France: Far-right party’s ‘de‑demonisation’ strategy rattled by antisemitism scandal Submitted by Tassa Adidi on Wed, 10/14/2026 - 08:44 Allegations of antisemitism targeting National Rally president Jordan Bardella have undermined the party’s attempt to move beyond its extremist past France's far-right Rassemblement National leader Jordan Bardella (R) attends a conference on antisemitism in Jerusalem on 27 March 2025 (Menahem Kahana/AFP) Off “Nature always returns,” says the proverb - a phrase that perfectly captures the current predicament of the president of France ’s far-right Rassemblement National (RN). Jordan Bardella is facing serious allegations published by the investigative outlet Mediapart, which attributes to him antisemitic messages exchanged on social networks in 2013, when he was 17 and already a party member. According to Mediapart, Bardella allegedly wrote on Messenger: “Banks are all owned by Jews,” “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and steal from them; a Zionist is necessarily Jewish, and deeply so,” and “The most important ministries go to people for whom Israel and banking interests take precedence over French interests.” Bardella, an MEP since 2019, has denied the accusations, denouncing “crude fabrications, obscure and manipulable screenshots reproducing vile statements I obviously never made.” He has filed complaints for defamation, forgery and use of forgery. RN officials have rallied around him, with Marine Le Pen leading the charge. The party’s candidate for next year’s presidential election said she trusts Bardella “a thousand percent”, accusing Mediapart of a “vile manoeuvre”. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Amid the turmoil, Bardella also received support from an unexpected figure: Amichai Chikli, Israel ’s minister in charge of combating antisemitism, who described him as “one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas”. “No one will convince me that Jordan Bardella hates the Jewish people or the Jewish state,” Chikli said . In 2025, during an International Conference on Combating Antisemitism, the Israeli minister hosted Bardella, who has consistently presented himself as a friend of Jews and Israel. The event, held in Jerusalem and attended by other European far‑right figures as well as numerous supporters of US President Donald Trump, was boycotted by several European and international Jewish organisations. From antisemitism to Israeli alignment In recent years, Israel has drawn closer to several European far‑right parties, united by a shared agenda on security and opposition to Islamist movements. For French Green MP Sabrina Sebaihi, Israel’s continued support for Bardella despite Mediapart’s revelations stems from the fact that he “supports its genocidal project” in Gaza . ‘The most important thing for the Israeli government is not the fight against antisemitism, but the eradication of the Palestinian people and the occupation of their land’ - Sabrina Sebaihi, Green MP “The most important thing for the Israeli government is not the fight against antisemitism, but the eradication of the Palestinian people and the occupation of their land,” she told Middle East Eye. She pointed to “an alliance of convenience” between Israel and the RN, recalling that the party was founded by members of the Waffen‑SS, the armed military units of the Nazi. Before changing its name in 2018, the RN was called the Front National (FN). The FN was founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen , Marine Le Pen’s father, along with members of various far-right movements, including Pierre Bousquet and Leon Gaultier, both former Waffen-SS, and supporters of French Algeria . Jean‑Marie Le Pen himself had been a lieutenant in a paratrooper regiment during the French colonisation of Algeria, where he allegedly tortured independence activists. A notorious antisemite, he once declared that gas chambers in Nazi concentration camps were “a detail of history”. Despite Le Pen’s record and six criminal convictions, Bardella defended him in 2023, even denying that he was antisemitic. He later paid tribute to the former FN leader after his death in 2025. A widely shared photograph also shows an 18‑year‑old Bardella waiting in line to meet Le Pen, whom he regarded as a key figure of the movement. At the time, Bardella also associated with members of the Group Union Defense (GUD), a violent far-right student group, and with one of its former members, Frederic Chatillon, a close associate of Marine Le Pen. Mediapart also attributes to Bardella a fascination with Alain Soral, a Holocaust‑denying polemicist repeatedly convicted by French courts. “His analyses are accurate because everything is confirmed by the facts,” Bardella allegedly wrote. Jean-Marie Le Pen, who brought French far right into the mainstream, dies at 96 Read More » Close to Jean-Marie Le Pen, Soral joined the party’s central committee in 2007. But Marine Le Pen pushed him out two years later as part of her so-called “de-demonisation” strategy. The goal of this policy, which became the goal of Marine Le Pen’s leadership, was to shed the party’s image as a radical far-right movement and break its association with antisemitism, seen as a major obstacle to electoral success. This involved removing candidates who displayed racist, antisemitic, homophobic or neo-Nazi messages, and even excluding the party’s founder - her own father - in 2015 over his antisemitic and Holocaust-denying remarks. Marine Le Pen chose to form a duo with Bardella, encouraging his rise to the RN presidency to present a youthful, suit-and-tie image far removed from the party’s historical far-right figures. Elected RN president in 2022 at age 27, Bardella became a pillar of the party’s de-demonisation strategy. Gone were the provocations and scandals: the RN sought to appear as a moderate, respectable party ready to govern, presenting itself as a bulwark against antisemitism while embracing an overtly pro‑Israel stance. Cosmetic change However, experts on the party argue that the strategy is primarily a media smoothing operation. Historian and political scientist Sylvain Boulouque explains that this “facade of normalisation” does not alter the party’s deep ideological foundations. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “Despite the change in rhetoric, the RN’s core programme - national preference, sovereignty, opposition to immigration, identity politics, hardline security - remains rooted in the historical identity of the far right,” he told MEE. ‘Antisemitism is a founding dimension of the far right and has never disappeared’ - Sylvain Boulouque, historian and political scientist “Antisemitism is a founding dimension of the far right and has never disappeared,” Boulouque added. “A portion of the RN electorate fully identifies with the statements attributed to Bardella,” he said. Outraged by the Mediapart revelations, Sebaihi took the matter to court. Backed by a dozen left‑wing MPs, she announced plans to refer the case to the Paris public prosecutor. In a letter seen by AFP, she cited facts “likely to receive criminal qualification due to their antisemitic nature”. “It is our duty as political leaders to never let antisemitic, Islamophobic, racist or xenophobic statements go unchallenged. The lack of systematic condemnation of such remarks contributes to the liberation of racist speech and deepens fractures in our country,” she said. Sebaihi argues that the messages attributed to Bardella show that the RN’s de-demonisation is a sham. “They changed the shop window, but the core of this party remains the same - fundamentally racist and antisemitic,” the MP told MEE. The president of the Representative Council of Jewish Institutions of France (CRIF), Yonathan Arfi, also notes that “antisemitism remains widespread among RN supporters and even among its officials”. “It seems illusory to believe that the RN could protect Jews,” he added. In a column published in Le Monde, Judith Cohen Solal, a psychoanalyst, and Jonathan Hayoun, a documentarist, recall that the far right’s deep DNA is structured around hatred of Jews. ‘Policing thought’: French bill to fight antisemitism accused of silencing Israel critics Read More » “The man who walked through Jerusalem in March 2025 claiming that ‘the fight against antisemitism must tolerate no ambiguity’, the man meant to embody the very face of de-demonisation, is today caught up by his own antisemitic writings,” they wrote. In 2019, they published a book showing how far‑right leaders like Marine Le Pen and Bardella seized on the rise of violent militant groups such as the Islamic State to court a previously hostile Jewish electorate, framing Muslims - or “Islamism” - as “the real antisemites”. The narrative helped the RN appear more respectable while deepening hostility toward Muslims. But this philosemitic posture, which the RN embraced more strongly after 7 October, has not fooled observers. Cohen Solal told MEE that the party sought to shed its antisemitic image solely to expand its electoral base. “There has been no work of repair or reflection on antisemitism within the RN,” she said, adding that Mediapart’s revelations “support the arguments of those who were already convinced” of the party’s antisemitic nature. Will these revelations harm the RN ahead of the 2027 presidential election? Cohen Solal does not think so: “We can see that Bardella denies the facts and his supporters back him, crying conspiracy.” For his part, Boulouque notes that studies show the RN’s electoral base is antisemitic. According to a recent poll , only 45 percent of RN voters consider the antisemitic statements attributed to Bardella “serious”, compared to 74 percent for the general population and approximately 95 percent on the left and centre of the political spectrum. Meanwhile, despite a slight drop in popularity this month (-4 points), Bardella remains, alongside Le Pen, one of the frontrunners in polls for the presidential race. Yemen hospitals overwhelmed by surge in war casualties, Red Cross warns Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to treat a sharp rise in people wounded in fighting along several front lines, the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Wednesday. Facilities in areas including Marib, Taiz and the Red Sea coast have reported unprecedented numbers of casualties, with some admitting more than 700 in a week. “Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” said Feras Abusamra, the ICRC’s health coordinator. The agency warned that shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicines are further straining a health system already weakened by years of conflict. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting renewed in recent weeks, according to the UN’s migration agency.

Azerbaijan's headscarf row: Were the girls excluded from school asked what they think? Submitted by Ayşe Duran Yilmaz on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 15:01 The debate over Muslim women's clothing should begin with the children standing at school gates - not with abstract arguments among adults Pedestrians walk past Azerbaijan’s Government House in Baku, on 10 November 2024 (Alexander Nemenov/AFP) Off The clothing worn by Muslim girls has once again become a political controversy. In Azerbaijan, an amendment last month to uniform rules at state schools introduced requirements linked to the secular character of education. The text does not explicitly name the headscarf, yet reports of Muslim girls being turned away from schools, followed by the introduction this month of rules governing teachers’ clothing, have intensified the debate. The difference between what a regulation says and how schools enforce it matters profoundly to the children affected. Asking a girl to remove her headscarf before entering a school is not simply a question of dress. It raises a more fundamental question: can access to education depend on making religious identity invisible? (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); This debate should begin not with abstract arguments among adults, but with the girls standing at school gates. Decisions made in the name of secularism, religion or public order shape their everyday lives, educational opportunities and sense of belonging. The controversy is larger than one country’s school policy. Why does Muslim women’s clothing so often become a test of modernity, freedom and social progress? Ideological contest A headscarf can signify devotion, cultural belonging or personal identity. Where covering is compulsory, it can also become an instrument of coercion. None of these meanings can be presumed for every woman or girl. There is a contradiction when authorities claim to liberate women from religious pressures by imposing another rule about their bodies. Requiring a headscarf, or requiring its removal, arise in different historical and legal contexts - yet both demand scrutiny of whose choices count, whose voices are heard, and who has the authority to decide. For girls, this is especially urgent. Too often, a girl becomes a symbol of her family’s religious values or the state’s secular identity, rather than a person with her own developing convictions. No child should be reduced to a symbol in an ideological contest among adults. Instead of asking who gets to decide what Muslim girls wear, we should ask why their own voices are so rarely heard Secularism can help to ensure that children of different faiths learn together, without the state imposing religious beliefs. But institutional neutrality is not necessarily the same as demanding that students conceal individual religious identities. The distinction matters when a school’s dress rules affect attendance. Governments may regulate uniforms for reasons of equality, order and belonging. Those aims, however, cannot end the discussion. If a dress code excludes some children from classrooms, it raises a question about the conditions attached to their right to education. In Azerbaijan, the crucial test is not only the wording of the rules, but their applications and consequences. Officials, parents, religious authorities and commentators are all allowed to speak. Yet how often are the girls whose lives are being debated asked what they think? Listening to girls A rights-based approach to the headscarf issue should take into account both of the above aspects: the ways in which familial and social pressures can shape a child’s decisions, and the reality that removing an item of clothing under institutional pressure is not automatically an act of liberation. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognises children’s right to express their views in matters affecting them, along with their freedoms of thought, conscience and religion, and their right to access education. These rights must be considered together. Listening to a girl is not the same as leaving her unprotected; protection should be attentive to her evolving capacities and circumstances. The world must stop trying to 'rescue' Muslim women Read More » States should not dismiss a girl’s beliefs in the name of education. Equally, a family’s religious preferences should not silence children. The task is to create conditions in which they can speak, receive support and continue learning. Excluding a girl from school because of her headscarf means more than losing a day of lessons. It can damage her relationships, confidence and sense of belonging, especially during adolescence, when identity matters deeply. Schools should be places where children encounter differences and learn to live with them. If the stated aim of education is to help girls think independently, consider different worldviews and make their own decisions, then exclusion is a troubling way to pursue it. Girls’ freedom cannot be defended at the cost of their right to learn. What should be left at the school gates are not headscarves, but rather these exclusionary policies. Instead of asking who gets to decide what Muslim girls wear, we should ask why their own voices are so rarely heard. SOCIETY: THE KITCHEN OF ISLAMKOT. As the sun sets over the Tharparkar desert, casting a warm golden hue across the landscape, the courtyard of a little-known ashram [hermitage] in Islamkot transforms into a lively haven. Flocks of birds arrive to roost, filling the air with their chirps and songs, as locals bring grain offerings. “This ashram is run on pure faith and love,” says Lachman Das, now in his eighties. He has spent the last two decades as the caretaker of the Sant Nenuram Ashram. The ashram feeds more than a thousand people a day, as well as tens of thousands of animals and birds, almost entirely through community support and without government funding. “When Sant Nenuram was alive, he would walk through the town’s streets, visiting different shops to collect donations and flour to serve the needy,” Das tells Eos. “To keep his sacred memory and mission alive, we continue this work today.” For Das, the hermitage embodies Tharparkar’s long tradition of coexistence and seva [service]. This tradition of seva — or sheva as it is pronounced in Thar — dates back generations and is deeply intertwined with the mystical, pluralistic culture of Sindh. The tradition continues to thrive in Islamkot, a historic desert town shaded by ancient neem trees. For decades, the Sant Nenuram Ashram in Thar has offered free meals to anyone who arrives at its doors, continuing a tradition of community service that extends from people to animals and birds A BAREFOOT PILGRIM RETURNS Born in 1898, Sant Nenuram developed a strong commitment to humanitarian work and a deep love for nature from an early age. Though he received little formal education, he was deeply influenced by the inclusive poetry of Sindh’s Sufi traditions, including the works of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast and Sami. He was also well versed in the writings of regional mystics such as Bhagat Kabir and Baba Bulleh Shah. According to accounts of his life, he once joined a group of pilgrims on a barefoot journey that took him to the village of Kekri in Rajasthan. There, he stayed at the ashram of a famous spiritual figure, Guru Kaniram, and absorbed the principles of devotion. In 1935, he returned to Islamkot and established his base at the site of another ashram, Puran Bharti Madhi. Initially, it served as a resting place for seasonal migrants travelling towards the irrigated barrage areas, where they could feed and water their livestock free of charge. Witnessing the extreme poverty around him — most locals could barely afford one meal a day — Sant Nenuram started a langar [free communal meal] that has operated continuously since then. “The Sant’s legacy transcends religious and social boundaries,” says Das. “Everyone is welcome and no one is ever asked about their faith or caste.” This ethos extends beyond humans to the desert’s wildlife. Inside the premises, clay pots placed across the courtyard are kept constantly filled with fresh water, and the areas designated for feeding birds are kept covered with grain. The ashram also maintains its own livestock, ensuring a steady supply of milk for visitors and pilgrims. Dileep Kumar, a devoted follower of the saint, spends his evenings here. “Here, the hunger of every creature matters,” he tells Eos. “Humans, animals and birds all find sustenance in this courtyard.” A KITCHEN WITHOUT A LEDGER Keeping such a large operation running in the middle of the desert is no simple task. The ashram relies on an unusual system of anonymous donations, managed entirely by the local community. Whether the contribution comes from a local resident or an outsider, no donor’s name or address is recorded in any ledger. Instead, every offering is acknowledged on its receipt with the phrase: “Nenuram ne diya, Nenu ne liya” [Given by Nenuram, received by Nenuram]. Volunteer Lachman Das prepares a plate of food for a visitor at the ashram | Photos by the writer Beyond serving as a place of sustenance, the ashram is also a repository of regional culture and history. It preserves personal items used by Sant Nenuram so that younger generations can learn about his austere life. The original well, dug when the ashram was established, is another important part of the site. According to local lore, the wells in Islamkot yielded bitter, brackish water before the ashram was built. When Sant Nenuram had this well dug to provide drinking water for people and animals, local accounts hold, its water became sweet. The site also holds spiritual significance for devotees from different religious communities across Sindh. Before setting off for various regional festivals and fairs, devotees of all backgrounds visit the ashram to light a sacred fire behind the samadhi [tomb] of Sant Nenuram. Only after performing the ritual and receiving the saint’s blessing do the pilgrims proceed on their journeys. A LIFELINE IN THE DESERT For low-income families in Thar, the ashram is not just a spiritual sanctuary; it is a vital economic lifeline. As rising prices make basic necessities increasingly difficult to afford, the free kitchen keeps hunger at bay. Santosh, a 35-year-old labourer, visits the ashram every afternoon for lunch. “This is a monumental service,” he tells Eos. “By eating here, we save money that would otherwise be spent on food. A large number of people from nearby neighbourhoods rely on this kitchen to survive.” Similarly, the ashram plays a quiet but pivotal role in supporting the dreams of the region’s youth. Meghraj, a student hailing from a family of farmhands, has to travel 15 kilometres daily from his remote village to study in Islamkot. Meghraj says the ashram’s free kitchen is what makes it possible for him to continue his education. “A single meal at a local hotel costs at least 300 rupees today,” he tells Eos. “If I had to pay for my food daily, my family wouldn’t have been able to afford my education.” Every year, the birth and death anniversaries of Sant Nenuram draw thousands of devotees from distant areas across Pakistan to participate in a mela [festival]. For as long as the kitchen continues to serve anyone who arrives at its doors, Sant Nenuram’s tradition of seva will live on — one meal and one offering at a time. The writer is a freelance journalist from Tharparkar, Sindh. He can be contacted at gr.junejo123@gmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, October 11th, 2026

PTI protest in KP's Bara turns violent as demonstrators clash with police. KHYBER: A protest demonstration by the PTI workers in Khyber’s Bara tehsil turned violent on Tuesday as protesters clashed with police and government buildings were set ablaze. There were reports of police firing live rounds and tear gas and protesters manhandling law enforcers. Dawn was able to confirm injuries to at least five protesters, based on accounts by eyewitnesses, who asked not to be named, while police said 50 people had been arrested. However, a doctor at Hayatabad Medical Complex, one of the city’s three major hospitals, told Dawn that more than a dozen injured, including four policemen, had been brought to the facility. The protest was held against the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkwa — a move that has rendered PTI’s Sohail Afridi non-functional as the province’s chief minister — and emergency in 12 of its districts, including Khyber. Scores of PTI workers assembled at the Khyber Chowk in Bara Bazaar in the afternoon for the protest, following which police reached the site. There were reports of police initially resorting to baton-charge and tear gas shelling to disperse protesters. Eyewitnesses told Dawn that police managed to disperse some protesters but later local MPA Abdul Ghani Afridi also reached the site with more PTI supporters. The protesters forced police to retreat, with some of the law enforcers taking shelter in nearby shops and commercial buildings, according to eyewitnesses. Reports received from the area said protesters manhandled police and dragged them out of shops, following which law enforcers fired tear gas shells and live rounds in the air. There were also reports of the nearby National Database and Registration Authority’s office and a portion of the Rescue 1122 building being torched. Police eventually dispersed the protesters from Khyber Chowk but all roads leading to Bara Bazaar were closed even as the demonstration ended. Meanwhile, leaders of the Bara Siyasi Ittehad urged both PTI workers and police to avoid violent confrontation. Arrests Capital City Police Peshawar said in a statement that 50 “miscreant elements” in Bara who “attempted to spread unrest” had been arrested. Separately, the newly appointed adviser on information and broadcasting in KP, Samar Haroon Bilour, said, “Forty-two PTI-affiliated miscreants associated with vandalism and unrest have been arrested, of whom 25 are illegal Afghans.” She accused the protesters of damaging public and government property. The adviser alleged that some individuals, reportedly led by PTI leaders, attempted to create unrest at Bara Chowk. She added that police made arrests over the incident and brought the situation under control. Dawn could not independently verify the number of arrests, the extent of the damage and the nationality and immigration status of those detained.

PM Shehbaz takes allies into confidence on KP governor's rule, says Centre made every effort to avoid 'extreme step'. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday took the allies of the ruling PML-N into confidence on the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, saying that the Centre had made every effort to avoid this “extreme step”. The Centre on Sunday imposed governor’s rule in KP and emergency in 12 of its districts, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. PM Shehbaz held a meeting with leaders of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), as well as a separate huddle with a parliamentary delegation comprising representatives of PML-Q, Balochistan Awami Party (BAP), Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP) and PML-Zia. During the meeting with the MQM-P delegation led by Education Minister Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui, the two sides exchanged views on the country’s overall and political situation, the PM Office (PMO) said. The prime minister said the government had to take this “most difficult decision” in the interest of the people of KP. “We made every effort to avoid taking this extreme step in any way. We engaged in negotiations with an open heart, but did not receive a positive response from the other side,” he was quoted as saying. The premier noted that rising terrorist attacks in KP were targeting ordinary citizens and security forces, while the provincial government “failed to openly raise its voice against terrorist groups”. PM Shehbaz also termed the PTI’s long march a “conspiracy to destroy the country’s improving economy”. According to PMO, the MQM-P delegation assured the prime minister of its full support for the government’s decisions regarding KP. On the MQM’s side, the delegation included Health Minister Mustafa Kamal, Senator Amir Waliuddin Chishti, Senator Khalida Ateeb, MNA Farooq Sattar, Syed Waseem Hussain, Aasia Ishaque Siddiqui, Javed Hanif Khan, Muhammad Moeen Aamir Pirzada, Muhammad Iqbal Khan, Hassan Sabir, Sadiq Iftikhar, Arshad Abdullah Vohra, Syed Hafizuddin, Syed Aminul Haque, Khawaja Azharul Hassan, Ahmad Saleem Siddiqui, Farhan Chishti, Nighat Shakeel Khan, Sabheen Ghoury, Rana Ansar, Sofia Saeed Shah, and Sanjay Perwani. In the second meeting with other parties, PM Shehbaz explained the reasons behind the federal government’s decision to take constitutional measures, state-run APP reported. He said the conduct of the PTI-led KP government in the province and its failure to adopt an unequivocal stance against terrorism had posed risks to Pakistan’s growing economy. The premier highlighted that the federal government had provided more than Rs800 billion to KP under the National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangements to support efforts against terrorism. However, he said, the provincial government had failed to take effective measures to strengthen the capacity of its Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and establish Safe City projects to improve its counterterrorism capabilities. According to the PM’s Office, the parliamentary delegation expressed its support for the federal government amid the prevailing situation and appreciated the prime minister’s leadership during what it described as difficult circumstances. The delegation also said the people of KP had remained deprived of adequate development in health, education and infrastructure during the PTI’s tenure in the province. It expressed confidence that, with the federal government’s cooperation, development and prosperity in KP would advance in line with other parts of the country. The delegation included BAP President and Science and Technology Minister Khalid Magsi; former Senate chairman Sadiq Sanjrani of BAP, senators Manzoor Kakar, Abdul Qadir Baloch, Dinesh Kumar and Samina Mumtaz Zehri; PML-Q President and Human Resource Development Minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain; and representatives of the IPP and PML-Zia. From the government, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry and PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah attended both meetings. ‘What other path did we have?’ Later, he addressed a parliamentary meeting of his PML-N and said, “When terrorism is spreading, sacrifices are being made day and night, and this party (PTI) is exhausting all its resources and time round the clock to create instability.” The premier emphasised that the people of KP had been wanting “projects of development and prosperity for the past 13 years”, such as schools, universities, hospitals, better law and order, and an end to corruption. However, he contended, there was “not zero, but negative attention” towards these matters, and “all attention and resources” were instead diverted towards long marches and protests. “Can any respectable society tolerate this? Even the question does not arise. So what other path did we have?” he asked, quipping if the Centre should have remained as “silent spectators”. The prime minister noted that the Centre was “compelled to make this decision” after the Oct 3 talks between the government and the opposition collapsed . Elaborating on the dialogue process, PM Shehbaz said, “There was a moment when it was set in stone that an agreement was about to be reached, all demands were settled.” He added that a consensus-based draft was ready, but the PTI team sought some more time to consult Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role now stands non-functional. “The rest is history. […] They were ordered that you have to create another May 9, even go beyond it and wreak havoc; you must not accept anything,” the premier added. He went on to recall his engagement with Jamiat Ulemai-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman to reduce tensions , which was followed by the Oct 11 cabinet meeting. “After all consultations and arguments, it was decided that this is the moment to save Pakistan. We must not wait any further, else everything will be set on fire and we will be left with regret.” PM Shehbaz reiterated, “We were compelled to make the decision of imposing emergency. This is no other choice because Pakistan is first.” He expressed his hope that the newly appointed KP Advisory Council , which will work under the governor, would work to improve the living conditions and safety in the province. The prime minister asserted that terrorism had been eradicated in most parts of the country several years ago, but had resurged recently. He lamented that law enforcers were being martyred daily in KP and Balochistan. “If this bloodshed is not brought to an end like it was in 2018, then the journey of development made in the past 2.5 years… this journey is continuing gradually.” “If one provincial government is not only determined to end that journey […] but that party is determined on destruction and comes to thinking that if they make progress, what will be our value; how regrettable it is.” The prime minister recalled the November 2024 protest by the PTI in Islamabad, as well as its 2014 rallies at the federal capital’s D-Chowk. “When someone is bent on ending the country’s progress, they are engaged in sit-ins, verbal abuse and allegations, instead of standing with the Centre and the armed forces and empowering the police and CTD,” he said. PM Shehbaz said even an enemy would not make the remarks made by Afridi in recent weeks. He criticised the PTI leader for not expressing sympathies with the martyrs’ families and for “not willing to say a single word” against terrorists. At the outset of his address, the premier highlighted his government’s efforts to cooperate with the PTI-led governments in KP. He recalled his meeting with former KP chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur , saying, “We told him in every way that we will cooperate with them … combatting terrorism is our shared responsibility.” He noted that he had also met with Sohail Afridi — whose role as the KP CM is currently non-functional due to governor’s rule — and asserted that the Centre tried its best to work with the KP government. At one point, the premier said International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva recently told him, “This is a new Pakistan”, as she praised the country’s economic reforms. He recalled his meetings last month with international financial institutions and stressed that praise from such independent firms for Pakistan “restored” his faith in the country’s progress.

try { if (window.ResizeObserver && iframe.contentDocument && iframe.contentDocument.body) { new ResizeObserver(updateHeight).observe(iframe.contentDocument.body); } } catch (e) {} } })(); The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Rs2.71 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs0.03 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs392.66 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.82 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 14 (Wednesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

PTI seeks production orders for nine ‘detained’ MNAs. ISLAMABAD/PESHAWAR: The PTI has urged National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq to issue production orders for its nine detained MNAs ahead of the National Assembly and Senate sessions scheduled for Tuesday. In a letter to NA Speaker, Chief Whip Amir Dogar claimed that the nine MNAs were “currently detained” and requested him to issue production orders for them to enable them to attend the 30th session starting on Tuesday. The lawmakers include Haji Imtiaz Ahmad Choudhry, Muhammad Jamal Ahsan Khan, Mian Ghous Muhammad, Sanaullah Khan Mastikhel, Dawar Khan Kundi, Junaid Akbar, Amjad Ali Khan, Fazal Muhammad Khan and Adil Khan Bazai. The PTI chief whip urged the speaker to take immediate notice of the matter and issue production orders to ensure the detained lawmakers’ attendance in the House. Afridi’s brother, speaker’s cousin move high court to trace their relatives CM, speaker’s family move PHC The brother of non-functional Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi approached the Peshawar High Court to trace his whereabouts, while Waqar Ahmad Khan, a cousin of KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, also filed a petition before the court seeking similar relief. The federal government had imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP on October 11. On the same day, the PTI claimed that Mr Afridi, along with some of his cabinet ministers and party leaders, had been abducted. The next day, officials, however, confirmed that Mr Afridi and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody. Muhammad Amir, Mr Afridi’s brother, filed a petition in the PHC, seeking multiple directives for the respondents, including the KP inspector general of police, Peshawar capital city police officer and others, to immediately take all lawful and effective measures to trace and recover his brother and, if he was found to be in custody, produce him before the high court so that the legality of his detention could be examined in accordance with Article 199(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution. The petition was filed through senior counsel Bashir Khan Wazir. He contended that the impugned detention and disappearance of the abductee were “wholly illegal, unlawful, without lawful authority and of no legal effect”, as the respondents had “failed to disclose any lawful order, warrant, abduction order or other legal authority under which the abductee was taken into custody”. Separately, in his petition, KP speaker’s cousin Waqar Ahmad Khan states: “That, on 11.10.2026, at approximately 7:00pm, the detenue was allegedly abducted by certain unknown, armed and masked individuals from the premises of the Provincial Assembly of KP, Peshawar, in the presence of CCPO Peshawar. The precise sequence of events, the identities of the persons involved, and the circumstances in which the detenue was taken away require immediate verification through the relevant official record, eyewitness accounts, and other available evidence.” Published in Dawn, October 14th, 2026

US may have ‘gone too far’ in targeting Iran leaders. OHIO: US President Donald Trump said that the United States “might have gone too far” in targeting Iran’s leadership. “We might have gone too far with the leaders because we don’t know who the hell we’re dealing with any more,” he said during a campaign rally in Ohio, according to Middle East Eye. “Nobody wants to be the president of Iran,” he added, claiming that potential candidates did not want to take up the position. Trump made this remark despite Masoud Pezeshkian being Iran’s president since July 2024. “We’re having a hard time figuring out who the hell to deal with, to be honest with you. I think we went too far,” the US president said. Trump says he doesn’t believe China, Russia are helping Iran Meanwhile, Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have “too much to lose.” Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops. Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: “If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!” Trump said in July that he did not believe China and Russia were selling weapons to Iran, warning that “it would be very bad for them” if they did. China and Russia both maintain strong ties with Iran but have refrained from getting directly involved in the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28. Since the outbreak of the war, Russia has sent humanitarian aid to Iran, but has otherwise not officially announced any concrete assistance. The Kremlin has denied US media reports claiming that Moscow passed sensitive intelligence to Iran, including the locations of US warships and aircraft in the region. China has sharply condemned US and Israeli strikes while also criticising Iranian attacks on Gulf states and the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz. China has previously supplied Iran with drones as well as equipment that can be used for both civilian and military purposes. Beijing has denied reports that the country’s top semiconductor firm, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, has sent chipmaking tools to Iran. China and Russia have also been accused of helping Iran circumvent international sanctions targeting its oil sales. Trump has frequently taken a more deferential tone toward Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin than he has toward some of Washington’s own allies, saying that they must be respected as the leaders of major world powers. Joint opposition flays move to ‘usurp KP govt mandate’. ISLAMABAD: A joint meeting of opposition parties on Tuesday demanded the immediate withdrawal of the emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and called for respecting the democratic mandate of the people of the province. According to a statement issued after a meeting of the opposition parliamentary parties at Parliament House, the participants strongly condemned the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in the province, the removal of its elected government, and the arrest of political leaders and workers. The meeting was chaired by NA Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai, and attended by Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, PTI secretary general Salman Akram Raja and other opposition leaders. The statement said that Oct 11 would be remembered as a black day in Pakistan’s democratic history. It called the removal of the elected government in KP, the arrest of PTI leaders, including Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, and action against political workers contrary to the mandate given by the people of the province, and democratic values. The participants demanded that the fundamental rights of the arrested leaders and workers be protected and that the supremacy of the Constitution and the law be upheld, the statement said. According to the statement, Maulana Fazlur Rehman briefed the meeting on his negotiations with the government, saying the step in KP was taken despite the talks having been completed. The participants appreciated his role in promoting the democratic process, easing political tension and seeking to resolve issues through dialogue. The statement said questions were also raised at the meeting over what participants described as double standards in the government’s handling of Balochistan and KP. If the provinces faced law and order or constitutional problems, uniform principles should be applied to resolve them, it said, adding that dissolving an elected government or taking undemocratic action on the basis of political differences was not a solution. The rights of the people and the mandate of elected representatives in all provinces, including KP and Balochistan, must be respected equally, the statement said. Instead of unilateral decisions, the statement added, a comprehensive national strategy against terrorism should be formulated in consultation with all relevant stakeholders, and the province should be given the resources it needs. Online abuse puts 1.5m Pakistani children at risk: study. WASHINGTON: About 1.5 million internet-using children in Pakistan experienced sexual exploitation or abuse facilitated by digital technology in a single year, according to new research, as a senior United Nations official warns that artificial intelligence and overlapping global crises are creating new dangers for children. Presenting her final report to the UN General Assembly on Monday, Najat Maalla M’jid, the secretary general’s Special Representative on Violence Against Children, urged governments to strengthen protections for children facing multiple and overlapping crises. “Almost 45 million children are displaced because of conflict, but also because of natural disasters, because of the climate crisis,” she told journalists at UN Headquarters in New York. Rapid advances in technology are creating new risks alongside opportunities for children to learn and communicate. Artificial intelligence has opened what Ms M’jid described as “huge avenues for child sexual exploitation”, as well as “cyberbullying, deepfakes and the recruitment of children into criminal activities.” Her presentation marked 20 years since the first UN global study on violence against children. Despite progress, she warned, the world continued to face complex and overlapping crises in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic. Troubling picture Nearly one in 16 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 in Pakistan — approximately 1.5 million children — experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse in a single year, according to Disrupting Harm in Pakistan, a study published by Unicef, ECPAT International and INTERPOL in September 2026. The UN General Assembly on Monday identified AI-generated sexual material as an emerging risk. The abuses include unwanted sexual images or conversations, demands for intimate photographs, the non-consensual sharing of children’s images, and sexual threats or blackmail. The findings challenge the perception that online abuse is mainly perpetrated by strangers. In 85 per cent of the incidents cited by ch­­­­­­i­­­l­­dren, the perpetrator was someone they alre­ady knew. Social media accounted for 44pc of reported instances of abuse, making it the most commonly reported digital setting. Fear, stigma and possible repercussions at home often prevent children from seeking help. Victims may fear being blamed, humiliated or subjected to restrictions by their families. Boys, too, risk being overlooked because of social expectations about masculinity and the reluctance to discuss sexual abuse. Unicef says more than half of children who experienced technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse did not tell anyone. None of the children surveyed reported their experiences through formal channels such as helplines, social workers or the police. These findings highlight the need for safe, confidential and accessible reporting systems, as well as support that allows children to seek help without fear of blame or punishment. Poverty and displacement Online abuse is part of a wider child-protection challenge shaped by poverty, displacement and disrupted access to essential services. Ms M’jid warned that poverty, food insecurity and rising prices were deepening children’s vulnerability worldwide. Economic hardship can expose children to exploitation, while conflict and natural disasters can disrupt education and weaken family support systems. Climate-related emergencies add to these pressures across South Asia. Unicef estimates that weather-related disasters displaced 15.6m children in the region between 2016 and 2022. In Bangladesh, climate-related events disrupted schooling for 35m children in 2024. These figures concern different as­­p­­­ects of children’s vulnerability; th­­­­ey do not establish a direct link bet­w­­een displacement and online sexual abuse. They nevertheless underline the importance of maintaining child-protection services during emergencies and ensuring that vulnerable families can access support. For Pakistan, the challenge is to address both the risks created by digital technologies and the social and economic circumstances that can leave children without adequate protection. The Pakistani study identifies we­­a­­­k­­­­n­­esses in the systems intended to pr­­­e­­­­­­v­­ent online abuse, investigate cas­es and support victims. Children ne­­­­­­­­ed safe and accessible ways to rep­ort abuse, while investigations must be conducted by appropriately train­­ed personnel. Victims must also be able to obtain support without being exposed to further humiliation or trauma. The study identifies gaps in Pakistan’s legal framework. Legisl­ation does not require child forensic interviews to be systematically conducted by specially trained professionals, increasing the risk of secondary victimisation during investigations. Court acquits Sharjeel Memon in liquor case. KARACHI: After eight years, a judicial magistrate on Tuesday acquitted Senior Sindh Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon and five others in a case pertaining to the recovery of liquor from his Dr Ziauddin Hospital room. The then chief justice of Pakistan, Mian Saqib Nisar, had raided the room and allegedly found the liquor. Later, a case was registered at the Boat Basin police station under Section 4 (owning or possessing intoxicant) of the Prevention (enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance 1979 read with Section 201 (causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender) and 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. On Tuesday, after hearing and examining the records, Judicial Magist­rate (South) Aasim Aslam acquitted Mr Memon and five others for lack of evidence against them. In its order, the court observed that the prosecution alleged that the suspected liquor bottles were recovered from the possession of the accused persons. However, the chemical examination report of the recovered bottles does not support the prosecution allegations. Rather, it mentioned that the bottles contain honey and olive oil. “Thus, both the reports being material pieces of evidence have failed to corroborate the prosecution version. It is settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the prosecution is bound to establish the case beyond the reasonable doubt and the burden of proving the guilt of accused cannot be shifted upon him,” the court observed. It added that mere allegations of the police officials in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence were insufficient to sustain a conviction particularly when the scientific evidence available on record contradicts the prosecution story. The judge also noted that the prosecution case in these circumstances has failed to establish the essential ingredients of the alleged offences beyond a reasonable doubt. According to the prosecution, on Sept 1, 2018, the then assistant superintendent of Karachi Central Prison received information that illegal activities were taking place in a private hospital room where Mr Memon was staying due to illness. The room had been declared a sub-jail as Mr Memon was in judicial custody in connection with a NAB reference. The prosecution added that jail police went to the room and recovered two bottles, one allegedly containing alcohol and the other apparently containing honey. Later, a case was registered against Mr Memon and his employees at the Boat Basin police station. During the trial, defence counsel Uroosha Memon argued before the court that Mr Memon was falsely implicated in the case for political victimisation. She further argued that as per chemical reports the alleged bottles contained honey and olive oil, adding that despite it being a crowded place, the police did not associate any private witness. Section 144 imposed in DI Khan, pillion riding and public gatherings banned. DERA ISMAIL KHAN: The district administration imposed Section 144 across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Dera Ismail Khan district, banning pillion riding and public gatherings, rallies and processions until Nov 11, citing law and order concerns. The restrictions were imposed through an order issued by Deputy Commissioner Hikmatullah on Oct 13 and took immediate effect. Under the order, public gatherings, meetings, processions and rallies that could potentially disturb public order, disrupt traffic or obstruct the movement of citizens have been prohibited. The administration has also imposed restrictions on the display of weapons and the installation of tents and temporary structures on public roads, according to the notification. The order said the measures had been taken in view of the prevailing law and order situation in the district. Those found violating the restrictions would face legal action under Section 188 of the Pakistan Penal Code, the administration warned. The restrictions will remain in force across the district until Nov 11, unless withdrawn or modified by the competent authority before that date. Section 144 is a provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which empowers local authorities to ban public gatherings such as rallies, processions and sit-ins, as well as the open display of weapons. Currently, Section 144 remains in effect in several areas of the country. On Sunday, it was imposed in Karachi , set to remain in effect till Oct 20. On Saturday, Section 144 was imposed in Rawalpindi district for a period of 30 days. Punjab Home Department also imposed Section 144 across the province until Oct 15 in view of serious threats to public peace, tranquility and the safety of life and property.

What we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer operation. Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour surgically removed from his right lung on Tuesday in a 90-minute operation described as “ successful ” by the Vatican. Here are what several medical experts told AFP about the surgery and diagnosis. What is pulmonary adenocarcinoma? Pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the type of tumour removed from the Pope, generally comes from “a primary cancer,” said Dr. Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association. She told AFP that “is a good thing” because it means the tumour is from lung cancer instead of generating from the spread of another cancer. There are two main types of lung cancer: “small cell” cancers, which spread aggressively and make up about 10 to 15 per cent of diagnoses, and “non-small cell” cancers, which make up the vast majority. “Adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of what’s called non-small cell lung cancer,” David Spigel, a medical oncologist specialising in lung cancer research at Nashville’s Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told AFP . Promising outlook David Carbone, director of the Oncology Center at Ohio State University, noted that while smoking is the most well-known risk factor for a lung cancer diagnosis, “most lung cancers that we diagnose today are in people who haven’t smoked, or (stopped) many years ago.” Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO), but the prognosis can vary significantly depending on the type of lung cancer and how advanced it is when first detected. “When we look at five-year survival rate from lung adenocarcinoma, and it’s nicely localised, the rate is approximately 63 to 67pc,” Mora said. “But if we catch it early, it becomes 80 to 98pc, especially after surgical removal.” In such a case, the patient “will achieve a cure and never have their life threatened by cancer,” Spigel added. A standard procedure Pope Leo XIV announced the presence of the lung nodule on Sunday, saying it had been “detected at a very early stage” and was localised. The Vatican said “the lower lobe of the right lung was removed” during Tuesday’s operation to remove the mass. “He had part of his right lung taken out, which is the standard procedure,” Carbone told AFP . “There’s a lot of reserve in the lung, and people can have an entire lung removed and live a normal life,” he added. “I would expect that he’d be back to completely full level of activity very soon.” What now? The question now is whether Pope Leo XIV will need additional treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation. According to the experts consulted by AFP , the answer will depend on several factors, such as the size of the cancerous mass removed, how aggressive it was, its genetic characteristics, and whether or not it has spread. A Vatican source indicated that additional testing is underway. For Carbone, the fact that the Pope has already undergone surgery is encouraging. “Because if it had spread to, for example, the lymph nodes in the centre of the chest, he would have had some treatment before surgery, which he didn’t have,” he explained. “They really do go straight to surgery only for the earliest stage tumours, which makes me think this was a very early stage tumour, and has a quite good prognosis.” He stressed that treatment for lung cancer has improved considerably over the past few decades, “and the prognosis is better than ever. So I would be hopeful for a full recovery”.

India shuts down iconic Delhi protest site after three decades. For more than three decades, a stretch of road in central New Delhi was where Indians came to be heard, staging rallies to press their demands and hold those in power accountable. Trade unions, retired soldiers, anti-corruption campaigners, women’s rights groups and student activists all protested beside the capital’s iconic 18th-century Jantar Mantar observatory, drawn by its location near the city’s commercial heart and the seat of political power. But this week, the country’s most recognisable stage for public dissent officially lost its status as an authorised protest venue, prompting concerns among activists over shrinking democratic space. “Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified,” Delhi Police said in an order issued Monday. Police detain All India party supporters during a protest demanding the resignation of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Ahmedabad on October 13, 2026. —AFP The move comes days after a confrontation between authorities and anti-government protesters led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement. The youth-led group has mobilised thousands to take to the streets over a revision to electoral rolls that critics say could disenfranchise eligible voters, months after separate protests over exam irregularities forced the education minister to resign. While authorities have designated three alternative demonstration venues in Delhi, campaigners say visibility and proximity to lawmakers are central to the right to protest in the world’s largest democracy. “Jantar Mantar is in the centre of the town, it is connected, it is next to parliament… it was a very important space for all protests,” human rights activist Shabnam Hashmi told AFP. “This is nothing but a move to curb dissent.” ‘Spirit of resistance’ Jantar Mantar, meaning an instrument to calculate in Sanskrit, is designed for the observation of astronomical positions with the naked eye. The roughly 1.6-kilometre (one-mile) street next to Jantar Mantar became synonymous with protest after being designated a demonstration site in 1993. In July, thousands of students led by the “cockroach” movement gathered there before attempting to march towards parliament over irregularities in competitive examinations. Security personnel try to prevent detained protesters from escaping from a bus during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 13, 2026.—AFP For nearly a month, Jantar Mantar transformed into a vibrant hub of Gen-Z dissent , its walls transformed into canvases for angry slogans, defiant messages and graffiti challenging the government. Tensions resurfaced this month when police denied permission for a CJP protest at the site demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner over the contentious voter roll revision. On Wednesday, two of CJP’s top leaders, who clambered over the barricades to “reclaim Jantar Mantar” a day before, were sent to jail for five days for alleged trespassing. “Jantar Mantar is not just a location but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away,” the group’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, said. Delhi Police on Tuesday defended their move, citing a directive from the Supreme Court that “suitable alternative sites” for protest “need to be identified and designated”. The developments have reignited debate over where citizens can now take their grievances. Activist Hashmi said protests at Jantar Mantar had already become increasingly restricted in recent years through limits on space and timings. But its location, she said, made it uniquely effective because demonstrators could easily reach parliament, government ministries and media houses. “In a democracy, you require spaces where you can protest,” she said. “This is absolutely unacceptable.” Neighbours complain Authorities have said demonstrations can be held at two venues on the capital’s outskirts, while a third site closer to the centre, Ramlila Maidan, remains available for larger gatherings. But activists argue that moving protests away from the city centre risks reducing turnout and visibility, particularly for campaigners travelling from distant states. Greater transport costs, longer journeys and reduced media attention could all diminish the impact of demonstrations, they say. Some of those living in the Jantar Mantar neighbourhood, however, welcomed the police order. Security personnel try to prevent detained protesters from escaping from a bus during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 13, 2026.—AFP “Roads leading to our homes are barricaded, there is noise and garbage, and our daily lives are disrupted,” Varun Seth, a resident, told the Hindustan Times newspaper. Former Delhi Police commissioner Kiran Bedi also defended the move, saying Jantar Mantar’s “sensitive” location made it poorly suited to hosting protests. “Every city does require an open space for democratic expression… but forgets to provide for (it),” she said on social media. A protester told AFP on Tuesday that demonstrators would continue to gather at Jantar Mantar despite the police order. “With great resolve, we will carry out civil disobedience,” she said. “We will sit here and protest,” she added, before being whisked away by police as she attempted to march towards the site.

HOCKEY: HOPE AND REALITY. Pakistan’s hockey team won the bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games. Is this satisfactory or unsatisfactory? The answer to this is not straightforward. A medal is always welcome. Pakistan failed to win a medal at the previous two Asian Games. Yet, for a country with an enviable Asian Games record of eight gold medals — compared to India’s five — a bronze hardly represents a return to the top. There is another, more important, way of looking at it. The Asian Games winner earns direct qualification for the 2028 Olympics. Pakistan has missed that opportunity and will now have to negotiate the Olympic qualifying process in early 2028. Sixteen teams will compete in two eight-team tournaments for four or five Olympic berths. That is a daunting prospect for a country that has failed to qualify for the last three Olympics. So, purely in terms of results, there appears to have been little progress. But results alone do not tell the whole story. Pakistan’s hockey team managed to snag a bronze at the recently concluded Asian Games. What does it tell us about the trajectory of Pakistan Hockey? ASIAN GAMES ASSESSED Pakistan began the Asian Games ranked third in Asia and 14th in the world, behind India, which is ranked eighth in the world and Malaysia, ranked 12th. In its pool games, Pakistan had a comfortable passage against the lower-ranked sides, beating Thailand 9-0, Uzbekistan 5-1, China 3-0 and Oman 7-2. Malaysia was the only genuinely testing opponent. It was a pulsating contest, with the lead changing hands repeatedly. Pakistan led 4-3 with only four minutes remaining and, on the run of play, deserved to win. All four Pakistani goals came from penalty corners. Pakistan earned eight penalty corners; Malaysia had only three but converted all of them. Malaysia created only four or five clear chances from open play and scored twice. Pakistan, meanwhile, dominated the third and fourth quarters — apart from the final four minutes — but squandered several opportunities, including some sitters. The contest eventually ended with Malaysia edging Pakistan 5-4. That defeat forced Pakistan into a semi-final against India, the overwhelming favourites and the Pool B winners. Pakistan have not beaten their traditional rivals for more than a decade, and recent encounters have frequently produced one-sided scorelines. Once India surged into a 3-0 lead, it seemed that history was about to repeat itself. But then Pakistan came alive. Captain Abu Bakar Mahmood reduced the deficit with a penalty-corner conversion at the stroke of half-time. The match was transformed in the 45th minute, when an electric move down the right flank ended with Abdul Hannan Shahid finding the net. Soon it was 3-3. Rana Waheed completed another superb attacking move from the right to take Pakistan level. What followed was a thrilling, end-to-end contest, with chances at both ends. Then came the cruelest of endings. India’s winner arrived in the final minute, in bizarre circumstances. Abhishek’s attempted pass was deflected into the Pakistan goal by a Pakistani stick, turning what had seemed an amazing Pakistani recovery into another defeat. The bronze-medal playoff provided another comeback. South Korea led 3-1, but Pakistan recovered to win 5-3. There is a pattern here. Pakistan’s ability to fight back after falling behind has become one of the more encouraging features of the present team. As in the World Cup, the players repeatedly showed that they could recover from two or even three-goal deficits. Even when they could not turn those comebacks into victories or draws, they often transformed apparently lost contests into competitive matches. But the frequency with which Pakistan has to recover from poor starts is also a serious weakness. Why does this team so often concede early goals? Is it tactical? Is it psychological? Is it a problem with game management? The questions require serious technical analysis. But there are other positives. Sufyan Khan is developing into a world-class drag-flicker. His 12 goals made him the joint leading scorer at the Asian Games. Yet Pakistan’s use of its penalty corners against India raises questions. The team earned seven penalty corners but converted only one. Against Oman, three of Pakistan’s penalty-corner goals had come through a two-touch variation. Curiously, that indirect option was not employed against India. There is no shortage of individual talent. Hannan Shahid and Rana Waheed have established themselves as genuinely world-class forwards. Goalkeeper Ali Raza also produced an impressive performance. Captain Abu Bakar is a dependable defender who has the added value of scoring from penalty corners, and his recent signing for Melbourne Cobras in Hockey One — Australia’s premier domestic competition — is another indication of his growing stature. Meanwhile, Abdul Rahman’s goal against Wales at the 2026 FIH World Cup won him the Poligrass Magic Skill Award, selected by fans for the moments that best captured the magic of hockey. So, even during one of the darkest periods in Pakistan hockey’s history, individual talent remains available. Pakistan’s great teams have traditionally possessed a potent weapon: attacks from the right wing. The opponent’s left side is generally regarded as the more vulnerable defensive flank, making the right-wing route particularly effective. Pakistan’s second-half fightback against India provided a vivid demonstration. Both goals that brought Pakistan level originated from superb attacking movements down the right. The lesson is obvious: strengths must be identified, developed and repeatedly exploited. At the other end of the pitch, however, Pakistan continues to commit too many unforced errors. Mistimed tackles and poor clearances in deep defence gave away penalty corners and, on occasions, resulted in soft goals. The team management must address these deficiencies. The broader picture is also worth considering. The Olympics, the World Cup, the Asian Games, the Asia Cup and the Commonwealth Games are the sport’s principal title tournaments. In these competitions, positions matter. Pakistan did not achieve the desired finish in either of the two title events of 2026 — the World Cup and the Asian Games. Given Pakistan hockey’s decline over more than a decade, this was hardly unexpected. But what matters now is whether the current upward trend can be converted into sustained progress. There is no title tournament before the 2028 Olympics. That should simplify Pakistan Hockey’s priorities. From now until the Olympic qualifiers, virtually every major effort should be directed towards building a team capable of qualifying for Los Angeles. The performance graph does appear to be moving upwards. Pakistan went toe-to-toe with India despite the considerable difference in world rankings and a decade of adverse results. That should provide the players with a substantial psychological boost. But there is still a sizeable gap before Pakistan can seriously challenge the world’s top six. One indication of that gap was the difference in tempo between the 2026 World Cup and the Asian Games. The World Cup’s final and semi-finals were played at a frantic pace. The intensity and tempo at the Asian Games were nowhere near that level. Pakistan must bridge that gap. The next step should be extensive and meaningful international exposure. The PHF should seek matches against teams such as New Zealand, France and Ireland, ranked around ninth to 11th in the world. Matches against opponents of that calibre would provide a much more accurate measurement of Pakistan’s progress than victories over lower-ranked Asian sides. The objective should not merely be to play more international hockey. It should be to play the right opponents, under demanding conditions, and to learn how to compete for 60 minutes at the highest tempo. The bronze medal in the Asian Games is, therefore, neither a failure nor a triumph. Pakistan have demonstrated resilience, individual quality and flashes of the attacking hockey that once made them feared across the world. But they still concede too early, make too many defensive errors and struggle to maintain the intensity required against the very best teams. The Olympic qualifiers will tell us whether Pakistan has actually moved forward. For now, the most urgent question remains unanswered: why does a team with the ability to come back from the brink so often put itself there in the first place?
