Security forces kill 5 terrorists in Balochistan's Washuk: state media. Security forces killed five terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Balochistan’s Washuk, state-run Pakistan TV reported on Wednesday, citing security sources. Terrorist hideouts were targeted with advanced weapons, sources said. State media added that four terrorists were also injured, identifying them as belonging to Fitna al Hindustan . The state refers to designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. The IBO was conducted under Operation Raddul Fitna 3, state media said, adding that “advanced weapons and ammunition” were recovered. “Security forces remain determined to eliminate terrorism from Balochistan,” state media said. President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to security forces for the Washuk operation in a statement on X. “Effective operations against terrorist elements attempting to disrupt peace and security and spread fear and panic among the public in Balochistan will continue,” President Zardari was quoted as saying. He added, “Conspiracies by the terrorists’ foreign patrons and their local facilitators will be thwarted at any cost”. Terrorism in Balochistan Balochistan has witnessed terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. Ten terrorists were killed in a targeted IBO conducted by the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) in Balochistan’s Barkhan district , the Home Department said on Oct 10. In Chagai, security forces killed two terrorists on Sept 29. The military’s media affairs wing said on Sept 27 that more than 71 terrorists had been killed in Shaban and other areas of Balochistan. On Sept 17, three terrorists were eliminated in an IBO in Balochistan’s Awaran district’s Badrang area. Another three were killed i n Mastung on Sept 14. Earlier in September, 21 terrorists were killed in separate engagements in Nokcha, Chagai, Ziarat Cross, and Pishin. The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to PICSS’ monthly assessment . As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism.

Pope Leo has cancerous tumour removed in lung operation. Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and “woke up normally” after the procedure, the Vatican said. A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread. “To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed,” the Vatican said in a statement. The operation “confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests”, it said. The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time. “The surgery was successful and there were no complications,” the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure. Lamps and flowers outside Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is hospitalised to undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule, in Rome, Italy on October 13, 2026. —Reuters Juanita Mora, medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, told AFP that when this type of cancer is “caught in early stages, then it has a very, very good prognosis”. She said much would depend on the stage of the cancer found and whether it had spread. In cases of surgical removal and when the cancer is caught early and localised, five-year survival rates from lung adenocarcinoma were “80 to 98 percent”, she said. “They’ll determine if he needs chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy for the adenocarcinoma,” she said. ‘Thoughts and prayers’ US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a practicing Catholic, said after the surgery that he and his wife were “united in prayer for (Leo’s) health following his recent diagnosis”. “May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his “thoughts and prayers” were with the pontiff, calling him “a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world”. Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery. He is staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation. The Vatican has said it expects the recovery to take a week. His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month. The surgery marks Leo’s first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025. In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter’s Square that doctors had discovered a nodule “at a very early stage” during medical checks. “The doctors believe it would be right to intervene,” he said. The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments. Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope’s condition. Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried. “However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors,” she said. “I will pray a lot for him.” Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned. “He’s still quite young and I really wasn’t expecting this. I thought he was in better health,” he said, noting that “thankfully it was caught in time”. PM Shehbaz extends prayers for Pope’s recovery Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif prayed for a speedy recovery of Pope Leo XIV following his surgery. “On behalf of the people and government of Pakistan, I wish him strength, comfort and a speedy recovery,” the prime minister said in a post on X. He said Pakistan’s Catholic community, as well as the entire nation, joined him in praying for the pope’s good health. “His steadfast message of compassion, peace and human dignity resonates deeply with people across Pakistan and the world,” the prime minister said, adding that he prayed for the pope to continue his service to humanity with renewed strength and conviction. Latin America trip in doubt The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican. Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city’s parishes to join in. The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been “very calm” about his condition when they met on Monday. The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope’s lungs. Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health. He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

India festival boat capsize kills 13 children. Rescuers dragged out 13 dead children from India’s Ganges river after an overloaded boat capsized en route to a Hindu festival, officials said Wednesday, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressing grief over the “deeply painful” tragedy. The boat overturned late Tuesday in Vaishali district in eastern Bihar state, with locals rushing to pull people out of the water in the dark using mobile phones to find the bodies. “It was dark when we suddenly heard children screaming and crying for help as the boat capsized,” Ravi Yadav, a young villager who joined the rescue effort, told AFP. “We managed to rescue only three children, using the light from mobile phones and torches, because it was dark.” Villager Ramlakhan Rai said the boat was “small” and “not in good condition”, saying people were crammed onto a vessel suitable for just a handful. “It is devastating — a few families have lost all their children,” he said. Six people were pulled out alive, including two children reported to be in critical condition. Medic Nirmal Kumar, from the local health centre, said four children and two adults were sent to the district hospital. “We tried our best to revive them… but 13 were already dead,” Kumar said. Vaishali district magistrate Varsha Singh told AFP 13 bodies had been recovered. “The loss of lives in the boat capsizing incident in Vaishali, Bihar is deeply painful,” Modi said in a statement on Wednesday, announcing compensation for their families. “My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this difficult time.” Boat accidents are common on Indian waterways, often blamed on overcrowding, poor enforcement of safety norms and inadequate life-saving equipment.

Makkah Alliance secretary general meets PM Shehbaz, briefs premier on defence cooperation. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday met the newly appointed secretary general of the Makkah Defence Alliance, retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, and was briefed on the strategy to promote “defence and strategic cooperation” under the pact, state-run Radio Pakistan reported. Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary general of the defence alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye last month. The agreement — signed on August 7 — empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all. During the meeting held on Wednesday, the premier reiterated that the pact was a “historic milestone for peace, unity, and stability in the region” and wished the secretary general well for his new role. PM Shehbaz also reaffirmed Pakistan’s “unwavering commitment” to the protection of Saudi Arabia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” during the meeting as the Gulf state, which is a signatory to the pact, has faced escalating tensions with Yemen’s Houthi rebels in recent days. The premier said Pakistan “stands shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia, according to Radio Pakistan. The meeting comes amid heightened tensions in the Middle East. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a “harsh and painful” response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations. Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom’s eastern province and Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. Later, a Saudi energy ministry official confirmed the attack. Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On October 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, maintained that Pakistan and Turkiye had “presence in theatre” and only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

Deeper poverty. PAKISTAN’S poverty crisis is far deeper than official indicators suggest. While the government celebrates economic stabilisation, almost four in every 10 Pakistanis suffer from deprivation in health, education, and living standards. The latest UNDP figures put multidimensional poverty at 38.3pc of the population against 19.3pc for South Asia. We are worse off than nearby countries — poverty affects 16.4pc of India’s and 14.9pc of Bangladesh’s population. These estimates are based on surveys from different years, however, and should not be treated as a strictly contemporaneous ranking. Still, the comparison is an indictment of our development priorities. That Pakistan’s multidimensional poverty rate is almost twice the regional average is not simply a reflection of low incomes. The index captures deficiencies in nutrition, child health, schooling, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and other necessities. A family may earn enough to remain above an income-based poverty line and still lack access to these essentials. The intensity of deprivation for the multidimensionally poor is 51.7pc. Another 12.9pc of the population is vulnerable to such poverty. This means millions more risk falling into acute deprivation when faced with illness, joblessness, rising food prices, or climate-related disasters. Our poor performance exposes the limits of an economic strategy focused primarily on containing inflation, accumulating foreign exchange reserves and meeting fiscal targets. Though necessary, they cannot substitute for growth and development. An economy cannot sustain higher productivity when children miss school, malnutrition damages their development, and poor healthcare pushes households into financial distress. Economic stability should be judged by whether it improves people’s lives, not merely by whether the balance-of-payments holds or the budget deficit narrows. Pakistan’s widening development gap with India and Bangladesh is a warning that stability without investment in people will leave poverty entrenched. Published in Dawn, October 14th, 2026

Pakistan, Russia agree to finalise extradition treaty, to sign MoU on prevention of organised crime. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Russia on Wednesday agreed to finalise an extradition treaty and pledged to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on cooperation in preventing organised crime and exchanging information. Minister of Internal Affairs Vladimir Kolokoltsev arrived in Pakistan on Monday. He is undertaking a four-day visit at the invitation of Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, marking the first instance of a Russian interior minister visiting Pakistan. The understanding was reached during a meeting between Naqvi and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Kolokolstev in Islamabad. The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks, the interior ministry said in a statement. Naqvi, during the meeting, said the proposed MoU on prevention of organised crime would be an important milestone in cooperation between the two countries. The two sides pledged to enhance mutual cooperation in areas of shared interests as they agreed to finalise an extradition treaty and an agreement on the exchange of criminals. Both sides resolved to promote cooperation in areas of mutual interest and decided to ensure early implementation of a readmission agreement, according to the statement. They also agreed to enhance cooperation between the Anti-Narcotics Force and relevant Russian institutions. It was agreed in the meeting that working groups from the interior ministries of both countries would soon visit each other. The two sides also discussed sending skilled manpower from Pakistan to Russia and facilitating visa acquisition for tourists and the business community, as per the statement. They agreed to enhance cooperation for the prevention of cybercrime between the National Police Academy and the Russian Police Academy, the statement said. Naqvi said easing the visa regime would increase people-to-people contact between the two countries. He also expressed desire to benefit from Russia’s experiences in curbing cybercrime. He further noted that at present, 1,300 Pakistani students were studying in Russia and Pakistan wanted more students to study there. Russian Interior Minister Kolokolstev, for his part, said joint measures were essential for the prevention of all organised crime, including terrorism, drug smuggling, and illegal migration. He said Russia had brought a 33 per cent reduction in cybercrime through effective measures. The meeting was attended by Minister of State Tallal Chaudhry, the Russian ambassador in Pakistan, special and additional secretaries to interior and other senior officials. In recent years, Pakistan and Russia have significantly strengthened their economic ties, driven by mutual necessity. In January, Russian President Vladimir Putin had said Moscow’s relations with Pakistan were “ genuinely mutually beneficial ” and that it maintained close ties with Islamabad. Last July, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk called Pakistan and Russia “ natural allies ”, stressing that Putin viewed Islamabad as an important strategic partner in the areas of economy and energy. Following Western sanctions related to the Ukraine conflict , Moscow turned toward new energy outlets, while Islamabad simultaneously sought more affordable fuel sources to reduce national import expenses. This diplomatic shift culminated in 2023, when Pakistan officially integrated Russian crude oil into its energy portfolio.

Automating death: Israel’s AI-powered genocide in Gaza. On February 29, 2024, Israeli forces fired at civilians as they gathered around an aid convoy. At least 115 people were killed in what has since become known as the ‘Flour Massacre’. Survivors recalled the involvement of armed tanks and quadcopters. “When the aid entered, the tank and quadcopter started firing at the people gathered, the people who went to get food for themselves and their children. They started shooting at them,” Mahmoud Ahmad, a Gaza resident, told Reuters shortly after the incident. Screenshot from video released by Israeli forces/Anadolu Agency Powered by artificial intelligence (AI), Israel’s strategy of keeping soldiers “out of harm’s way” while they kill Palestinians relies on quadcopter drones and various AI systems to identify and target people. Quadcopters such as the ‘Bird of Prey’ — designed by Elbit Systems, the apartheid state’s largest arms manufacturer — have contributed to the deaths of Palestinians in Gaza, where more than 70,000 people have reportedly been killed since the beginning of the genocide. According to the manufacturer, the ‘Bird of Prey’ quadcopter drone is designed to enable “fast and accurate” targeting and is light enough to fit into a soldier’s backpack. The drone can transmit high-quality footage in real time, facilitating precision targeting. According to the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor , at least 60 civilians have been killed by fire or munitions dropped from these drones since the October 2025 ceasefire till early September 2026. Palestinians inspect the site of a house targeted by Israeli airstrikes after the Israeli military warned residents to evacuate late on Saturday, in Al-Zawayda, central Gaza Strip on October 11, 2026. —Reuters Lavender According to Palestinian-Israeli news outlet +972 Magazine , the Lavender system was designed to identify suspected members of the military wings of Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) as potential targets for air strikes. The publication reported that human oversight of the system was minimal, with one intelligence officer describing his role as little more than a “stamp of approval” for attacks. According to the report, Lavender’s accuracy was estimated at 90 per cent, meaning that around 10 per cent of those it identified as targets were incorrectly classified. The report also said that, during the early weeks of the war, Israeli military officials permitted strikes against suspected junior-level fighters even when they risked killing up to 15 to 20 civilians. The report alleged that these policies facilitated attacks that caused extensive civilian casualties in Gaza. “They could target someone who is a photography personnel or a truck driver and take another 15 people down with him,” a testimonial on Breaking the Silence — a digital archive of Israeli atrocities against Palestinians — revealed. Twenty seconds. That’s the time given to consider whether a target should be bombed and if that target is male. The Israeli army’s use of AI systems such as Lavender further enabled blanket targeting of Palestinians. Another entry spoke of how a single target could result in hundreds of ‘casualties’. “That they knowingly authorised a strike. I don’t know what number they authorised exactly, but they knew it would be more than a hundred [civilian deaths].” The entries dated 2023 are an astonishing admission of targeted strikes on civilians. Where’s Daddy? ‘Where’s Daddy?’ is an automated system used to track people and identify them for targeting when they enter their homes. According to reports, the system was designed to target individuals at their residences. It has been linked to the deaths of thousands of civilians, including women and children. “It’s much easier to bomb a family’s home,” an Israeli officer told +972 Magazine . Habsora A third system, Habsora, also known as ‘The Gospel’, was designed to identify buildings and infrastructure allegedly linked to Hamas for targeting. Israel has accused the Palestinian group of using essential infrastructure, including hospitals, schools, UNRWA buildings and mosques, for military purposes. These allegations have been disputed, and the resulting attacks have caused extensive destruction across the besieged enclave, where approximately 82 per cent of buildings have reportedly been damaged or destroyed. Who is responsible for these AI controlled attacks? The Israeli military’s main intelligence unit, Unit 8200, has been at the centre of cyberwarfare. Other systems include facial recognition systems such as Red Wolf and Blue Wolf. A 2020 testimony published by Breaking the Silence describes Israeli soldiers photographing Palestinians’ identity cards and compiling a database for the Blue Wolf system. Blue Wolf then displays different colours depending on whether it recognises an individual. A yellow light gives Israeli forces the option to detain that person, while a red light signals that they should be arrested. In its 2023 report, Israel and Occupied Palestinian Territories: Automated Apartheid: How Facial Recognition Fragments, Segregates and Controls Palestinians in the OPT , Amnesty International found that Israeli soldiers used a gamified system to map Palestinian identities. Soldiers were reportedly rewarded for photographing Palestinians without their consent. In 2024, Muhammad Ahmad Odeh recounted to Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor how a quadcopter killed his sister in Gaza and described what happened afterwards. “After just two or three hours, a small aircraft flew in and took pictures of us inside the house. The army forces then moved in and started shooting at us. They fired sound shots, causing a state of panic among the women and children.” Terror beyond Palestine Ambulances arrive at American University of Beirut Medical Center (AUBMC) as more than 1,000 people, including Hezbollah fighters and medics, were wounded when the pagers they use to communicate exploded across Lebanon, according to a security source, in Beirut, Lebanon on September 17, 2024. —Reuters/File Israel’s AI warfare systems have been used beyond Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia 'totally unacceptable', says Dar. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday said that Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia were “totally unacceptable”. He made the remarks while addressing a joint press conference alongside Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, who is currently on an official visit to Pakistan, following the eighth session of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC). At the outset of the press conference, Dar said that the two sides would sign a protocol relating to the commission. He said that this reflected “a shared resolve to further strengthen and expand bilateral cooperation in areas of mutual interest”. He said that the two sides would also sign an agreement for mutual visa exemption for holders of diplomatic and official passports. “Pakistan-Oman friendship remains strong and forward-looking,” he told media. The two ministers would after the press conference sign “a number of bilateral agreements”, Dar said. He added that the two ministers had also agreed to hold a business-to-business investment forum in Pakistan. The ministers discussed the situation in Gulf as well, he said, adding that “Pakistan remained committed to contributing constructively to diplomatic efforts aimed at promoting peace and stability in the region”. Dar said that the two sides also exchanged views on recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. He said that he conveyed Pakistan’s condemnation of the attacks. “I underscored that attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure are totally unacceptable. My brother [Albusaidi] actually fully endorses this. Violations of international law pose a serious threat to regional peace and security,” he said. “I reaffirmed Pakistan’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and our unwavering commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security in accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” he said. They also “emphasised the urgent need for unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance to the people of Gaza”, Dar said. DPM Dar also stressed that India’s unilateral abeyance of the Indus Water Treaty was “a material breach of international law”. “This action threatens the water, food and energy security of Pakistan’s 250 million people,” Dar said. Speaking at the occasion, Albusaidi said the JMC had “provided an important opportunity to review the state of bilateral relations”. He said that two sides “reaffirmed the strength of the longstanding ties” between the two countries. “Both Oman and Pakistan attach great importance to dialogue and diplomacy as essential means of addressing regional challenges, easing tensions and promoting peace and stability,” Albusaidi said. He also appreciated Pakistan’s diplomatic role in the US-Iran war . He reaffirmed the two countries’ “shared commitment to further deepening our bilateral partnership and broadening cooperation across centres of mutual benefit”. The two countries agreed that dialogue and diplomacy were “the only way forward” to resolve regional conflicts, Dar said in response to a reporter’s question. “We are both on the same page,” he said. Meanwhile, Dar told reporters that a free trade agreement between Pakistan and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) would help expand business activities, adding that he was told that barring one, all countries had consented to the agreement. Responding to a question about the gaps in between bilateral talks between the two countries, Dar said Albusaidi’s visit was previously delayed because Pakistan had been involved in mediation efforts between US and Iran. Albusaidi added that discussions had continued “behind the scenes”. Responding to a question about the Strait of Hormuz, Albusaidi said that Oman was committed to “unhindered navigation” through the strait “because of its vitality to the global economy and the region”. Dar commends Albusaidi’s efforts towards regional peace Albusaidi arrived in Pakistan on Tuesday on a two-day visit. Speaking at the outset of the 8th session of the JMC, Dar said the two had “worked out” certain areas of bilateral interest and discussed global issues in detail, including the US-Iran war, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab and Gaza in their restricted meeting. Dar said the two sides had also discussed Jammu and Kashmir and other pressing regional issues. He commended Albusaidi’s leadership and efforts towards regional peace in the Middle East. “I personally greatly admire your efforts. I know how much hard work you have put in,” he said, noting that Pakistan’s position on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) was “very unique”. “We are members of both the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and, obviously, the United Nations and other multilateral bodies,” Dar said. He stressed, “There should not be any long gaps between bilateral engagements,” noting potential in the areas of trade, economic activities and investment opportunities. Dar said he had promised to visit Oman in 2027 to hold the next session of the commission there. He added that both sides had identified areas of mutual interest and discussed possible meetings. He said Pakistan and Oman cooperated closely and cordially, adding that although their diplomatic relations had completed 55 years, their ties went back “centuries”. Dar said the two countries shared a history of “love and affection”, particularly in relation to Balochistan and Gwadar. Referring to discussions on Bab al-Mandeb and recent developments involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, Dar said both sides shared similar views on resolving regional issues. He said the impact of regional tensions was also visible in Pakistan, where energy supply chains had been affected, and fuel prices had skyrocketed, adding that the “common man could not afford the resulting burden.” Speaking on the occasion, Albusaidi said Oman was committed to further strengthening bilateral engagement and cooperation in various fields that could bring greater benefits to the people of both countries. “I am delighted to be here with my delegation in Islamabad this morning, in this very warm, friendly and brotherly country, Pakistan, with which, as you have rightly said, we share bonds of history, culture, tradition and unity,” he said. He said the Pakistan-Oman JMC was one of the mechanisms for exploring further avenues of collaboration, adding that the two countries also had a business council and a political consultation mechanism between their foreign ministers. “We can do much more, and as we made a joint commitment this morning to make this meeting a success, I believe the more we do, the more we can deliver on the promise and the aspiration of our leaderships and our people,” Albusaidi said. He also commended Pakistan’s role in supporting dialogue and diplomacy in the region. “Your efforts to encourage engagement, understanding, respect and recognition are commendable, and I salute you for all your efforts,” he said, adding that Oman greatly appreciated Pakistan’s role in providing space for dialogue between Iran and the US. Albusaidi said there was significant potential for economic cooperation between Oman and Pakistan, particularly in trade, logistics, port connectivity, energy and food security. “The potential exists, and our task is to remove any obstacles and create the conditions that allow businesses to thrive so that we can fully benefit from this potential,” he said. He also called for greater cooperation in tourism, academic and technological fields, as well as more regular exchanges between the people of the two countries. “Once again, I appreciate the efforts of our private sector and industrial partners,” Albusaidi said, adding that he looked forward to further discussions on strengthening bilateral cooperation. Dar, Omani FM call for sustained bilateral engagement Earlier in the day, Dar held a meeting with Albusaidi ahead of the JMC session, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The two ministers reaffirmed the close, fraternal ties between Pakistan and Oman and underscored the importance of sustained high-level engagement to deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest, particularly trade, investment and people-to-people contacts, according to the FO. “The two sides also exchanged views on regional developments and emphasised the importance of dialogue and diplomacy in advancing lasting peace and stability”, the FO said. Albusaidi commended Pakistan’s efforts to promote regional peace and security, while Dar acknowledged and appreciated Oman’s constructive role and shared aspirations for regional peace and stability, the statement added. A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) said the JMC session would review the entire spectrum of Pakistan-Oman bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation. The visit “reflects the longstanding fraternal relations between Pakistan and Oman and is expected to further deepen mutually beneficial cooperation Last week, DPM Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting in Islamabad to review preparations for the upcoming JMC session, according to state-run Radio Pakistan. The meeting reviewed the agenda, bilateral agreements, and arrangements for the co-chairing of the JMC session, it said.

KP Police administrative staff not entitled to risk allowance, rules FCC. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) ruled on Wednesday that the administrative staff of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Police were not entitled to risk allowance. The judgment was issued by a two member bench headed by Justice Aamer Farooq and including Justice Syed Arshad Hussain Shah. In its ruling, the bench set aside an April 10, 2025 order of the Peshawar High Court’s Mingora Bench (Dar-ul-Qaza), Swat, which had granted the administrative/ ministerial staff of police the benefit. The judgment, authored by Justice Farooq, stated that there was a clear distinction between “uniformed police personnel” performing active operational duties involving risks and hazards and administrative/ministerial staff working in the same department under the KP Police Act, 2017, as well as the KP Police Department Ministerial Service Rules, 1974. The question before the FCC was whether the respondents qualified as police officials entitled to the allowance under the relevant laws or whether a distinction existed between uniformed police personnel and administrative/ministerial staff. The respondents, who were employees of the KP Police establishment, claimed entitlement to risk allowance on the grounds that it was being paid to other employees and staff of the department and that denying them the benefit amounted to discriminatory treatment in violation of Article 25 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality. After the police department denied the grant of the allowance, the respondents challenged the decision before the PHC, which allowed their petition. In its judgment, the FCC observed that administrative/ministerial staff had their own set of rules governing their terms and conditions of service. Under the relevant rules, the FCC stated, such employees had their own method of recruitment, eligibility and composition of service. “Nowhere was it provided that a person appointed as ministerial staff under the rules will be expected to perform active police service”, the judgment said. It added that it was a settled constitutional principle that the guarantee of equality did not mean that all persons must invariably be treated alike, irrespective of the nature of their duties, responsibilities, classifications or conditions of service. The court observed that while Article 25 of the Constitution prohibited discrimination, it did not prevent reasonable classification based on “intelligible differentia having a rational nexus to the object”. “In the case at hand, there exists a clear distinction between uniformed police personnel performing active and operational duties and employees forming part of ministerial establishment,” the court noted, adding that the former may be required to perform duties involving physical danger, law and order operations, arrests, raids, security assignments, crime control and other functions associated with active policing, whereas the latter performed administrative, clerical and ministerial functions. The fact that both the categories were administratively associated with the police department did not obliterate material distinction in the nature of their duties, the judgment said, further stating that the “allowance, which was sanctioned on account of nature, character and hazards of a particular duty, cannot automatically be claimed by every employee serving in the same department”. “The high court appears to have proceeded primarily on the fact that both categories of employees are serving in the police department,” the FCC noted. “Such an approach did not adequately address the material distinction in their relevant service functions,” the judgment said. The FCC observed that the respondents had essentially sought parity on the basis of departmental affiliation. “Such a claim cannot succeed unless basis requirement of similarity of duties and service conditions is established,” the FCC emphasised. “The constitutional prohibition against discrimination does not require the state to treat the dissimilar classes although they are identical.” The judgment concluded that the high court “fell into error” in allowing the writ petition merely on the basis of alleged discrimination without examining whether the respondents were similarly placed with the employees who were being paid the risk allowance and whether the classification made by the government had a rational basis. Dismissing the plea, the FCC observed that the denial of the allowance to the respondents did not constitute hostile discrimination or offend constitutional guarantees of equality.

FCC rejects Bushra Bibi's petition seeking suspension of 7-year Al-Qadir Trust sentence. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Wednesday rejected a plea moved by the spouse of incarcerated former premier Imran Khan, Bushra Bibi, seeking suspension of her seven-year sentence in the £190 Al-Qadir Trust case . “We find no sufficient ground warranting interference with the April 30 Islamabad High Court (IHC) order at this stage,” Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, who headed a two-judge FCC bench, observed. The court also expressed the expectation that the high court would endeavour to decide the main appeal, affording both sides adequate opportunity of hearing while discouraging unnecessary adjournments. Earlier in the day, a two-judge FCC bench comprising Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan and Justice Ali Baqar Najafi had reserved its ruling. The court had taken up Bushra Imran’s criminal appeal, in which she contended that, being a woman and in view of her serious medical condition, she was entitled to suspension of her sentence, as similar relief was contemplated under the first proviso to Section 497(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). Bushra had moved the FCC in July seeking the suspension of her sentence, with her criminal appeal contending that the appellant, being a woman with a serious medical condition, was entitled to the suspension of her sentence. On Sept 17, Safdar moved an application before the FCC, seeking early hearing of the appeal, citing a rapidly deteriorating ocular condition that threatens the appellant’s remaining eyesight. In a three-page order, the FCC noted that the application for suspension of sentence had remained pending before the IHC on account of successive adjournments sought by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB). The FCC said that, without entering into the merits of the application under Section 426 of the CrPC, the IHC had declined suspension of sentence, principally on the ground that the main appeal had already been fixed for hearing and the appellant’s counsel was not extending the requisite assistance towards its adjudication. The record further reflected that the appeal, initially fixed for April 30, was subsequently adjourned to May 7 and thereafter to Oct 5. The principal grievance urged by counsel representing the appellant pertained to the repeated adjournments allegedly sought by NAB, resulting in the prolongation of proceedings on the application for suspension of sentence, the FCC observed. “Be that as it may, the main appeal having already been fixed for hearing, the appropriate course would be to secure its expeditious adjudication rather than undertake a parallel examination of the merits of suspension of sentence at this stage,” the FCC observed. The appellant’s assertion that the appeal involved a voluminous record necessitating elaborate arguments did not, by itself, furnish sufficient justification for interference with the impugned order, the order said. It was, therefore, incumbent upon the appellant’s counsel to extend full assistance to the IHC in hearing the main appeal, whereafter NAB would be equally obligated to advance its arguments without unnecessary adjournments, the judgment said. The FCC also noted that the present criminal appeal was barred by 61 days, for which the appellant had sought condonation of delay. The explanation furnished, particularly the appellant’s incarceration at Central Jail, Adiala, Rawalpindi, constituted sufficient cause warranting condonation, the FCC observed while condoning the delay of 61 days in filing the appeal. Appeal Moved under Section 32-A of the National Accountability Ordinance read with Article 175F(1)(a) of the Constitution, the criminal appeal pleaded before the FCC that, despite earlier directions issued by the IHC to the authorities of Central Jail Adiala to facilitate a meeting between the appellant and her counsel, the jail authorities were not complying with the directions. Her counsel was instead permitted to meet the appellant’s husband, Imran Khan, who disclosed that both he and the appellant were being illegally kept in solitary confinement. They were allegedly denied access to family, friends, counsel and political party members, as well as to each other, and were not provided with books or television, thereby subjecting them to complete isolation from human contact and depriving them of information about the outside world. The same was subsequently confirmed by the appellant’s daughters upon meeting her after her eye surgery on April 17, the appeal stated. Such treatment amounted to an unauthorised enhancement of sentence, violated the prisoners’ fundamental rights to life and dignity guaranteed under Article 9 of the Constitution, and warranted immediate intervention by the FCC, the petition argued. The appeal stated that the appellant had been subjected to continuous solitary confinement, which had demonstrably taken a grave toll on her physical and mental health. This was evident from the fact that she had to be taken outside the jail premises for eye surgery. In view of her deteriorating medical condition, she ought not to be subjected to solitary confinement even if such punishment had been awarded by a court. However, in blatant disregard of the applicable law and prison rules, she continued to be subjected to such unlawful confinement, the petition pleaded. The appeal contended that NAB had selectively prosecuted the appellant and her husband while deliberately excluding six other individuals who were allegedly implicated in the matter. The core allegations revolved around the Malik Riaz family and other persons who had conspicuously not been subjected to prosecution. This selective and incomplete approach had resulted in a defective and biased investigation, culminating in the unjust framing of charges and subsequent conviction of the appellant, the appeal contended. Thus, the prosecution had failed to present cogent, reliable and legally admissible evidence to substantiate the allegations in their entirety. Earlier this month, senior members of the PTI’s legal team approached the FCC for early fixation of the criminal appeal. However, no fresh application was filed, and only a verbal request was made for early registration and fixation of the case. The former first lady was handed the sentence in the case in January last year, and remains imprisoned at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. The court found Imran and Bushra guilty of giving undue favours to property tycoon Riaz in retrieving his laundered money from the United Kingdom. Bushra, along with the ex-PM, had initially moved the Islamabad High Court (IHC) for the suspension of her sentence in July last year. But the high court dismissed their requests in May 2026, observing that their appeals against their convictions had already been fixed for hearing. Subsequently, the two approached the Supreme Court against the IHC decision, but the SC office returned the petition as being not maintainable, explaining that since the IHC had passed the impugned order while exercising jurisdiction under Section 32 of the National Accountability Ordinance (NAO), 1999, the remedy lay exclusively before the FCC under Section 32-A of the ordinance. Bushra then moved the FCC on July 30, with her criminal appeal contending that the appellant, being a woman with a serious medical condition, was entitled to the suspension of her sentence, as similar relief was contemplated under the first proviso to Section 497(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). Her latest application for the appeal’s early hearing, which was rejected on Monday, also stated that her rapidly deteriorating ocular condition threatened her remaining eyesight.

National Assembly passes resolution endorsing Centre's imposition of emergency in KP. ISLAMABAD: The National Assembly on Wednesday passed a resolution endorsing the federal government’s imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Centre had imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Sunday, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The NA question hour session was suspended due to discussions on the emergency. Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled a motion regarding the proclamation of emergency, which was adopted with a majority vote after a discussion opened by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar. “The National Assembly approves the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on the 11th October, 2026 in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution,” read a post by NA’s official X account. According to Article 232 , if the “president acts on his own, the proclamation of emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days. The proclamation of emergency is now pending approval by the Senate. Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months. Throughout Wednesday’s proceedings, opposition members participated calmly and did not stage any loud protest, unlike past instances of ruckus when PTI objects to the Centre. Federal ministers defended the emergency imposition while assailing what they described as the PTI-led KP government’s lack of will to combat terrorism. In tune with that, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari blamed the PTI for the circumstances that compelled the Centre to impose emergency in KP and termed it a “political suicide attack” for the party. However, he also urged the treasury and the opposition to get back on the path of dialogue and make joint efforts against terrorism. At one point during the proceedings, the NA speaker noted that the Oct 3 dialogue was held in a cordial atmosphere. Sadiq praised both sides for “attempting more than their capacity so that the matter is settled”. However, he said some matters were beyond the parties’ control and voiced his support for forming the same committees for negotiations if ever needed in the future. Addressing PTI lawmakers, the speaker said, “Everyone’s response was that this [process of dialogue] should continue, but you also understand that your hands were tied.” He took note of the PTI’s complaints regarding the jail conditions of party founder Imran Khan, adding that he had even provided details of facilities provided to the jailed ex-premier. The session was adjourned to meet again at 11am on Oct 16 (Friday). ‘Political suicide attack’ Bilawal began his speech by highlighting that emergency and governor’s rule in KP were measures taken under the Constitution . Reading the relevant provisions, he asserted that the Centre tried its best to “engage the opposition so this step did not have to be taken”. “They will have to accept, even if not publicly, but the responsible leadership of the opposition knows that the PTI itself carried out a political suicide attack on its KP government,” he remarked. The PPP chief maintained that the PTI could not deny that its “leadership, particularly in the province had a key role in the political, constitutional and legal circumstances” at present. Bilawal emphasised that the PPP’s stance was that “before employing this constitutional atomic bomb, we must engage with PTI and the opposition and try to address the federal government’s reservations that they were not supporting them in the war against terrorism”. He observed: “If political space is restricted for one political party, it is impossible that it remains restricted for that particular party; it is limited for every political party, political worker and Pakistani citizen. “We are responsible for this, but you cannot deny that you are also responsible for it,” he said. Terming the imposition of emergency a “difficult decision”, Bilawal recalled alleged remarks by Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional — that he would not combat terrorism the way the Centre wanted. “If this was not a political suicide, then what else was it?” The Bhutto scion wondered if the opposition and Afridi had left any reason for President Asif Ali Zardari, who he said prides himself on passing the 18th Amendment, to “refuse to sign” the emergency proclamation. He argued that due to the PTI’s actions and statements, neither the president, the Centre, nor he had any legal or political reason left for not imposing emergency in KP. “But even today, I would recommend to the federal government that we extend our hand forward once again for negotiations, political discussions and try to find a resolution and a middle path,” Bilawal added. The PPP chairman noted that emergency was “always a stopgap measure”. “We cannot sustain the emergency forever,” he added, emphasising that while the counterterrorism fight would be better than before, an “all-of-society and all-of-country response” was needed to eradicate it completely. Regarding the Oct 3 talks of a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition, Bilawal said, “Late at night, I was informed that congratulations, negotiations are succeeding.” He said the PTI was willing to declare the areas in KP with surging terrorism as “terrorist areas”, and the opposition was about to agree that the federal and KP governments would sign a pact on joint efforts against terrorism. However, the dialogue collapsed. The former foreign minister pointed out that the security challenges Pakistan was facing were “way more complicated” than before, adding that India “could still not digest […] its embarrassment” from the May 2025 conflict . Referring to remarks by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that its ‘ Operation Sindoor ’ was still ongoing, Bilawal said: “It means that India is still sponsoring terrorist incidents in Pakistan, sometimes in the form of TTP (Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan) and sometimes in the form of separatist terrorist groups.” He reiterated Pakistan’s stance that India was involved in terrorist activities being conducted from across the Afghan border. The ex-foreign minister then highlighted Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran war. “But there is a state — which we do not recognise as a state — that will neither be happy nor ever forget that you took this step. And those Zionist forces will and are interfering in Pakistan’s internal politics and state.” Concluding his speech, the PPP chairman emphasised the need for building consensus on “some fundamental issues” for an empowered lower house. “Even today, we are saying, come and at least begin from this house,” he said while addressing the opposition benches. Gohar demands implementation of NAP Speaking on the NA floor, PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan’s said his party “rejected” the Centre’s move to impose emergency in KP. He asked what “terrorism” Imran’s wife or sisters had allegedly been involved in that they had been put behind bars, or what the accusations were against the PTI MNAs and MPAs who he said were detained. Gohar further said, “One person is not present in the house currently. When he comes during a joint session, then I will reveal the reality of the negotiations.” He affirmed that the PTI had raised its voice against terrorism, adding that measures against the scourge must be taken according to the National Action Plan (NAP). Gohar argued that the PML-N opposition during the PTI’s tenure carried out “14 long marches in two years, but you did not let us stage even one long march”. Presenting his version of the Oct 3 talks with the government, the PTI leader said his party was being asked to immediately call off the long march . “I said where did [the topic] of terrorism arise from suddenly.” Noting that the government had put forward “five reservations”, Gohar said PTI was willing to make the KP Police Act similar to that of Punjab and Sindh. The PTI leader reiterated his party’s request for the production of certain MNAs it says were taken into custody. Gohar also welcomed Bilawal’s proposal to continue dialogue. Responding to Gohar’s remarks, the PPP chairman said the PTI was busy in its long march while the people of KP were being targeted by terrorists. Bilawal reiterated that the opposition could keep arguing against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, but no one could deny that the decision was grounded in the Constitution. “I cannot insist on the government to continue talks with PTI despite being defrauded multiple times,” the PPP chairman said. Pointing towards Gohar and NA Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai, Bilawal said: “I believe that none of them is allied with terrorists. I believe that they will definitely want to combat terrorism; however, they cannot deny the fact that their former chief minister contradicted this fact.” Bilawal again requested all the stakeholders to unite and combat terrorism collectively. He also called for the provision of all facilities to the incarcerated PTI founder. ‘Threat to national security’ Addressing the house, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar explained that emergency was imposed in KP as the security situation there was becoming a threat to “national security”. Tarar noted that after the proclamation of emergency was issued, the Constitution’s Article 232 required that both houses of the parliament approve the measure. He recalled that the federal cabinet examined “material” regarding terrorism in the province during its Oct 11 meeting and then advised Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to recommend the imposition of emergency. He noted that some people compared the measure to the emergency imposed by former dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf on Oct 12, 1999. The minister particularly noted “internal disturbances” and cross-border infiltrations. He contended that the situation since Oct 15, 2025, when Sohail Afridi’s government came into power in KP , was “turning into a threat to national security to an alarming extent”. He went on to highlight that there was a rise in terrorism in KP, especially after 2021, due to the approach of the provincial government. “Perhaps there might be foreign, diplomatic and political reasons behind it, which got inflamed due to a political party’s point of view.” Tarar stated that 2,911 incidents of terrorism took place between 2021 and 2024 in KP, but they surged to 3,787 incidents between Oct 15, 2025 and Oct 9, 2026. He criticised the KP chief minister for ignoring martyred security and police personnel, and for instead preferring to promote his political designs and make visits across the country. “Even this was announced that the federal capital will be conquered,” he said, referring to the party’s plan to hold a protest long march towards the federal capital. The PML-N leader expressed his government’s gratitude to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq for providing a platform for dialogue between the Centre and the opposition. He reiterated the government’s stance that the PTI had the agreement draft changed multiple times, but even then backed off from it. Tarar observed that the PTI demanded the release of their party founder Imran Khan and his treatment in a private hospital despite knowing that only courts could provide such a relief. He said two days would be “remembered in the country’s democratic history with regard to misfortune and a political party”. On the emergency measure, the law minister noted that a special mechanism has been introduced for 12 districts of KP. Speaking after Tarar, Achakzai criticised him for trying to prove that terrorism was not tackled in KP. The opposition leader questioned the government’s mandate in the February 2024 general elections, quipping that the opposition would “surrender” if the minister could swear that the government won those polls fairly. Achakzai alleged that the incumbent ruling coalition was formed “illegally”. ‘You do not have clean hands’ Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif went on to recall the tenure of the PTI government in the Centre and assailed the party’s past actions. Referring to ex-prime minister Imran Khan’s plan to resettle members of the TTP, he said PTI tried to convince the then-opposition that “bringing these terrorists back would be better for Pakistan”. The PML-N leader mentioned the 2019 episode of an Indian pilot’s capture in Pakistan: “They had threatened and we were surrendering. The then-prime minister was saying, ‘What should I do? Attack India?’” Asif urged the opposition to reflect on its past actions, adding that Imran often used to praise former army chief retired General Qamar Javed Bajwa. “As long as this contradiction remains in our words and actions and in our society, the circumstances of this country will not fix.” He narrated his time behind bars during the PTI government, when Shehbaz “smuggled a blanket” to him to brace the low temperatures. “I used to eat the jail’s food,” he said, claiming that orders were given to remove the geyser when it was installed. “But we did not hold rallies or mourn at D-Chowk or dig graves. We did not martyr police and law enforcement personnel,” Asif remarked. “You demand equity when you have clean hands. You do not have clean hands, you cannot demand equity; this is a thousand-year-old principle,” he contended. “You know very well what Gen Musharraf did to me. There was a 4x6 cell in Attock jail,” the PML-N politician said, emphasising that he stood with his party and ex-PM Nawaz Sharif. Speaking on the current political situation, Asif alleged that Afridi used to “take directives […] from a person sitting in Afghanistan”. He referred to a statement by the TTP condemning the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops in certain places. “Who is their ally and who is their rival?” he said. The minister further countered the PTI’s stance that its leaders have not been able to meet Imran, who is imprisoned in the Adiala jail. “Meetings are held, [but] a lot of them are not publicised or brought on record,” he maintained. Farooq Sattar urges PTI to ‘openly condemn terrorism’ In his remarks on the floor of the lower house, Farooq Sattar expressed Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan’s (MQM-P) confidence in the decision taken by the prime minister. “This was an extremely difficult decision, but so unavoidable that you had no other option,” Sattar said about imposing emergency and governor’s rule. “We trust your decision as we trust your experience, capabilities, political acumen, and that you made this decision in the interest of the nation,” he added. The MQM-P lawmaker contended that the PTI was “on the wrong side and does not have concrete arguments” to declare that the decision was baseless or made with political motives. “The main issue is of the mindset,” he declared, adding that Imran had “publicly said that the war on terror is not ours”. “This is their policy. This is their mindset.” Sattar questioned whether the KP government had ever published reports to expose terrorist hideouts and extremist trends. He further raised questions about the government’s pursuit of cases against suspected terrorists. “Openly condemn terrorism; else, the allegation of backing [it], if a commission is formed and God forbid, it is proven in the inquiry that there is political extremism and terrorism complicity, there is a nexus, then where will you go?” Sattar recounted his past MQM experiences, saying, “I have also suffered such times. A lot of times, the narrative coming from the top was difficult to defend. Today, I feel that Barrister Gohar is also not in the position to defend his [party’s] position on KP.”
