In his reasoning, the 27 December joint statement provision that troops must remain where they are supersedes MOU 43, which says neither side may “carry out any work resulting in changes of environment of the frontier zone”. 156 Ibid.; MOU 2000, Article V. 2. MOU 44 In December 2025, the same senate committee had also recommended withdrawing from MOU 44. Anutin, who had promised to annul it during his campaign, included the decision in his government’s policy statement following the February election, which the National Security Council endorsed on 23 April. 157 “Anutin pledges to scrap maritime MOU in final election rally push”, op. cit.; Mongkol Bangprapa, “Security Council scraps MoU 44, citing stalled talks, rising tensions with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 23 April 2026. Two weeks later, the government formally withdrew from MOU 44. 158 “For Thailand, MoU 44 no longer exists, Thai PM says”, Thai PBS World, 5 May 2026. Anutin has since been at pains to explain that the decision was unrelated to the Cambodia conflict, but instead based on the memorandum’s failure to produce results after only five meetings over 25 years. 159 “Fence project under way – Thailand moves to secure vulnerable crossings”, The Nation , 24 April 2026. Cambodian officials had warned that Thai withdrawal from MOU 44 would leave them with “no choice” but to pursue compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS. 160 “Cambodia to pursue compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS if Thailand revokes MoU”, Phnom Penh Post , 4 May 2026. In announcing the decision to invoke compulsory conciliation on 2 June, Hun Manet said it would “[bring] dialogue into a structured international framework recognised by both countries”. 161 “UNCLOS underway; Cambodia lodges formal request for maritime reconciliation”, Phnom Penh Post , 2 June 2026. Established under UNCLOS Annex V, compulsory conciliation is a dispute settlement mechanism in which parties select two experts each to sit on a commission, who then select a fifth to chair the body; the resulting recommendations are non-binding but serve as a basis for negotiations. Bangkok has acquiesced to compulsory conciliation, but made its dissatisfaction clear, with Foreign Minister Sihasak noting it would “unavoidab[ly] … affect talks on restoring relations, border security and … boundary issues”. 162 “Thailand to join UN maritime arbitration with Cambodia, halts other two-way talks”, Reuters, 5 June 2026; “Sihasak warns Hun Manet’s maritime move could shut door on wider Thai-Cambodian talks”, The Nation , 3 June 2026. Thailand appointed Rüdiger Wolfrum (Germany) and Albert J. Hoffmann (South Africa) as its two conciliators, while Cambodia appointed Peter Taksøe-Jensen (Denmark) and Jean-Marc Thouvenin (France). In mid-August, these experts selected Australian diplomat Katrina Cooper as the commission’s chairperson. Anutin later affirmed that Thailand would suspend participation in the JBC and GBC. He added that Bangkok would not discuss renewing relations until conciliation concludes. 163 “Thailand to join UN maritime arbitration with Cambodia, halts other two-way talks”, Reuters, 5 June 2026; “PM appoints Sihasak to lead UNCLOS process, vows to freeze JBC and GBC talks with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 5 June 2026. A Thai analyst observed that, as there was no legal rationale for linking compulsory conciliation with discussions of the land border, this stance reflected Bangkok’s anger with Cambodia. 164 Crisis Group interview, Thai journalist, Bangkok, June 2026. The compulsory conciliation process commenced on 15 September in Singapore, with opening statements by the two foreign ministers. Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn called the process “a means to rebuild trust”, expressing hope that the commission could help the parties “turn a new page for their mutual benefit”. 165 “Opening statement of the agent of the Kingdom of Cambodia, first meeting of the Conciliation Commission”, 15 September 2026. His counterpart Sihasak’s remarks struck an uncompromising note, citing the “broader context” of Cambodian provocations as the cause of the breakdown in relations. 166 “Thailand’s statement at the first meeting of UNCLOS Conciliation Commission”, 15 September 2026. VI. Averting a Third Round Demarcating the land border is essential if the two countries are to remove disputed territory as a source of conflict, leading to the loss of hundreds of lives over the past eighteen years. The means of specifying the land border already exist: the JBC has already demarcated three quarters of it. The main impediment is not technical complexity – the revised 2003 Terms of Reference and advantages offered by light detection and ranging should suffice – but rather the mistrust between Bangkok and Phnom Penh. Given events of the past year, there are genuine worries on both sides that a third round of fighting is likely – a former high-ranking Thai officer even called the prospect “inevitable”. 167 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Ex-deputy commander of Second Army Area warns third round of fighting ‘will happen’”, The Nation , 28 January 2026. Ideally, third-party mediation would make the necessary compromises more politically palatable. As Hun Sen noted in June 2025, any Cambodian or Thai leader who retreats from maximalist positions at this point would risk incurring public disapproval. 168 “Selected Comments of Samdech Akka Moha Sena Padei Techo Hun Sen, President of the Senate, on the Cambodia-Thailand Border Issue”, 2 June 2025. A disinterested third party could shield decision-makers from some of the political costs of compromise. The most logical candidate to play such a role remains the ICJ. Even if many in Thailand regard the ICJ’s 1962 ruling on Preah Vihear as unjust, it does not establish a binding precedent for other disputed areas of the land border. If Cambodia and Thailand agreed to have the court rule on all these areas, it could very well lead to an equitable resolution. 169 William Roth, “Tackling Thai-Cambodian border row”, Bangkok Post (editorial), 12 November 2025. Unfortunately, such a path is, for now, politically untenable in Thailand, both because of bitterness over the 1962 ruling and the establishment’s objections to internationalising the conflict. The reality of heightened nationalism is that the Thai government is unlikely to attempt to sell the public on trading even a small amount of territory for peace. 170 Jones and Narut, “The Sovereignty Straitjacket”, op. cit. Prime Minister Anutin was rewarded at the polls for maintaining a hard line on Cambodia. In turn, he is intent on keeping the Thai military’s support. He also does not wish to run afoul of right-wing nationalists who perceive bargaining as a betrayal of sacrifices, military and civilian, in the 2025 fighting. 171 “New government faces MOU 43 dilemma as Cambodia pushes JBC talks”, The Nation , 2 January 2026. Furthermore, conflict with Cambodia has allowed the Thai military to burnish its image, which had been sullied by its overt political role, including coups d’état. 172 Crisis Group interviews, journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. In this charged environment, those advocating compromise risk being labelled traitors. 173 Crisis Group interviews, Western diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. The costs of conflict are not high enough to impel [Thai and Cambodian] leaders toward a resolution. More broadly, political elites in both countries perceive benefits from the conflict, principally from popular support arising from nationalism and as a distraction from domestic economic and political problems. For decision-makers, especially in Thailand, these benefits continue to outweigh the conflict’s costs, whether economic or reputational. In any event, the costs of conflict are not high enough to impel leaders toward a resolution. Cambodia adapted to the border closure better than many anticipated, though it has compounded pre-existing economic pressures as time goes by, contributing to a marked slowdown in growth. 174 Crisis Group interview, government minister, Phnom Penh, February 2026. See also “IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Cambodia”, International Monetary Fund, 28 September 2026. The IMF projects growth to slow to 3 per cent in 2026, from 5.3 per cent in 2025. In any case, disruptions of bilateral trade have been damaging, but not bad enough to trigger a policy change. 175 Closure of the land border caused trade to decline by 40 per cent to $1.3 billion for the first half of 2026, year-on-year, according to Cambodian government data. “Cambodian economy suffers as Thai conflict blights bilateral trade”, Nikkei Asia , 24 July 2026. Some 900,000 Cambodian migrant workers returned from Thailand in 2025; two thirds of them found employment, though generally lower-paid. The UN estimated remittance losses at $277 million in 2025 and $665 million in 2026. “Socio-economic Impact Assessment of Cambodia–Thailand Border”, UN, April 2026, p. 10. Perhaps the most significant obstacle is that, for now, political elites in Bangkok appear to see greater reward in hardline policies than in the risks of reconciliation. Cambodia’s leadership likewise sees benefit in confrontation, in the form of popular nationalist fervour, though another round of fighting could shift Phnom Penh’s calculus, as further military setbacks could fracture the Hun family’s coalition. 176 Crisis Group interviews, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. Hun Sen told local officials that the CPP’s policy on the border dispute would be a campaign issue in the 2027 commune elections. “Ruling CPP to use border dispute issue as 2027 commune election campaign material”, CamboJA News, 1o June 2026. In these circumstances, reconciliation in the near term is unrealistic. Some argue that the conflict cannot be resolved until politics in both countries become more pluralistic and democratic, thereby weakening the hold of established elites. 177 Crisis Group interviews, academic, Phnom Penh, February 2026; journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. Yet, given the dismal state of bilateral ties, modest steps toward improved relations are as imperative as they are difficult. Until the land boundary is agreed upon, the issue will remain a potential trigger for war. Even in the absence of further combat, the border closure and suspension of trade is immiserating people living along the frontier, depriving both countries of revenue and eroding ASEAN cohesion in a period of major-power competition and flux in the international order. Delaying border demarcation [between Thailand and Cambodia] only heightens the risk of renewed fighting. To begin with, Bangkok and Phnom Penh should restore normal diplomatic relations by exchanging ambassadors, signalling a desire to improve the relationship, enhance communication and start rebuilding trust. Secondly, the JBC should resume its work as soon as possible, and the GBC should convene as necessary. 178 In July, Prime Minister Anutin appointed retired General Somsak Rungsita, a former director of the National Security Council, to lead Thailand’s JBC delegation. Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. The December 2025 ceasefire commits both parties to “refer to the Joint Boundary Commission to resume, at the earliest, the survey and demarcation works … to achieve lasting peace along the border”. 179 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. Given the prohibition on the use of force in determining international boundaries, there is no legitimate alternative to jointly negotiating the boundary line and withdrawing Thai troops from areas that are indisputably Cambodian territory. Delaying border demarcation only heightens the risk of renewed fighting. Thirdly, the neighbours have a politically acceptable platform for cooperation on demining and disposing of explosive remnants of war, which is a priority for both countries. 180 Thailand acknowledged using cluster munitions in 2025, defending their use as directed at military targets. The Cambodian Mine Action Centre estimates that Thai M42, M46 and M85 submunitions affected nearly 300,000 hectares in 349 villages. Neither Cambodia nor Thailand is party to the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions. “Cluster Munition Monitor 2026”, Cluster Munition Coalition, September 2026, pp. 24-25; “Third Review Conference condemns cluster munitions use, CMAC chief highlights impact of Thai shelling”, Agence Kampuchea Presse, 29 September 2026. The December 2025 ceasefire agreement stipulates that the two countries “work together to make timely progress on demining efforts along the border”. 181 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. To date, however, no such cooperation has taken place. 182 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. To some extent, Thailand has lessened the urgency by unilaterally clearing mines in the disputed areas it holds, but nevertheless the two sides should undertake whatever joint efforts they can. Cambodia should destroy any remaining antipersonnel mine stocks, reaffirm to its forces that mine use is prohibited and report these steps in its annual transparency reports under Article 7 of the Mine Ban Treaty. 183 “Investigation into New Use of Antipersonnel Landmines on the Thai-Cambodia Border”, op. cit. These actions could help build trust with Thailand. Both governments would serve their own interests by toning down statements that have hardened opinion and narrowed the room for compromise. Cambodia, in particular, would benefit from speaking with one voice on the border. Hun Sen’s statements, especially in 2025, attacked Thai leaders personally and raised tensions. Hun Sen often speaks before the prime minister, setting a line from which Hun Manet cannot easily depart. 184 Crisis Group interviews, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. Leaving border matters to the prime minister, the foreign ministry and the bilateral mechanisms would give Cambodia a more coherent posture and Hun Manet room to seek a new relationship with Bangkok. Restraint is also needed on the Thai side, where senior military officers accused Hun Sen of lying and labelled him the real commander of Cambodian forces during the December fighting. 185 “RTA says Hun Sen lied, ordered provocative acts against Thailand”, The Nation , 10 December 2025. Such charges may play well at home, but they make it harder for Thai officials to treat Hun Manet as the preferred counterpart. 186 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, September 2026. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push [the Thai and Cambodian officials] to the negotiating table. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push the sides to the negotiating table or otherwise decisively influence the course of events. U.S. diplomats remain engaged, but Washington is preoccupied with the Middle East war and shows little appetite for leading mediation efforts. 187 “US to provide $45m for Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire”, Nikkei Asia , 9 January 2026. For its part, China is unlikely to risk souring its relationship with either country by attempting to impose an agreement touching on the sensitive issue of sovereignty. Beijing should nevertheless intensify its Track II efforts, which have provided a welcome platform for civil society engagement and could furnish creative ideas for mending people-to-people ties. 188 “Summary Report: The Second China-Cambodia-Thailand Track II Dialogue, 20-21 April 2026, Beijing, China”. On file with Crisis Group. For its part, ASEAN should play a greater role. Ceasefire monitoring could help build confidence between the two sides, but the current configuration of the ASEAN Observation Teams leaves that potential unrealised. The teams, staffed by military attachés and ASEAN representatives based in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, can observe border areas only with the host country’s permission and coordination. 189 “Domestic pressure holds Thailand-Cambodia peace deal hostage”, Thai PBS World, 30 October 2025. Consequently, the teams have become implicated in the rival information strategies, with both Bangkok and Phnom Penh using site visits to cast blame on their adversary. 190 Crisis Group interview, analyst, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Can ASEAN keep the Thailand-Cambodia peace?”, South China Morning Post , 5 July 2026. Both sides should permit observers greater independence. 191 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. VII. Conclusion The fighting in 2025 has given way to an uneasy ceasefire that leaves Cambodia and Thailand no closer to resolving the underlying border dispute. With nationalism running high on both sides, political elites in Bangkok and Phnom Penh perceive greater rewards in hardline posturing than in compromise. To prevent the recurrence of a conflict that has already caused hundreds of deaths and displaced over a million people, Cambodia and Thailand will eventually have to survey and demarcate the land border, requiring compromise on both sides. Current prospects for a rapprochement are poor, however, and foreign states lack the leverage or commitment to impose a settlement. In the near term, the priority should be modest steps: restoring normal diplomatic relations by returning ambassadors, resuming the JBC’s technical demarcation work without preconditions and expanding cooperation on demining. The two sides should also permit ASEAN Observer Teams a more independent monitoring role. None of these measures will resolve the territorial dispute, but they could help rebuild the trust and communication needed to manage tensions and reduce the risk of renewed violence while a comprehensive settlement remains politically out of reach. In this episode of Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, Alan Boswell, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, the risk of direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and what may prevent further escalation. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Horn of Africa Ethiopia/Eritrea This week on Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Alan Boswell, Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and the risk of an all-out war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. They examine federal forces’ recapture of Tigray’s capital Mekelle and what has changed since the previous war. They explore Eritrea’s calculations in backing its former enemy, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, and whether Ethiopian advances toward the Eritrean border could bring the two countries into direct conflict. They also discuss Ethiopia’s push for Red Sea access and how it has further fuelled tensions with Eritrea. Turning to the wider region, they assess how Middle Eastern powers’ competing interests could shape their responses to a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, and the risk of such a conflict becoming entangled with wars in Sudan. The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict cmoore Fri, 10/09/2026 - 17:45 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) Mil Mi-8 helicopter lands on the Moroccan side of the border crossing point between Morocco and Mauritania, in Guerguerat located in the Western Sahara. 25 November, 2020. AFP / Fadel Senna Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 09 October 2026 17 minutes The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict Talks between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front over Western Sahara have hit a wall, with U.S. and UN representatives pushing for Rabat’s autonomy plan as the centrepiece of negotiations. If they are to broker a compromise, the mediators will have to slow down. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Riccardo Fabiani Project Director, North Africa https://twitter.com/ricfabiani Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Western Sahara Morocco Mauritania For some time after October 2025, it seemed that the long diplomatic stalemate over Western Sahara might have been broken. This desert territory is claimed by Morocco but sought by the Algeria-based Polisario Front as the home of an independent state for the Sahrawi people. A UN Security Council resolution passed in October 2025 strengthened international backing for a Moroccan autonomy proposal while remaining vague enough to allow for the possibility of other outcomes. Working together with the UN envoy to Western Sahara, Washington used this narrow opening to bring Morocco and the Polisario back into direct discussions for the first time since 2019. Algeria and Mauritania, both neighbours of Western Sahara, also joined. Three rounds of talks in Washington and Madrid allowed the parties to explore practical elements of a possible settlement without forcing either Morocco or the Polisario to abandon its stance on Western Sahara’s sovereignty, autonomy and self-determination. But the opening is now in danger of closing. The U.S. and UN tried to move too fast, from exploratory discussions to negotiations centred on Morocco’s autonomy proposal, meeting with firm resistance from the Polisario, which insists on a self-determination vote. Meanwhile, a series of diplomatic and military incidents sullied what had been a constructive atmosphere. Washington has responded by applying increasing pressure on the Front, entertaining alternative Sahrawi interlocutors and considering changes to the diplomatic framework. Uncertainty about the U.S. position on the future of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) adds another complication. The U.S. concededly has a difficult diplomatic task. It needs to show both resolve and a capacity for patience if it wants to coax the parties toward progress – and right now the balance is off. Why the U.S. decided to become so seized of this issue is unclear, but if the objective is a quick diplomatic win, then it is looking at the wrong file. Indeed, there is a significant risk that, if the administration persists in trying to force a quick settlement, it will risk deepening the mistrust that has long impeded progress in negotiations. Rather than searching for shortcuts, the U.S. and UN should seek to rebuild confidence among the parties, preserve an open negotiating framework and gradually create the political conditions under which substantive compromises might eventually become possible. Creating Space for Talks The Western Sahara conflict dates to 1975, when Spain withdrew from the territory and Morocco and Mauritania moved to divide it between them. The Polisario Front, backed principally by Algeria, launched an armed struggle for independence. Thousands of Sahrawis fled to Algeria. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 envisaged a referendum on self-determination, but disagreements over who should be able to vote have prevented it from taking place. Morocco has instead promoted a plan that would devolve powers to an autonomous Western Sahara under Rabat’s sovereignty, while the Polisario continues to demand a route to independence. The ceasefire collapsed in 2020, though fighting has remained limited. That same year, during President Donald Trump’s first term, the U.S. recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, in exchange for Morocco’s normalisation of relations with Israel; during Trump’s second term, the administration has strongly endorsed Rabat’s autonomy plan. In October 2025, the UN Security Council agreed to renew MINURSO’s mandate for another year, with new language more explicitly supporting Morocco’s autonomy plan. As the penholder, the U.S. had tabled a first draft that called autonomy “the basis” for future negotiations and “the most feasible solution”; but consultations among Council members led to watered-down language. The final version’s ambiguously (and awkwardly) worded text says autonomy will be taken “as basis” for negotiations and represents “a most feasible solution”. The Council thus gave its strong backing for the autonomy plan, while leaving the door ajar for discussion of other proposals. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. The former reiterated its demand for a self-determination referendum to settle the conflict, while the latter – then an elected member of the Council – took the politically unsurprising but exceptionally rare step of not voting on the resolution to register its opposition to a reference to “Moroccan sovereignty” in one of its preambular clauses. Nonetheless, U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos used the resolution’s ambiguity to press Algeria and the Polisario to return to negotiations. In the weeks after the Council vote, Boulos signalled to both actors that, though Washington clearly supported autonomy, the UN resolution did not preclude another solution if the conflict parties agreed to it. At the time, a Polisario official told Crisis Group that “Boulos’s language is more neutral than the UN Security Council resolution” – an expression of growing confidence in Washington’s role. Between January and February 2026, ministerial-level delegations from Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and the Polisario gathered twice in Washington and once in Madrid, the first direct meetings between the conflict parties in seven years. The co-chairs were Boulos, U.S. Ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz and UN envoy Staffan de Mistura. These rounds differed from previous efforts in at least three ways. First, Washington was directly involved in the discussions, marking a break from its traditional role as the UN envoy’s external supporter, with U.S. officials both driving the conversation and giving de Mistura space to help do the same. Secondly, Algeria and Mauritania participated in the talks – though only as ostensible “observers”. For years, Rabat has wanted Algiers and Nouakchott involved in negotiations, claiming that the Polisario is an Algerian proxy and that, to be durable, any agreement will have to be part of a grand bargain with countries abutting Western Sahara. Algeria and Mauritania have countered that they are merely neighbours interested in the conflict’s resolution (hence their insistence on “observer” status). Thirdly, ahead of the talks and responding to a demand repeatedly put forward by the U.S. and its European partners over the years, Morocco expanded its four-page autonomy proposal floated in 2007 into a comprehensive 40-page blueprint to guide negotiations. The co-chairs insisted on confidentiality from the participants to protect discussions from political pressures at home. Though news broke that the four parties were talking, the contents of the three rounds have remained mostly secret, with Morocco’s expanded autonomy plan still under wraps. That said, diplomatic sources have told Crisis Group that the talks, which apparently touched upon organising elections and reintegrating Sahrawi refugees, among other things, went well overall. In a conversation with Crisis Group, a Polisario official was keen to stress that these exchanges were “a discussion, not a negotiation”. The open-ended format seemed to suit both sides, making it possible for them to re-engage with each other, however warily. From Progress to Stalemate The talks subsequently hit a wall, however. After the three meetings, the U.S. and UN repeatedly asked the Front to offer its comments on Rabat’s plan with the aim of kickstarting a more substantive discussion of how to end the conflict. The Polisario baulked, with an official explaining to Crisis Group that the Front “has not accepted the Moroccan autonomy plan as the basis for negotiations and the UN Security Council does not require us to accept it”. While this position should not have been surprising – the talks gained momentum only because of the ambiguity that the U.S. had managed to create around this key issue – U.S. and UN diplomats seemed both frustrated and bewildered by the Front’s attitude. A U.S. official noted that “Algeria showed much more flexibility than the Polisario” by encouraging the Front to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan, rather than rejecting the proposal out of hand. Between May and June, relations between the parties – as well as between the U.S. and the Polisario – quickly deteriorated. On 5 May, after a long period of quiet, the Front fired rockets at the city of Smara, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, wounding a civilian and damaging a number of buildings. The U.S., France and several other countries, along with the EU and UN, immediately condemned the attack, calling it an attempt to undermine negotiations . The next day, U.S. Ambassador to Morocco Duke Buchan III visited Dakhla, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, reiterating the Trump administration’s recognition of Rabat’s sovereignty and criticising the Polisario. On 7 May, the Polisario issued a statement denouncing Buchan’s visit and justifying the Smara attack as legitimate resistance to colonialism. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. According to several U.S. and European diplomats, Waltz wrote to ask whether the Front’s leaders were still committed to a negotiated solution after Smara. The Polisario reportedly responded with a long missive about the dispute’s complexity that Washington saw as obfuscatory. At that point, a number of administration insiders turned against the group. Tensions escalated further when, on 7 June, Moroccan forces killed Lahbib Abdelaziz, son of former Polisario leader Mohamed Abdelaziz and a potential future leader of the Front. His killing shocked pro-independence Sahrawis, who complained that (in contrast to the outcry that followed the Smara attack) there was precious little international condemnation. Then, on 8 June, Sahrawi activist Naama Asfari – who was arrested in 2010 in connection with protests at Gdeim Izik – began a hunger strike , which lasted 47 days and ended only after Rabat granted him a transfer to a jail closer to his family. By late June, U.S. frustration with the Polisario had begun to show. On 30 June, Waltz met with a delegation of the Sahrawi Movement for Peace (MSP), founded in 2020 as a self-styled moderate alternative to the Polisario, expressing willingness to negotiate with Morocco over autonomy. Waltz praised the MSP as an organisation committed to “peace, compromise and a durable solution” that “the world should hear”. Another meeting between a U.S. embassy official and an MSP delegation followed on 28 July. With these steps, the U.S. was breaking with a well-established practice of recognising the Polisario as the representative of the Sahrawi people (even if there was some dispute over whether it should be considered the sole, exclusive representative) and raising the spectre that it might bypass the Front absent greater cooperation. The Front reacted dismissively. A Polisario official told Crisis Group that U.S. officials “should come on the ground and see who really represents the Sahrawis. The Polisario comes from the people and remains representative. The groups they want to promote are nothing”. Summing up the U.S. approach, a Western diplomat told Crisis Group that Washington believes the Polisario’s choice is between “the hard way and the harder way”, meaning that continued resistance by the movement to engaging with Morocco’s plan will bring more adverse consequences upon it. In another sign of tougher steps to come, and in parallel to the talks, a group of U.S. members of Congress introduced two bills that would require the Secretary of State to designate the Polisario as a foreign terrorist organisation (FTO) due to its alleged links with Iran and Lebanese Hizbollah. For legal and political reasons, it is hard to imagine these bills passing into law and being enforced, and the administration has expressed no support for them. But the administration could be working with Congressional allies to signal what might come next should the impasse persist. Searching for Alternatives Faced with a diplomatic deadlock ahead of the expiry of MINURSO’s mandate at the end of October, U.S. officials have been weighing other options, including replacing the Polisario with more flexible Sahrawi representatives, such as the MSP, in the talks. A Western diplomat observed that Washington could use the mandate renewal to try including new language that creates space at the negotiating table for the MSP and others (eg, elected Sahrawi officials who reside in Morocco) – for instance by referring to “Sahrawi representatives” rather than “the Polisario Front” when describing the concerned parties. That said, not all U.S. officials seem ready to drop the Front or give up on the current format. In a 25 September interview with France 24 , Boulos stressed that the U.S. was still hoping the Polisario would engage in talks, praised Algeria’s stance and highlighted that more work was needed to achieve a mutually acceptable settlement. The pro-Polisario media welcomed these remarks. In his 28 September speech to the UN General Assembly, Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf reiterated his country’s rejection of any shortcut to a deal: “Algeria warns that any attempt to bypass this framework of reference or marginalise the holders of the inalienable right, the people of Western Sahara and their sole, legitimate representative, the Polisario Front, will not contribute to resolving the conflict; rather, it will further exacerbate tensions”. Meanwhile, Morocco has been assiduously currying favour with the Trump administration, even if it has not openly backed the idea of opening negotiations to other Sahrawi groups. In July, King Mohamed VI announced that the Tiznit-Dakhla road connecting Morocco to Western Sahara would be renamed the Donald J. Trump Highway as “a personal expression of my high regard”. On 15 September, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and U.S. Ambassador Waltz agreed in New York on upgrading Israel-Morocco relations by appointing ambassadors and working toward a series of economic agreements to be signed by year’s end. In their official statement, the three countries reaffirmed Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and support for the autonomy plan. “The tripartite agreement with the U.S. and Israel is an essential part of Morocco’s approach to Western Sahara”, a Moroccan expert told Crisis Group. “The diplomatic upgrade is a gesture addressed to Washington, as we need the U.S. on our side ahead of the next Security Council meeting”. According to Moroccan and European sources, Rabat is hoping that the MINURSO renewal will, among other things, include clearer backing for the autonomy plan as “the only basis” for resolving the conflict. MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. At this stage, MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. In October 2025, Washington tried to shorten the mission’s mandate to three months, hoping that more frequent Security Council involvement might increase pressure on the parties to reach a deal, thus allowing MINURSO to wind down, in line with the U.S. agenda of reducing spending on peacekeeping missions. Eventually, the U.S. settled for a twelve-month renewal in parallel with a strategic review conducted by the Secretary-General. Meanwhile, in anticipation of U.S. requests to trim peacekeeping spending, MINURSO underwent cuts , removing 23 civilian posts, reducing flying hours and slashing its own budget by 11.5 per cent. In an April Senate hearing , Waltz mentioned MINURSO as a mission that – in the Trump administration’s eyes – has outlived its purpose. Several European diplomats told Crisis Group that they suspected Washington would once again push for a major cut in the mission’s expenses or (less likely) its termination during the next renewal debate. MINURSO’s political mandate has changed beyond recognition since its inception, insofar as it presently plays only a marginal role in diplomacy. But European officials who spoke to Crisis Group share the conviction that its presence remains critical to avoiding escalation. In 2022, Morocco made clear that, should MINURSO withdraw from the UN buffer zone separating the territory held by Rabat from the Algerian and Mauritanian borders, the kingdom would occupy this strip of land. If that were to happen, the Polisario would likely attack Moroccan installations from Algeria or Mauritania, rather than using the buffer zone as its launchpad, as is now the case. In turn, Rabat might decide to pursue Polisario units into Algerian or Mauritanian territory, potentially dragging its neighbours into conflict. Rebuilding Confidence among the Parties With the October deadline for renewing the MINURSO mandate fast approaching, U.S. officials could be tempted to either strong-arm the Polisario into accepting Morocco’s autonomy plan or replace the Front with a more accommodating alternative. They may hope that this small organisation will eventually buckle under Washington’s pressure, fearful of the consequences of continued obduracy, which might range from being cast aside to being designated as an FTO, with the severe attendant sanctions. For an administration keen to secure quick deals to end wars, ending the Western Sahara conflict might look like low-hanging fruit. Taking this tack would be highly risky. Since the breakdown of the UN-organised referendum scheme in the early 2000s and, in particular, the resumption of hostilities in 2020, confidence between Morocco and the Polisario has been running low, a by-product of the conflict’s five-decade duration, the accumulation of failed diplomatic initiatives, competing legal and historical narratives, and repeated periods of military confrontation and political deadlock. The two sides continue to approach negotiations from fundamentally different premises: Morocco sees autonomy under its sovereignty as the sole viable end state, while the Polisario insists on a process that preserves the option of independence. In addition, since the 2021 diplomatic rupture between Algeria and Morocco, the conflict has been nestled within a regional dispute , further complicating efforts to resolve it. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. The Polisario regards self-determination for all practical purposes as an existential issue, meaning that it is more likely to dig in than concede in the face of coercion, with much of the cost of any standoff being borne by vulnerable Sahrawi refugees. In such a scenario, the risk of escalatory violence would also increase. For leaders on both sides to make difficult concessions, and for public opinion to accept them, at least some preliminary steps are needed. Otherwise, both will view negotiations as a zero-sum game, dimming prospects for a resolution. “We need a minimum of trust”, a Polisario official commented to Crisis Group. Against this backdrop, Washington should drop any illusion of reaching a swift deal. Instead, it ought to embrace a more patient approach that, for now, focuses on clearing the air among parties whose relations have soured. The co-chairs should look to four confidence-building measures that might create a better atmosphere for future talks. They should: First, press Morocco and the Polisario to allow Sahrawi families in Algerian refugee camps to visit Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, and vice versa, resuming a program that was suspended in 2014. These exchanges would create regular, low-risk cooperation among Morocco, Polisario and the UN in service of a concrete humanitarian need, while reconnecting people divided by the conflict and helping reduce both mistrust and the political cost of engagement; Secondly, urge Morocco to release some or all the Sahrawi prisoners it has held since the 2010 Gdeim Izik protests – or at least to honour prisoners’ requests for transfer to jails closer to their families; Thirdly, push the Polisario to declare a unilateral truce in return. Even though the Front rejects returning to the 1991 ceasefire, it might be persuaded to temporarily suspend its attacks to avoid undermining talks; and Finally, arrange for U.S. and UN officials to visit the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, meeting the Polisario leadership and holding town hall-style meetings with refugees to listen to their concerns. The co-chairs also should revise their diplomatic approach to get out of the current cul-de-sac. Rather than pushing the Polisario to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan – which it rejects as a sole basis for negotiations – they should revert to the format of the three rounds held in Washington and Madrid, thus creating space for the parties to continue a less structured exchange of views on their respective plans. The co-chairs could facilitate these conversations and advance bridging proposals on the specific issues discussed. The most difficult questions relating to sovereignty should be left for the end. Over time, such an approach – pursued on the basis that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed” – might eventually allow for more in-depth discussions. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the [Polisario] Front. Crucially, the U.S. should stop suggesting it might replace the Polisario with other Sahrawi representatives in the talks. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the Front. Besides, any settlement reached with such alternative groups would almost certainly lack popular buy-in and would fuel tensions among Morocco, the Polisario, Algeria and Mauritania. That said, the co-chairs might create a purely consultative parallel track bringing together other Sahrawis, from elected officials in Morocco to the MSP to civil society groups from the Tindouf camps – all of whom might have more political flexibility to put ideas on the table than Morocco and the Polisario. These Sahrawis could contribute their ideas on specific issues such as elections, natural resource management and refugee reintegration – as well as on the sovereignty-related endgame issues. For its part, the Polisario should engage more earnestly in the process. Whatever the Front thinks of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign, both the Polisario and Sahrawi refugees would benefit from seeing it defused. Showing some flexibility would have the dual advantage of helping stave off this threat while taking advantage of U.S. engagement to advance diplomacy. For example, the Polisario could present a new proposal based on a 2003 plan advanced by James Baker, the former U.S. secretary of state who was then UN envoy. Under that plan, which combined autonomy and self-determination, Western Sahara would have had five years of substantial self-rule, with an elected local executive and legislature, while Morocco would have retained responsibility for foreign affairs and defence. After that transitional period, the UN would have held a referendum on the territory’s final status. At the time, the Front accepted the plan, while Rabat rejected it. Such a counteroffer would at least provide the co-chairs with a document they could use in trying to bridge the gap between the two sides’ positions. Morocco should also find ways to show flexibility. While one concrete way to do that might be releases of Gdeim Izik prisoners, it will also need to set something of a different tone in negotiations, resisting the temptation to treat autonomy as an outcome that can be fast-tracked. A more durable settlement will require Rabat to accept a long, difficult negotiating process in which trust gradually is rebuilt and the terms of any eventual compromise are worked through with the Polisario, rather than presented as a fait accompli . Meanwhile, the UN Security Council should refrain from sunsetting MINURSO and ensure that any effort to streamline its mandate or reform the mission preserves its military monitoring component to manage the risk that fighting will spill into Algerian or Mauritanian territory. Washington may reasonably seek to review the mission’s costs and functions, but reforms that significantly weaken or eliminate this military role could remove one of the few remaining stabilising mechanisms in Western Sahara. Finally, Washington should maintain a balanced approach to regional diplomacy – engaging regularly with both Algeria and Morocco, as it has sought to do during the current diplomatic effort, rather than allowing its closer ties with Rabat to feed perceptions that it is taking sides in an increasingly polarised regional competition. Maintaining credible channels with both capitals could help contain bilateral tensions, limit the Western Sahara dispute’s entanglement in wider rivalries and protect the political space needed for an eventual negotiated settlement. Should U.S. diplomats instead choose to intensify pressure on the Polisario and its backers in hopes of forcing rapid acceptance of Morocco’s autonomy framework, they are likely to find – potentially at high cost to the parties and to the region – that a conflict more than five decades old is unlikely to be resolved through coercion alone. A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? cmoore Mon, 10/12/2026 - 13:35 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? Online Event Tuesday, 20 October 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Tel Aviv Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. The Knesset elections on 27 October could be the most consequential in Israel’s short history. After four years of hard-right government under Benjamin Netanyahu, and three years of war on multiple fronts since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israelis head to the polls with starkly different hopes for their future. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the threshold needed to enter the 120-seat parliament. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Whichever bloc comes out on top, a question hangs over the vote: has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change – at least, not on big issues that matter to the rest of the world, such as accommodating the 7.5 million Palestinians that live under Israeli rule? In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading Israeli political analysts who will tackle this and other questions. Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea Back from War cmoore Mon, 10/12/2026 - 21:44 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Members of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) gather in front of Mekelle Alula Aba Nega International Airport after federal forces retook control of the facility in Mekelle on 6 October, 2026 AFP Alert / Africa 12 October 2026 11 minutes Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea Back from War Addis Ababa and Asmara are edging closer to a direct conflict, which would cause further mayhem in the troubled Horn of Africa and the Red Sea basin. It is not too late to avert disaster. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Horn of Africa Ethiopia and Eritrea stand perilously close to all-out war as heavy fighting inches close to their shared border. The threat of resurgent interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa follows several weeks of fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an armed rebellion on 23 September. The Ethiopian military has gained the upper hand in those clashes, moving northward after capturing Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and deploying military personnel on its soil, a claim that has been backed up by media reports and other accounts, though it appears that Eritrea subsequently pulled its troops back toward the border in the face of an Ethiopian advance and reported drones strikes on its forces. The effects of these cross-border movements could be dire: they could trigger a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea that, in turn, could spiral into a wider conflagration along Eritrea’s Red Sea coast. A push at the highest political and diplomatic levels to prevent this budding confrontation is a matter of extreme urgency. The Resurgence of Conflict The risk of direct conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea has risen sharply since late September as war has engulfed Tigray. On 20 September, the TPLF and six other groups announced a new “alliance for survival” aimed at toppling Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, which they see as authoritarian and bent on centralising power. Two days later, Ethiopia conducted a large drone raid on sites in southern Tigray, where officials believed the TPLF was massing for an attack. On 23 September, the TPLF mounted large-scale offensives against the federal government. It was apparently trying to join forces with two of its allies, the Amhara Fano and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, which commenced their own assaults on Ethiopian military positions near Tigray’s boundaries. This first wave of attacks made gains, but Ethiopian forces quickly regrouped. They have steadily pushed the Tigrayans back since then, recording a string of battlefield victories and capturing most of Tigray. On 3 October, federal forces and their allies took Mekelle without a fight. As the TPLF withdrew, the war’s front line shifted toward the group’s strongholds in the northern mountains, near the border with Eritrea. At the same time, tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea reached fever pitch in the wake of reported Eritrean troop deployments to northern Tigray in support of the TPLF’s rear guard. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. Frictions between the two are neither sudden nor surprising, even if the present rift between them in some ways marks a radical turnaround. For more than a year, Addis Ababa has been denouncing Asmara, and more recently its allies in the Sudanese army, for backing rebel groups in Ethiopia, particularly the TPLF. This antagonism stands in sharp contrast to what prevailed during the last Tigray war, which raged between 2020 and 2022, when Ethiopia and Eritrea had become friends rather than foes. That conflict came on the heels of Abiy’s ascent to power, which in turn dethroned the TPLF, a pivotal force in national politics for decades, and set the stage for a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF high command in Tigray. Eritrea, which had fought its previous war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 while the TPLF was in charge in Addis Ababa, sought common cause with Abiy in confronting the group after Tigrayan forces attacked Ethiopia’s Northern Command in November 2020. A seesaw battle ensued, with Addis Ababa and its allies eventually beating back the TPLF ahead of the signing of the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022. This agreement left the TPLF largely intact, however, and its commitment to fully demobilise its armed forces was never fully enforced. Eritrea, which was not involved in the Pretoria negotiations, had been pushing for the group’s complete elimination. Asmara was incensed at the outcome. In its view, its critical national interests had not been respected during the talks. Eritrea’s relations with Ethiopia subsequently began to deteriorate. Some say Abiy was quietly courting the TPLF in order to establish a new alliance with it against Eritrea in the acrimonious aftermath of the peace deal. TPLF leaders apparently rebuffed these advances. Abiy also began to argue in public that Ethiopia needed to restore sovereign access to the sea. He said Ethiopia had a historical claim to the Red Sea coastline, which it had lost when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Since then, Ethiopia, the world’s largest landlocked country by population size, has been relying almost exclusively on Djibouti to export goods by sea. Officials in Abiy’s government have stressed that Ethiopia will not be satisfied merely with access to a wider range of ports, a course some have suggested it pursue, but needs a sovereign seaboard with a naval base. Asmara has viewed this rhetoric as a threat to seize Eritrea’s coastline, especially its southern port of Assab, by armed force. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. Asmara appears to have seen Tigray in the TPLF’s grip as a potential geographic buffer between it and the Ethiopian heartland, as well as a military counterweight to Addis Ababa. The TPLF, for its part, was keen to break the encirclement it endured in the 2020-2022 war. As a sign of their strengthening ties, Eritrean and Tigrayan authorities promoted new cross-border “people-to-people” exchanges known as tsimdo (“engagement” in Tigrinya), providing further ballast for their switch from adversaries to allies. Meanwhile, the 2022 peace deal began to fray. The TPLF complained that the government had failed to resolve major issues stemming from the conflict, including the status of disputed territories occupied by Amhara forces during the war and the return of displaced people to their homes in these areas. Little effort was made to remedy the antipathy between the TPLF and Abiy: Addis Ababa never reintegrated Tigray back into the national political federation, with the region remaining without representation in parliament or other institutions in the capital. In March 2025, the TPLF ousted the first post-war interim Tigray administrator, Getachew Reda, who had been a lead negotiator in the Pretoria peace negotiations for the TPLF and was chosen ahead of TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael. The group claimed that Getachew was too close to the federal government and had not defended Tigray’s interests sufficiently during his time in office. (Getachew fled to Addis Ababa, where he joined Abiy’s administration.) Abiy then appointed Tadesse Werede, a top Tigrayan general, in Getachew’s place, but the relationship between Tigray’s new ruler and the TPLF also began to worsen. In May 2026, the TPLF retook power in Mekelle, dismantling the interim administration, reinstalling its leader Debretsion as regional president and placing Tadesse under house arrest. The federal government responded by tightening its economic restrictions on the region and launching a campaign of airstrikes inside Tigray. In August, a major clash broke out between TPLF and federal ground forces before quickly subsiding. Shuttle diplomacy by the African Union and others aimed at restarting negotiations failed to gain traction. Simultaneously, mediators found their efforts thwarted by rising hostility among powers across the Horn. Addis Ababa began to denounce Asmara for trying to coordinate a transnational alliance against it, and accused the Sudanese army , an ally of Eritrea and Egypt (another Ethiopian foe), of supporting meetings of a nascent alliance of opposition groups in eastern Sudan. Ethiopia also complained that Sudan was harbouring a group of Tigrayan troops, known as Army 70, in Sudanese territory, where they were said to have stood alongside the army in fighting its enemy, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Ethiopia, on the other hand, began allowing the RSF to base itself in its Benishangul-Gumuz region close to the Sudanese border, from where it could launch attacks into Sudan’s Blue Nile state. Ethiopia’s relations with the Sudanese army, which had continued to function despite the chill between them, became icy as a result. Sudan has also claimed that drones attacking Khartoum were dispatched from Ethiopian territory. Neighbours at Loggerheads This mosaic of enmities and alliances has come into sharp relief since war broke out in Tigray. As hostilities have intensified, Ethiopia and Eritrea have edged ever closer to conflict. Ethiopia considers Eritrea to be masterminding the TPLF’s war effort. Soon after fighting broke out, Ethiopian federal officials and Afar’s regional president accused Eritrea of deploying forces in the Afar region. On 1 October, Ethiopia expelled all Eritrean diplomats from the country, accusing Asmara of “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”. All diplomatic ties between the two states have since been severed. After Ethiopian federal forces began advancing north of Mekelle, the first reports emerged of alleged Eritrean deployments in northern Tigray, seemingly with the aim of bolstering the TPLF’s defensive lines. Several media reports indicated on 7 October that Eritrean units had passed through Adigrat, 30km south of the Ethiopian border. Accounts also suggest that Eritrean forces took up positions south of Adigrat in the Edaga Hamus area. A day later, after reported drone strikes on Eritrean vehicles, some of its forces reportedly withdrew to the border. With Ethiopian forces currently approaching the frontier at several points, the two armies are positioned in alarmingly close proximity. Asmara’s apparent gamble to intervene more directly in the war, even if the incursion was brief, could well backfire. On 9 October, Ethiopia wrote a letter to the UN Security Council saying it was “taking measures” of self-defence in response to Eritrea’s deployment of infantry and mechanised units across the border and occupation of Ethiopian territory. The letter also accused Eritrea of “harbouring, supporting, financing, arming and directing armed insurgent groups operating within Ethiopia”. On 10 October, Eritrea responded with its own letter, accusing Ethiopia of declaring a “war of aggression” against it three years ago and using self-defence as a pretext for acts of war. The Security Council has scheduled a closed-door session to discuss the crisis on 13 October. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. The last major interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa, in which hundreds of thousands perished in trench warfare, was fought along precisely the same border. One flashpoint could be Eritrean military positions inside Ethiopian territory; another could be disputed territory along the border. Should Eritrean forces fully withdraw to their side of the border, Ethiopia could point to Eritrea’s apparent incursion and alleged harbouring of TPLF fighters as justification for seeking to cross into Eritrea. Even if Ethiopia stops short of a land invasion of Eritrea (and Ethiopian officials maintain that they have no intention of fighting a war on Eritrean soil), aerial warfare using drones and other long-range strike weapons could cause devastating harm. Ethiopia possesses the larger air force and drone arsenal, and it could try to quickly overwhelm Eritrea’s air defences. Should the two states lock horns, war could also extend across the region. The Sudanese army and Egypt look primed to jump to Eritrea’s defence, though it is uncertain how much support they would be willing or able to give. On the other side, the United Arab Emirates could be expected to back Ethiopia with more arms transfers. Saudi Arabia is keen to prevent a new front from emerging along the Red Sea, especially one involving the UAE, and has tried in the past to de-escalate tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On this occasion, however, Riyadh might be tempted to throw its weight behind Eritrea should a larger conflict erupt, given that its own Red Sea security would be at stake. That said, Saudi Arabia is also embroiled in a fresh round of fighting in Yemen and may not want to rally to the side of what might be a losing cause. Halting the Slide to War Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea back from the brink of war should be the priority for all those interested in preventing a deadly chain of interconnected conflicts from snaking across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea regions. Capitals such as Washington, Nairobi, Pretoria, London, Paris, Rome, Riyadh, Ankara and Abu Dhabi should press both sides to avoid escalation. In particular, they should urge Abiy to refrain from advancing into Eritrean territory. They should also appeal to Asmara to respect Ethiopian sovereignty and withdraw any remaining troops from Ethiopian territory, should they still be stationed there. Despite their rift, Saudi Arabia and the UAE could also use this moment to work together to staunch a new conflict along the Red Sea, which could otherwise cause even more trouble in their bilateral relations. Should efforts to avert an outright war prevail, diplomats should not desist until they manage to achieve a durable de-escalation of tensions between the two capitals. The heart of any settlement between the two countries is likely to be respect for each other’s sovereignty and restoration of diplomatic ties. In focusing on calming regional tensions, mediators should not forget the dispute between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF, should the latter manage to avoid complete collapse following its reversals. African leaders still look best placed to restart the Tigray peace track, even if neither federal officials nor TPLF leaders appear ready for direct talks any time soon. Prior to the start of hostilities, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the Pretoria negotiations that ended the last Tigray war, had been acting as the African Union’s peace envoy for the region. He visited Addis Ababa and Mekelle several times earlier in the year but had little success in bringing the two sides together. Efforts should be made to reactivate Obasanjo at the earliest opportunity. Other African leaders or ex-leaders could also be dispatched, such as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made a quick stop in Addis Ababa on 5 October to speak with Abiy, or former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, who also played a key role in the Pretoria negotiations in 2022. The U.S. or European powers could also play a part behind the scenes in trying to rekindle peace talks. At a minimum, all sides should press the federal government and the TPLF to abide by humanitarian commitments under international law. The UN Security Council, which as noted will discuss the crisis on 13 October, should make a clear call for both sides to respect the UN Charter and instruct the Secretary-General to undertake urgent diplomacy to prevent a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Another war in the Horn of Africa may lie around the corner. Outright conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea would likely spread to the Red Sea, disrupting the African side of this strategic waterway. It could also prove to be yet another front in the Horn that is easy to open and hard to close, especially once it becomes entangled in the mesh of disputes among neighbours and across the region. The best time to stop the looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war is now, before any more damage is done. Louisiana Activists Draw Links Between Petrochemical, Climate Harm to Maternal Health. Click to expand Image Kaitlyn Joshua with her daughter, Lauryn, age 5, outside their home in Geismar, Ascension Parish, in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley. Joshua, a chronic asthma sufferer since childhood, said her physician told her, “Kaitlyn, it’s where you live. It’s the air quality. You’re going to have to move out of there.” October 20, 2023. © 2023 Eli Reed for Human Rights Watch Louisiana feminist activists came together on October 2 at the annual Black Birth Matters conference to demand that policy makers consider how toxic air pollution and other environmental damage negatively impact reproductive health. As part of a day-long examination of human rights in Louisiana, Kaitlyn Joshua, an environmental and reproductive rights expert, Shamell Lavigne from RISE St James, a key community-based environmental rights organization, and Tyra Gross, an academic with an interest in climate intersections with Black reproductive justice, led a panel on environmental justice. Joshua and Lavigne explained why industrial regulation is important for human and, specifically, maternal health, and Gross discussed ways communities can make sure pregnant people and new parents are better prepared for climate disaster. Louisiana is an especially pertinent place for this conversation. The state has the second biggest (after Texas) petrochemistry industry in the US with significant reproductive and other health consequences for fenceline communities. Public health in Louisiana is especially at risk from climate change impacts. Louisiana also has a maternal health crisis with worsening prenatal care access, large maternal care “deserts”, a premature birth rate that recently rose and devastating cuts to safe abortion and other lifesaving reproductive health care. There is evidence that petrochemical pollution can lead to an increased risk of reproductive harm. Local authorities should make sure impacted communities have the most up to date information on how emissions from extracting and burning fossil fuels, climate change, and the petrochemical industry might damage the health of pregnant women and other people. The collective work of Black Birth Matters’ participants shines a light on how communities sometimes face multiple and interlocked injustices. It’s time for the state government to take action to protect the environment and reproductive rights for the people of Louisiana and nationwide.

Niger’s Junta Tightens Its Grip on Free Expression. Click to expand Image Nigerien journalist Moussa Kaka, former correspondent for Radio France Internationale, February 12, 2007. © 2007 Seyllou/AFP via Getty Images A lawyer in Niger faces prosecution over comments about the army on social media while a prominent journalist and critic of the country’s military junta is being held in secret, with authorities refusing to identify his alleged offense. These cases together highlight a broadening crackdown in Niger, where the space for free expression is shrinking by the day. On September 21, police summoned Abrourahamane Lirwana, a well-known lawyer. A prosecutor in Niger’s capital, Niamey, charged him with “spreading data likely to disturb public order” under a broad cybercrime law and ordered him detained. Authorities have not explained the basis for the charge, though it appears linked to a September 12 Facebook post in which Lirwana described Niger’s army as divided, with some officers backing former President Mahamadou Issoufou and others former President Mohamed Bazoum. At an October 6 court hearing, prosecutors sought a five-year prison sentence for Lirwana. Meanwhile, Moussa Kaka, a journalist, went missing in Niamey on August 31, raising fears he had been forcibly disappeared. His family and colleagues received no information about his whereabouts until September 25, when Justice Minister Alio Daouda said during Niger’s Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations in Geneva that Kaka had been detained for an alleged “offense” and would “answer before the courts.” A Nigerien journalist told Human Rights Watch that Kaka “should never have been arrested, and authorities must now reveal where he is.” Lirwana and Kaka are hardly alone. The junta continues to arbitrarily detain former President Bazoum, his wife, the former Interior Minister Hama Amadou Souley, and Moussa Tiangari, a leading human rights defender. Since taking power in 2023, Niger’s military junta has entrenched authoritarian rule and curtailed fundamental rights and freedoms. The authorities have dissolved all political parties and several independent unions, suspended civil society groups, detained journalists under the cybercrime law, and stripped exiled opposition figures of their nationality. Niger’s authorities should drop the politically motivated charges against Lirwana and release him. They should immediately disclose where Kaka is being held and release him or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offense. Niger’s authorities should respect fundamental freedoms and ensure political opponents, journalists, and civil society activists can operate safely and freely.

Airstrike Damages Hospital in Central Ukraine. Click to expand Image A shattered window at the Consultative and Diagnostic Centre in the Podilskyi district of Kyiv, Ukraine, on September 24, 2026. © 2026 Ukrinform/NurPhoto via AP Photo A Russian airstrike damaged a hospital in the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih on October 6, according to reports from local officials and media outlets. The attack injured several people, including at least two hospital workers, and also damaged residential and administrative buildings and an art school in the city center. The strike is the latest in a long string of Russian attacks in Ukraine that impact health care workers and facilities and seriously threaten the right to health. In some cases, these attacks may constitute war crimes. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded more than 3,300 attacks impacting health care since the full scale February 2022 invasion, resulting in the deaths of 248 health workers with 1,095 injured. In September, a Russian strike damaged a maternity hospital in Kyiv and killed one person in its car park. It was one of a series of drone and missile attacks across Ukraine that day that killed eight people, most of them in Kharkiv and two in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, Ukrainian authorities said. Attacks impacting health care can have devastating effects beyond the immediate casualties. A survey of civilians conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières’ (Doctors Without Borders) showed that, since the invasion, the percentage of respondents who reported being able to access health care “always” or “most of the time” dropped from 77 percent to 35 percent, in part due to these attacks. Those who can “rarely” or “never” access care rose from 7 percent to 35 percent. After years of hostilities, the WHO estimated the cost of rebuilding Ukraine’s healthcare sector at more than US$23 billion. International humanitarian law grants special protections for medical facilities, healthcare personnel, and medical transportation units, such as ambulances. Attacks on health care can also violate international human rights law, in particular the right to health, but also the rights to life and security. Russian authorities and state media have alleged that Ukrainian strikes have also damaged medical facilities in Russia's border regions and Russian-occupied territories. All parties to the conflict should immediately cease all attacks on health care and ensure their conduct is in line with international law.

War’s Hidden Mental Health Toll on Children with Disabilities. Click to expand Image Ibrahim, a 5-year-old boy with autism, is held by his father in Idlib, Syria, June 2022. © © 2022 Human Rights Watch. As armed conflicts proliferate around the globe, World Mental Health Day is a reminder that the psychological toll stemming from hostilities result in mental health harms that have lasting effects on people’s lives. Insecurity, trauma, anxiety, and confusion are the norm for many who have endured armed conflict. Access to services is frequently inadequate—even though over a fifth of conflict-affected populations are estimated to experience mental health conditions such as post-traumatic stress, depression or anxiety. For people, including children, with intellectual disabilities, these harms can be compounded by social, attitudinal, and environmental barriers, which interact with their disability and can heighten their exposure to violence and exclusion. The father of a boy with an intellectual disability in Syria, described in 2020 the effects that the war there had had on his son. The boy, who was 13 at the time, had become increasingly withdrawn and isolated. “He sits alone, doesn’t want to interact with any other kids,” said his father, who also described the psychological distress affecting his other children. “You can see the fear in their eyes. They have no hopes for the future.” Because of communication barriers, a lack of accessible information, and inadequate communication support, people with intellectual and other disabilities are frequently excluded from humanitarian assistance and mental health services, even when such services are available to others affected by the conflict. Human Rights Watch has documented lack of inclusive psychological support for people with disabilities in other armed conflicts, including Gaza and Sudan. Governments should address these gaps by integrating disability-inclusive mental health support during conflict and recovery, in line with their international obligations. Humanitarian agencies providing such services should also take steps to ensure that their programs are disability-inclusive and do not exclude people with disabilities. This could include providing accessible communication methods, such as pictograms and play therapy for children, training staff to provide disability-inclusive support, and equipping them with tactile regulation tools—like weighted lap pads, squeeze balls, and noise-canceling headphones—to help manage sensory overload. Accessible, inclusive mental health care and support are policies that cannot undo the trauma of war, but they can help create the conditions for recovery, inclusion, and hope for the future.

US Sanctions on ICC Put Global Justice at Risk. Click to expand Image Permanent premises of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the Netherlands. © 2019 Peter Dejong/AP (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC) is an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations, including in Afghanistan, Darfur in Sudan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Ukraine, and Venezuela. The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries, including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties, the European Union, UN human rights experts, the UN secretary-general, the UN high commissioner for human rights, civil society organizations, and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said.
