Among those detained were 13 members of a nature conservation organization who were later released, along with 14 others who had been under house arrest. The continuing criminal investigations and arrests of environmental protestors since 2023 have created a significant chilling effect on the rights to expression and assembly, protected under international human rights law and the Turkish constitution. Many have ended in decisions not to prosecute or acquittals, but investigations impose an immense burden on those targeted, as they last for years and require them to appear repeatedly before law enforcement agencies. A 75-year-old woman in Denizli, in western Türkiye, was fined in May 2024 when she refused to allow two mining company staff access to her property in a protest against coal mining. She was accused of beating the staff members, allegations she strenuously denies. The decision is under appeal. Police and gendarmes have prevented journalists and bystanders from filming environmental protests in the affected areas, in some cases using violence, and arrested and opened investigations against journalists covering the protests, media reported. Human Rights Watch has previously raised concerns with Turkish authorities that its efforts to expand coal mining and coal-fired power capacity in Türkiye pose serious risks to public health, environmental protection, and the protection of other human rights. The crackdown on environmental defenders is part of a wider attack on civic space in the country, Human Rights Watch said, including the detention of activists in Istanbul protesting an anti-LGBT crackdown on September 15, 2026. Some of them allege that they were ill-treated during the more than 24 hours they were arrested. Civil society participation is important for holding states to account for their environmental policies, Human Rights Watch said. It is also essential in contexts where decisions made by the central government can have serious local environmental impact. As host of COP31 in November, Türkiye has an obligation to facilitate the participation of civil society in the conference. “The Turkish government has ignored environmental protections and turned on local people who are speaking out against environmental damage to their communities,” Bayram said. “States attending COP31 should speak out against Türkiye’s crackdown on environmental defenders and remind their hosts that civil society participation is critical to achieving COP goals.” For additional details, please see below. Methodology In August 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 23 people who had been at environmental protests: 15 community members, 6 lawyers, and 2 journalists. Human Rights Watch documented investigations and prosecutions related to long-running environmental protests in Akbelen forest in Muğla, western Türkiye, between 2023 and 2026, and protests in the eastern Black Sea region in 2026, as well as investigations linked to those protests. Human Rights Watch also reviewed media reports, indictments, traffic penalties, and other administrative fines issued against protesters; court decisions, court-appointed expert reports relevant to the protests, and forensic medical reports; and photographs from protesters documenting their injuries. Human Rights Watch examined the judicial proceedings against protesters in four cases in İkizköy village, in the Milas district of Türkiye’s southwestern Muğla province, including relevant investigation documents and the decisions on conviction and acquittal, and assessed the laws used to prosecute them. Akbelen: Protests Banned Over Coal Mining in Forest, Olive Groves Click to expand Image Since 2023, local residents have been protesting forest clearance for coal mining, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye, August‎ ‎6‎, ‎2023. © 2023 Kazım Kızıl Since 2019, residents of İkizköy have been pursuing court cases to prevent the expansion of an open-pit lignite mine into Akbelen forest, the clearance of the legally protected forest, and the expropriation of nearby olive groves. The forest clearing case is pending while a court halted the expropriation of the olive groves. On July 17, 2021, after the Muğla Forestry Directorate cut down about 30 trees, community members began to monitor Akbelen forest for potential unlawful activity. On August 10, about 250 gendarmes intervened and arrested 11 protesters, including Füsun Ergün, who was forcibly removed after tying herself to an olive tree. Ergün and another environment defender, Gülören Demir, were convicted of resisting public officials and sentenced to 6 months and 20 days in prison, subsequently converted to fines. Click to expand Image During protests, the gendarmerie intervened with riot shields and water cannon against demonstrators, July, 28, 2026, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye. © 2026 Kazım Kızıl When the authorities resumed clearing the forest in July 2023, police used tear gas and water cannons against protesting villagers. The media reported that at least 40 people were arrested, including 14 later charged with resisting police officers. A broad coalition of civil society groups from across the country soon joined the protests. By August 2023, the authorities had cut down about three-fifths of the forest, despite the pending court case. Click to expand Image Despite pending court cases challenging the forest clearance and urgent expropriation, large areas of Akbelen Forest have already been cut down, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye, July 30, 2023. © 2023 Kazım Kızıl The government has prosecuted six community members for their participation or presence at various protests since 2023. Four were convicted for resisting public officials and are appealing. Two of them, Ahmet Tatar, 63, who faced multiple charges of resisting public officials, and an 85-year-old man accused of insulting the president, were acquitted. At least 55 others have been criminally investigated, 3 lawyers representing community members said. Many of the investigations have remained open for years. İsmail Atal, a lawyer who is himself the subject of two investigations, said that “keeping the investigations [open] for years leaves the threat of prosecution hanging over protesters like a Sword of Damocles, deterring them from taking part in further protests.” The Human Rights Watch review of the cases and interviews with those investigated suggests a pattern of intimidation aimed at discouraging protests. The authorities have arrested Tatar three times, and he said prosecutors had opened ten criminal investigations against him, most for allegedly resisting public officials or preventing them from performing their duties. Eight are ongoing, and two resulted in prosecutions both ending in acquittals. The prosecutor appealed the acquittals, and to date one acquittal has been upheld. “Of course I will continue to join protests,” Tatar said. “It is my moral obligation to humanity. But it is difficult and burdensome to deal with all these investigations.” Prosecutors have, however, failed to effectively investigate allegations against security officers for violations of protesters’ rights in Akbelen. On September 13, 2023, Tatar said, gendarmes broke his camera, struck him with their hands on his back and ankles, forced him face-down to the ground, pressed on his neck and back, cuffed his hands behind his back, and searched his tent. Tatar said he identified the gendarmes by name and filed complaints, supported by medical reports documenting his injuries, but the court dismissed his complaints. İpek Sarica, another lawyer, also filed a criminal complaint about violence she says she experienced during a protest in 2023. After a prosecutor declined to prosecute the case, Sarica appealed, but her complaint has remained unresolved for over three years. In a third case, Nejla Işık, the village head of İkizköy, filed a complaint alleging a violation of her right to privacy after a siginal jammer and a large number of gendarmes were deployed very close to her house. Prosecutors declined to open a case, which Işık’s lawyers challenged. The case is pending before the Constitutional Court. Güven Göknar, 66, from Muğla, said he intervened in a July 2023 protest against deforestation when gendarmes used pepper spray against protesters at close range. He was sentenced to five months in prison for allegedly resisting public officials, after footage showing him raising his hand was misinterpreted as showing him throwing a stone. He said he raised his hand to tell the gendarmes to stop; his appeal is pending. On March 30, 2026, Esra Işık, 26, was arrested during a protest against an expropriation order covering 649 land parcels in İkizköy. She spent 42 days in pretrial detention. On July 6, the Milas Criminal Court convicted her of “resisting officials” and sentenced her to two years and one month in prison, together with a suspended sentence for insulting public officials. Esra Işık’s lawyers have appealed. Another lawyer interviewed said that community members have been fined between 40,000 to 250,000 Turkish lira (about US$825 to $5,160) for acts including putting up tents and banners in connection with the Akbelen protests. People who have been fined and their lawyers said that in some cases fines were finalized without proper notification, with officials falsely recording that recipients had refused to accept notifications being served. As a result, some community members faced seizures of their bank accounts and property, while some were forced to pay. A lawyer said they had succeeded in having some fines cancelled, but not all of them. In 2023, prosecutors investigated 25 environmental activists in Edremit, on the north Aegean coast, for an unauthorized protest in solidarity with environment defenders in Akbelen. The case was later dropped. The authorities have also exerted pressure on lawyers representing the Akbelen community. Atal said that gendarmes arrested him on allegations of obstructing public officials as he traveled to the village on July 29, 2023, held him for several hours, and that he has been kept under investigation. Prosecutors opened a criminal investigation against Arif Ali Cangı, another lawyer, for allegedly inciting hatred and hostility among the public after he posted a social media post criticizing continued mining activity in Akbelen in the aftermath of the 2023 earthquake. The investigation remains open. The experience of journalists covering environmental protests suggests that the authorities open criminal investigations deliberately to interfere with their work. Prosecutors summoned a citizen journalist, Zeynep Kuray, on August 3, 2023, while she was reporting on the Akbelen protests. She then learned that the Milas Prosecution Office had opened an investigation against her for “spreading misleading information,” a criminal offense punishable with a prison term of one to three years, which eventually closed in 2024. Two other journalists arrested at their homes in İzmir in February 2024 said that police had questioned them about their presence at the Akbelen protests. Eastern Black Sea: Crackdown against Gold Mining Protests In Türkiye’s eastern Black Sea region, residents of the Perşembe Plateau have been protesting gold mining exploration since early 2026. The high plateau is in the northern part of Korgan-Aybastı districts, about 110 kilometers from Ordu, the provincial capital. The residents raise livestock for their livelihoods. The area designated for gold exploration is classified as pasture under Turkish law and requires specific permits to be mined. Türkiye’s Environment Ministry issued a permit in 2024. Human Rights Watch interviewed 11 residents who said they had been excluded from consultation and information about the project, which could potentially force them to relocate. They became aware of the project after it began affecting water they needed for livestock and household use, as well as from public statements by environmental groups. The community challenged the Environment Ministry’s permit. A court-assigned expert report dated June 15, 2026, warned that the project could disrupt the area’s hydrogeology, or groundwater flow, and that local water resources were critical to pastoral activities, livestock farming, and the community’s drinking and domestic water needs. Click to expand Image Local residents of Perşembe Plateau, together with the Ordu Environmental Organization, gathered to make a press statement opposing the gold exploration project, July 19, 2026, Korgan, Ordu. © 2026 Private The authorities fined the protesting community members in June and August in Giresun and Ordu provinces for hanging banners and issued traffic penalties for alleged “improper parking,” which residents believe was retaliation for protesting. On July 29, more than 50 residents protested drilling in Perşembe Plateau. Gendarmes arrested about 15 people. Human Rights Watch interviewed four men who were among at least 11 taken to the Tepealan gendarmerie station in Korgan, some handcuffed. They said they were held for about eight hours without being told why or whether they were under investigation, then released. One said gendarmes made some arrestees sign a document stating that they would not attend any further protests. The men said they have received no information since about any investigation or legal basis for their arrest. Leyla Acerce, 40, attended the protest with her husband and four children. She said that gendarmes formed a large circle, their shields pointing outwards, and pushed her into the circle, where she fainted. She was dragged and left sitting in a chair outside in heavy rain for hours. She was later transferred alone to Korgan State Hospital by ambulance. Acerce said she called the police from the hospital to report that she had been beaten by the gendarmes. The police came to the hospital. The hospital gave the police the medical report documenting her injuries but refused her a copy. Her husband, Ali Acerce, 47, said that when he tried to help his wife, three gendarmes handcuffed him, twisted his arm, and forced him into a container, where he was held for about two hours. He was then taken to the Tepealan gendarmerie station, where he was held for six hours and then released. He said that their 22-year-old son, İlyas, was also arrested for about six hours. Police made the family wait for hours when they went to the police station to file a complaint about their treatment by the gendarmes. They are not aware of any action on their complaint. Nuriye Dilek, 48, and another woman in her 50s who requested anonymity out of fear for her family, said four gendarmes dragged them from the protest and forced them into an unmarked white van. “They threw me into the van like a sack,” Dilek said.” I thought they would break our arms as they twisted them.” Human Rights Watch observed bruising on Dilek’s wrists and on the other woman’s chest and arms six days after the protest. Interviewees also said that they saw gendarmes drag two girls, both under 18, by their hair and put them into an unmarked van. Dilek said she saw gendarmes and plain clothes officers pointing out community members who had spoken out about defending the plateau in videos shared on social media. Musa Duman, 60, said that during questioning in a separate investigation, a prosecutor asked him about photos and videos he had shared online from the protests. Click to expand Image Gendarmerie block local residents from Perşembe Plateau from reaching the gold mining drilling site to stage a protest, July 16, 2026. © 2026 Private Residents said that after the protest, they faced a range of apparent retaliatory measures by the gendarmerie, including repeated identity checks in the small community where they had lived for years. If they did not carry identification, gendarmes photographed their faces at close range “as if we were criminals,” one resident said. Residents also reported verbal harassment and that following a solidarity protest on August 1, 17 traffic fines were issued to protesters and visitors for alleged improper parking or tinted windows. Local activists also said gendarmes used a signal jammer during the protest to disrupt communications, and Human Rights Watch reviewed photographs showing gendarmes carrying jamming equipment. Jammers were also used at other protests in Akbelen. An 84-year-old woman who had been arrested said she was now hesitant to appear in protest photos or videos after gendarmes contacted her sons, who live in other cities, and told them not to let their mother attend protests. Dilek also said that authorities had contacted her son. Dilek said that her husband, Halil Dilek, 53, and another man were arrested on suspicion of theft of materials related to mining operations and detained overnight at the Tepealan gendarmerie station. Halil Dilek said that he was distressed because his wife was travelling and that his teenage daughter was alone at home. He said that the prosecutor who questioned him the following day asked about his participation in the protests and photos he had shared on social media, raising concerns of surveillance and pressure over his environmental activism. On August 27, residents of Perşembe Plateau, including Duman and Nuriye Dilek, met with Ordu’s governor to discuss the project and the excessive use of force and violence by the gendarmerie. When Dilek said that gendarmes had beaten and dragged her and that her clothes had been torn open during the altercation, she said the governor asked what she was doing there in the first place. Duman said that on September 9, gendarmes summoned him to give a statement about his Facebook post criticizing the governor’s response. He was told he was suspected of publicly disseminating misleading information. The authorities have sought to suppress environmental protests in other areas of the eastern Black Sea designated for gold mining exploration. On April 5, residents of Görele and Tirebolu in Giresun province, east of Ordu, gathered to protest work at a gold mining project, despite a court order suspending the work. A large number of gendarmes confronted them, said a lawyer, Sevda Karataş, and the company complained the protesters had interfered with its “freedom to work.” Subsequently, Karataş, Ömer Cebeci, a municipal council member, and Nihal Nakıpoğlu, a local environmental association member, were summoned for questioning by the prosecutor. Karataş, who represents two community members from Tirebolu in Giresun, said that a prosecutor investigated her clients for alleged threats, disseminating misleading information, and interfering with the company’s “freedom to work.” The investigation remains open. Mesut Yilmaz, a 33-year-old local resident who actively posts about the protests on social media, said that police questioned him for about six hours about more than 100 pages of his social media posts. On June 2, he was fined, paying the maximum penalty of 115,000 lira (about $2,500) for putting up banners announcing a gold mining protest for May 29. The Right to Protest Under Human Rights Law The right to peaceful protest is protected under international human rights law, including under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR); Türkiye is party to both. The right to peaceful assembly is closely linked to the right to freedom of expression. While the rights to freedom of assembly and expression are not absolute and can be subject to restrictions, both the ECHR and ICCPR require that any restriction must be prescribed by law to pursue a legitimate aim and to be necessary and proportionate to that aim. Blanket bans on protests are disproportionate and unjustifiable. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, in its General Comment No. 37 (2020) stipulates that peaceful assemblies should not be criminalized, and that states must facilitate and protect such gatherings. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found that Turkish authorities’ use of powers under the Law on Meetings and Demonstrations (Law no. 2911) to ban or disperse protests and punish protestors violated the right of assembly. The right to peaceful protest is also protected under the article 34 of the Turkish constitution, which guarantees the right to organize peaceful, unarmed demonstrations and marches without prior permission.

India: End Crackdown on Protesters, Arbitrary Detentions. Click to expand Image Police detain protesters during a demonstration demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Manish Swarup (New York) – Indian authorities are using abusive methods to crack down on thousands of peaceful protesters in New Delhi and other Indian cities, Human Rights Watch said today. The protests, led by the Gen Z Cockroach Janta Party, opposition parties, student organizations, and civil society groups, have demanded the resignation of the country’s top election official over alleged wrongdoing and the scrapping of a contentious voter list revision process. As the protests grew in October 2026, the police have beat protesters, forcibly dragged them on the streets and stuffed them into vans and buses, arbitrarily detained them, imposed excessive restrictions on movement, and suspended mobile internet services. The authorities have also harassed and arbitrarily detained journalists covering the protests. “Police in Delhi are responding to peaceful protests with seemingly unnecessary or excessive force and have wrongfully detained thousands of people,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections.” Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration should stop the ill-treatment and arbitrary detention of protesters, allow people to protest peacefully, and restore mobile internet services and freedom of movement, Human Rights Watch said. Since June 2025, the Election Commission of India has carried out a nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to clean electoral rolls, ostensibly to remove any dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters. But the process, which has deleted more than 130 million names so far, has been arbitrary and opaque, prompting fears of mass disenfranchisement, and is disproportionately affecting Muslims and other religious minorities, women, and people living in poverty. Protest leaders and opposition parties allege that the commission has manipulated the lists to benefit Prime Minister Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The protests began on September 25, soon after the Indian Express published its investigation into alleged irregularities in the revision process. The newspaper found that the Election Commission’s two commissioners had raised multiple objections against decisions by the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Petitions challenging the revision process and seeking Kumar’s removal are before the Supreme Court. As protests in Delhi grew in October, security forces arbitrarily arrested and assaulted numerous protesters each day, and took them to undisclosed locations, later releasing many of them. Those detained included journalists and political opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers and Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition. When the protests began, Delhi Police released a set of “guidelines,” instructing journalists to “carry valid identity cards” that are “visibly displayed,” to “not obstruct police operations,” and to “maintain a reasonable and safe distance.” On October 11, the Supreme Court directed that lawyers and journalists “should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties.” On October 10 and 11, officials arbitrarily detained at least 30 journalists who were covering the protests. Four journalists’ organizations condemned the police actions, saying that journalists were “bundled into buses” used to detain protesters, and that police seized some of their phones and equipment. Three female journalists alleged that Delhi police officers sexually harassed them during the protests. A journalist from the magazine Caravan said that on October 11, police officers in Delhi hit him on the head several times, slapped him, and assaulted him with a rifle butt while he recorded them detaining a protester. “My press card was hanging by my neck but they still dragged me into the bus, ripping my shirt buttons,” a 31-year-old journalist told Human Rights Watch. Police detained him in a bus on October 10, and he was released only after the bus overheated and caught fire. “We could smell the fumes and had to shout at them to get us out,” he said. “The police personnel assaulted me and pinned me to the seat,” said John Brittas, a member of parliament participating in the protests, in a letter to the chief justice of India. The Cockroach Janta Party called for a protest on October 10 at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in Delhi. In response the authorities deployed over 40,000 security forces, canceled trains, shut down 43 metro stations, and suspended mobile internet services. Police took three Cockroach Janta Party leaders into custody aboard an airplane after it landed in Delhi, dragged several protesters from trains and buses who were traveling to Delhi, and put some youth leaders under house arrest. Air India has sought a response from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security on how security forces entered its aircraft without prior authorization. On October 9, a police officer entered a Delhi mosque during Friday prayers to warn Muslims against participating in any “unnecessary protests.” The next day, police officials entered a Sikh temple in central Delhi to detain protesters who sought refuge there. Citizens for Fraternity-Bharat (CFF-Bharat), a civil society group that includes former government officials, has questioned why police entered religious premises and called for an independent inquiry. On October 11, India’s Supreme Court directed the authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained, internet services are restored, and people and traffic are allowed to move freely, subject to lawful restrictions. Thus far, the authorities appear to have ignored the directions. A journalist, 26, told Human Rights Watch he witnessed at least three instances in which BJP supporters and police chased protesters together. “It is collaborative,” said the journalist, who covered the protests on October 10. “The police looked on and did not stop the violence.” A female journalist, 27, said a group of about five men, some of them wearing saffron scarves, were beating protesters and targeting female journalists. “They were shouting at us, mocking us, and showing us the middle finger,” she said. “I saw two policemen laughing while the right-wing goons were kicking and beating protesters.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concerns over the mass detention of demonstrators and said that the government should engage in meaningful dialogue. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs called the statement “unwarranted” and “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India.” The Indian government should publicly direct security forces to respond to protests in accordance with international standards, notably the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, Human Rights Watch said. “Indian authorities should allow people to protest peacefully by resuming transport services, removing unnecessary barricades, restoring the internet, and ensuring media freedom,” Pearson said. “Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold.”

Japan’s Commitment to Sport Needs to Include Athlete Protection. Click to expand Image Photo montage of the Tokyo Olympic Stadium and youth in Japan training and playing popular sports. © 2019 imagenavi/Aflo; 2005 Doable/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2015 Satoru Kobayashi/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2016 RYO/amanaimages; Trevor Williams/Getty Images; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2016 Matsuo/Aflo; AdobeStock Every October, Japan celebrates Sports Day, a public holiday established to commemorate the 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games and Japan's longstanding commitment to sport as a national priority. There has been much to celebrate in recent years. For more than six decades, Japan has had dedicated legislation – now known as the Basic Act on Sports – to advance sports on a national level. By investing in facilities, athletes’ development, and public participation—and hosting mega-events like the 2020 Olympics—Japan has become a leading sports nation. Yet, one critical issue has received too little attention: protecting athletes and children from sports-related abuse. Human Rights Watch has documented the widespread physical, sexual, and verbal abuse many Japanese children and athletes experience when they participate in sports. A professional athlete described suffering abuses from his coach: “I was hit so many times, I can’t count ... the coach … hit [me] in the face in front of everyone. I was bleeding, but he did not stop.” Under public pressure from athletes and survivors to reform, the Japanese parliament passed in 2025 amendments to the Basic Act on Sport requiring the national government to prevent abuse in sport. So far, however, the government has not adequately implemented the law—largely relying, instead, on individual sports federations and organizations to handle complaints of abuse. But, as Human Rights Watch has reported, athletes and children are often hesitant to report abuse to these institutions because they fear retaliation and because federations often protect their leaders rather than athletes. Reporting mechanisms also vary widely by sport, creating unequal access to protection. The Japan Sports Agency is now drafting the government's five-year blueprint for sports policy, which will be implemented in 2027. This plan should better address abuse in sport, including by establishing an independent Safe Sport Center to receive complaints, investigate abuse allegations, and support those who have been harmed. Sport Day should be an opportunity not only to celebrate Japan’s athletes but to make them safer. Japan’s government should ensure that everyone can participate in sport safely, without abuse, and can report harm through a trusted system.

France Shouldn’t Return Afghans to Taliban Rule. Click to expand Image Afghan refugees board a truck with their belongings as they await deportation at the Pakistan-Afghanistan border in Chaman on October 19, 2025. © 2025 Abdul Basil/AFP via Getty Images France has confirmed that it has opened a “technical dialogue” with the Taliban authorities regarding forced returns to Afghanistan. The announcement marks a dangerous shift in policy that places Afghans in France at risk of persecution, torture and other grave abuses in contravention of France’s international human rights obligations. The “technical dialogue” follows in the wake of a Taliban delegation to Brussels in June in which migration and return policies were discussed with European Union officials. Germany has already deported 263 Afghans since last year. The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the talks aim “to facilitate the removal of Afghan nationals who are illegally on the national territory and who represent a national security risk.” French officials say the dialogue is narrowly focused but have not set out any guarantees that those at particular risk, including women, would be protected. Since taking power in August 2021, the Taliban have issued decrees and enacted laws that have deprived Afghans of their fundamental rights. Women and girls are restricted from exercising their rights to education, freedom of movement, and expression. There is also compelling evidence that Taliban forces have detained and tortured people who have been forcibly returned to the country. French cooperation with the Taliban on a returns process would be with full knowledge of the Taliban’s responsibility for grave human rights violations and systematic oppression. Earlier this month, the International Criminal Court publicly announced the arrest warrants for Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and three other senior officials for the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and political grounds. The warrants, issued in 2025, relate to the persecution of women, girls, and people who do not conform to the Taliban’s expectations of gender, and the political persecution of those viewed as “allies of girls and women.” No country should be forcing refugees to return to Afghanistan so long as the Taliban continues to commit widespread human rights abuses. France should suspend any plan for deportations, and any cooperation on migration control should not be used as a vehicle for sending people back to a country where they would face a real risk of persecution or worse.

Saudi Arabia: Death Penalty for Facebook Comment. Click to expand Image Anojan Sivarasa. © Private (Beirut) – A Saudi court has sentenced a Sri Lankan migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that was deemed blasphemous, Human Rights Watch said today. Saudi authorities should reverse the judgment and release him immediately. The Saudi Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region handed down the death sentence to Anojan Sivarasa, 24, on September 17, 2026, after two court sessions. An initial ruling had sentenced him to five years in prison. “Sentencing a migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that he has publicly apologized for is an outrageous overreaction from Saudi authorities amid a surge in executions,” said Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “No one should face execution for a comment on religion.” On June 28, Sivarasa replied to a video circulating on Facebook with a comment in Tamil deemed offensive to the Prophet Muhammad by some viewers. The comment quickly gained attention, and a screenshot was apparently sent to Saudi authorities and Sivarasa’s employer, a family member of Sivarasa’s told Human Rights Watch. Sivarasa deleted the comment and uploaded an apology video to his Facebook account. Sivarasa’s employer held him in its office for at least 24 hours and then took him to the Dammam police station, where he was arrested on July 1, the family member said. Sivarasa was working in construction and had arrived in Saudi Arabia just 10 months earlier. He is the sole breadwinner for his family in Sri Lanka, the family member said. The Al-Ahsa Public Prosecution charged Sivarasa with “verbally insulting and offending our Prophet Muhammad” and “producing and disseminating, through the information network, material prejudicial to religious values and public morals, by publishing a comment on a social media program containing words contrary to religious values and public morals,” according to court documents obtained by Human Rights Watch. On July 27, the Criminal Court of Al-Ahsa issued a judgment convicting Sivarasa under article 6 of the Anti-Cyber Crime Law and sentenced him to five years in prison and a fine of 3 million Saudi riyals (about US$800,000), according to court documents. The court also ordered confiscation of his electronic device and closure of his Facebook account. The Al-Ahsa Public Prosecution filed an appeal of the initial judgment. Sivarasa’s lawyer also appealed the initial judgment and sentence. On September 17, Sivarasa informed his family that he had been sentenced to death, the family member said. Court documents reviewed by Human Rights Watch show that Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region found Sivarasa guilty of verbally insulting the Prophet Muhammad on a social media post and sentenced him to death. “We never expected this situation,” the family member said. “This is a funeral house. The family is shocked and they still are recovering from that state of shock.” On October 5, a prisoner attacked Sivarasa in detention with a small weapon, injuring his head and face. the family member said. He received medical attention and has been moved to a different cell. Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people over the last decade, in many cases violating Saudi and international law. Authorities executed at least 356 people in 2025, setting a new record in the country for the highest number of executions in one year since monitoring began. International human rights law, including the Arab Charter on Human Rights ratified by Saudi Arabia, obliges countries that use the death penalty to only do so for the “most serious crimes” and in exceptional circumstances. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all circumstances because of its inherent cruelty. “Saudi Arabia should immediately quash this sentence and release Sivarasa,” Shea said. “Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections.”

Vietnam: Free Abducted Democracy Group Activists. Click to expand Image Nguyen Duc Thuan (left) and Tran Hiep. © Private (Bangkok) – The Vietnamese authorities should immediately release three activists associated with the overseas Viet Tan organization who went missing in Cambodia, and drop all charges against them, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities should also grant Norwegian and Australian consular officials and family members immediate access to the detained men. The Vietnamese police claim that Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen; Tran Hiep (also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy), an Australian citizen; and Thai Cong Truong Son are members of the outlawed Viet Tan organization and attempted to use fake documents to cross the border from Cambodia to Vietnam on September 18, 2026. The men’s relatives say they never attempted to enter Vietnam. The police announced that they have charged the three men with “terrorism” under article 299 of the penal code for their association with Viet Tan and with forgery of seals and documents under article 341. Viet Tan is an overseas political organization that advocates for democratic change in Vietnam. It contends that the men were abducted in Cambodia. “The apparent abduction and detention of the foreign nationals raises many questions about the roles of both the Vietnamese and Cambodian governments,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Norwegian and Australian governments should press the Vietnamese authorities to grant them immediate access to their nationals and to drop baseless charges against them.” Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep flew to Phnom Penh on September 15 and were reportedly in regular contact with family members outside of Cambodia until the morning of September 18, after which neither could be reached. Both men missed other scheduled appointments in Cambodia and the flight they had booked to leave Cambodia on September 19; they have not been heard from since. Their luggage and other effects except phones and passports were found in their hotel rooms in Cambodia. Nguyen Duc Thuan requires daily insulin injections for diabetes and medical attention for kidney problems. As of October 11, neither the Australian nor Norwegian embassy had been granted access to the detained men. The Vietnamese police claimed that the three men crossed the border into Vietnam at Tay Ninh province, and that “Nguyen Duc Thuan was carrying two fake Vietnamese citizen identification cards” under a fake name and a Norwegian passport under his real name. They said that Ho Pham Hiep Huy “was carrying an Australian passport in the name of Tran Hiep.” The police statement does not describe Thai Cong Truong Son’s identification. On October 7, Cambodia’s Ministry of Interior issued a statement saying it had confirmed that Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep had entered Cambodia but had not recorded their exit. And said it “categorically” denied any involvement in handing over the men to the Vietnamese authorities. In the 1980s, Viet Tan had engaged in armed resistance against Vietnam’s communist government. Viet Tan relaunched in 2004 as a political party committed to nonviolent change, but the Vietnamese authorities have arrested and imprisoned Viet Tan members. In 2016, Vietnam officially labeled Viet Tan a “terrorist group.” In 2019, an Australian member of Viet Tan, Chau Van Kham, and his colleagues Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen were arrested in Vietnam and sentenced to 12, 11, and 10 years, respectively, for their involvement with Viet Tan on terrorism-related charges. Their trial lasted only 4.5 hours, suggesting that the verdict was pre-determined. The activities listed in the government’s charges against Chau Van Kham and attributed to Viet Tan, such as making travel arrangements to Vietnam, organizing leaflets for protests, expanding the Viet Tan’s network, writing articles, and sending people abroad for IT training, do not constitute acts of terrorism. In 2022, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued an opinion stating that “the deprivation of liberty of [Viet Tan member] Chau Van Kham … is arbitrary.” Vietnam released Chau Van Kham in July 2023 and repatriated him to Australia. His Vietnamese fellow activists Nguyen Van Vien and Tran Van Quyen are still serving long prison sentences. In 2018, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Quoc Binh in Binh Dinh province and accused him of participating in Viet Tan and smuggling weapons from Cambodia into Vietnam to “carry out terrorist activities.” Viet Tan rejected the accusation, calling it “a ridiculous fabrication.” The then-public security minister and current Vietnamese president, To Lam, praised the police for arresting Le Quoc Binh. Later accounts in government media of his trial and conviction on charges of terrorism and illegal possession of weapons dropped all mention of Viet Tan. In May 2026, the Vietnamese police arrested Le Thanh Son and Nguyen Thanh Hung in Dong Thap province for their alleged affiliation with Viet Tan and charged them with “carrying out activities that aim to overthrow the people’s administration” under article 109 of the penal code. Also in May, the police reportedly detained, interrogated and beat a former political prisoner, Huynh Truong Ca, and forced him to admit that he was a member of Viet Tan, which he denied. After Huynh Truong Ca fled, police detained his family members, interrogated them on his whereabouts, and intimidated and pressured them to denounce him. In recent years, the Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression—government efforts to silence dissent by targeting dissidents and critics outside their territory. They have pressured other governments, including Thailand and Cambodia, to return Vietnamese citizens who fled Vietnam out of fear of arbitrary arrest, torture, or imprisonment. Vietnamese security forces have abducted Vietnamese citizens in Germany and Thailand, including Trinh Xuan Thanh, Truong Duy Nhat, and Duong Van Thai. In the past year, courts in Vietnam put on trial in absentia Vietnamese nationals who live overseas, convicting and sentencing them to long prison terms, including Le Trung Khoa, Nguyen Van Dai, Doan Bao Chau, Dinh Yum, Siu Di, and Dang Thi Hue. Since the trials, the police have issued numerous warnings and fined Vietnamese citizens for interacting with those convicted in absentia. Activists from Vietnam and Thailand have been forcibly disappeared in Cambodia in cases of suspected transnational repression. “Campaigning for democracy and pluralism is not a crime,” Pearson said. “The Vietnamese government should release Nguyen Duc Thuan, Tran Hiep, and Thai Cong Truong Son and end its practice of transnational repression.”

Libya: Eastern Authorities Carry Out Wave of Executions. Click to expand Image Military leader of Eastern Libya, Khalifa Haftar (center), attends a conference in Sabha, Libya, September 5, 2024. © 2024 Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Photo (Beirut) – The Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), which controls eastern and southern Libya, has executed at least 31 people since late August 2026 following grossly unfair military trials, Human Rights Watch said today. These are the first known executions in Libya since 2010, with at least 50 more people in Gernada military prison at imminent risk of execution. On August 23, the LAAF military prosecutor announced that 10 people had been executed by firing squad after being convicted of murder and terrorism-related offenses. Human rights groups have documented a total of at least 31 executions as of September 10. The LAAF, led by General Khalifa Haftar, should immediately halt all executions and impose a moratorium on the death penalty, Human Rights Watch said. “The Libyan Arab Armed Forces are putting people to death after secret trials built on confessions allegedly extracted through torture, in courts that Libya’s own Supreme Court has said should not be trying civilians,” said Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “Every execution carried out under these conditions is an irreversible injustice and every government with influence over the LAAF should be pressing hard to stop the next one.” Many of those executed had been arrested in the cities of Derna and Benghazi during or after the armed conflict between the LAAF and opposing armed groups between 2014 and 2018. Between 2018 and 2021, military courts in eastern Libya convicted hundreds of civilians in secret trials targeting real or perceived critics of the LAAF, sentencing at least 22 to death. According to Amnesty International, many of the sentences were based on confessions allegedly extracted under torture by the Internal Security Agency, an LAAF-affiliated armed group. At least two death sentences were reduced to life in prison on appeal by a higher military court in 2019, yet the defendants were put to death this year regardless. The executions also went ahead despite a November 2025 ruling by the constitutional chamber of Libya’s Supreme Court that Law No. 4/2017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants military courts jurisdiction to try civilians for terrorism and crimes against the state. Local human rights groups said that the military trials violated defendants’ due process rights. They were held in secret and without prior notice. Defendants’ families, journalists, and human rights organizations were not allowed to attend. Several defendants were denied lawyers of their choice and those who did have their own lawyers were refused visits before and during trial and could not speak with them privately. They were apparently not allowed to present their cases in court or examine the evidence against them. The verdicts were handed down without providing the defendants or their attorneys with written and reasoned judgments. Trying civilians in military courts is incompatible with the right to a fair trial under human rights law and such trials violate the right to be tried before an independent and impartial tribunal. In Libya, military prosecutors are often not qualified to investigate civilians and they lack independence. The military prosecutors and judges in eastern Libya are themselves affiliated with the LAAF or allied armed groups. Families of defendants were not notified in advance that the executions would take place. The authorities refused to hand over the bodies of those executed, asked relatives to confirm the identities of the dead, then buried them without families present and warned relatives not to hold funerals. Secret executions and denying families a last visit violate international law, including by inflicting severe mental suffering on those executed and their relatives in breach of the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. Libya remains split between two rival authorities. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU), which is internationally recognized, controls the west, alongside affiliated security agencies and armed groups. The LAAF and affiliated forces and militias control the east and south. Both sides operate with near-total impunity. The United Nations and the GNU condemned the executions. Governments that fund, train, and legitimize the LAAF have real leverage, and a responsibility to use it, publicly and privately, to press LAAF leaders to halt all executions, Human Rights Watch said. Libya’s justice sector is fragmented and deeply polarized. Human Rights Watch has previously documented outdated and repressive legislation, a lack of fair trial rights, and rampant due process violations. Unaccountable militias control prisons that are only nominally under state ministries. Libyan authorities in both the east and west should restrict the jurisdiction of military courts to military offenses committed by military personnel and stop trying civilians in military courts altogether. They should promptly review all cases of civilians wrongfully detained and prosecuted before military courts and provide effective remedies, including release, transfer to civilian courts, or retrial in line with international fair trial standards, with acknowledgment of time served. Human Rights Watch opposes the death penalty in all countries and under all circumstances because it is inherently inhumane, uniquely cruel and irreversible, and universally plagued by arbitrariness, prejudice, and error. Ninety-two countries have ratified a protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights that requires the abolition of the death penalty, recognizing that capital punishment violates the right to life and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman, or degrading punishment. Libya should abolish the death penalty and until then enact a moratorium on all executions. “Libya went more than 15 years without an execution, and the LAAF has shattered that moratorium in a matter of weeks,” Khawaja said. “The lives of at least 50 more people now depend on whether Haftar’s forces, and the governments that back them, choose to stop this.”

European Governments Fall Short on Reparatory Justice. Click to expand Image Secretary-General António Guterres addresses the 55th session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland, February 26, 2024. © 2024 Elma Okic/UN Photo A United Nations Human Rights Council resolution on October 7 calling for concrete action against systemic racism should have been an opportunity for governments to demonstrate their commitment to racial justice. Instead, the United Kingdom called for a vote, breaking from last year’s consensus on the annually tabled resolution. Citing concerns about the applicability of international law to establish responsibility and accountability for colonial harm, the UK objected to language on reparations and then abstained from the vote; European Union members of the Council also abstained. Regardless, the resolution passed with 30 votes in favor, 17 abstentions, and none against. The loss of last year’s consensus reveals the gap between the UK and other European governments’ stated dedication to combat racism and their actual political willingness to address its historical roots. European governments have present-day obligations to tackle racial discrimination and provide effective remedies. The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination requires states, including the UK, to ensure just and adequate reparation for harm resulting from racial discrimination. The experts who monitor this treaty earlier this year set out clear legal guidance on states’ obligations for such reparation. Enslavement and colonialism helped establish racial inequalities, the consequences of which persist today. Human Rights Watch has documented systemic racism, including racial profiling and barriers to economic and social rights in Europe. Reparatory justice is essential to confronting these enduring harms. Jamaica’s pursuit of an advisory opinion from the Judicial Committee of the UK’s Privy Council underscores the importance of examining governments’ legal arguments. Its petition asks whether the enslavement of Africans was lawful under English and international law, and whether the UK owes a reparatory remedy. Next month’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda offers another opportunity to change course. King Charles’s forthcoming Caribbean visit will, apparently, include an acknowledgement of Britain’s involvement in enslavement, although Buckingham Palace says decisions on reparations and formal apologies rest with the UK government. The UK and other European governments should engage meaningfully with African and Caribbean initiatives and affected communities to develop reparatory measures for the harms they were and are responsible for. These measures can include, according to UN principles, compensation, restitution, rehabilitation, acknowledgment of wrongdoing and reforms to prevent recurrence. Affected communities should shape the process and its outcomes. The United Nations Human Rights Council resolution calls on governments to move “from rhetoric to reality.” Those that are serious about ending systemic racism should embrace reparatory justice as part of that work.

French High School Student Protests Met with Excessive Force. Click to expand Image Students raise their hands in front of police officers as they demonstrate outside Sciences Po during a protest over school overcrowding and decay in Paris, France, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Tom Nicholson/Getty Images Images from ongoing student protests in France of heavily armed riot police using tear gas, stun grenades, batons, rubber bullets, and rough restraint techniques on children have sparked national and international concern. High schoolers across France have taken to the streets since September 21 frustrated with the government’s continued under-investment in their education, which has resulted in a shortage of teachers, too large classes, and inadequate school buildings. While schools have been blockaded and some protesters have engaged in violence, the protests have been overwhelmingly peaceful. Police use of force in response to the protests has resulted in serious injuries to children, including a 15-year-old boy who lost a hand to an explosive police stun grenade and a 14-year-old boy whose jaw shattered from a police tear-gas canister fired at close range. The government announced a temporary suspension of the use of stun grenades. Police have reportedly detained more than 6,800 people since the demonstrations started; with apparently 86 percent of them, children. Authorities have also reportedly opened 36 internal investigations into allegations of police misconduct. But internal reviews in France rarely translate into real accountability. Police use of excessive force during protests is not new in France. Human Rights Watch documented severe injuries caused by police during the 2018 “Yellow Vest” movement. And 2023’s pension reform protests and environmental demonstrations were also marked by such use of force. The current student protests began in schools in working-class neighborhoods, where racialized young people constantly experience and fear police harassment and state violence. Instead of addressing persistent problems with police using excessive force, the government is seeking to strengthen law enforcement’s right to use force. Under consideration since early 2026, a bill proposes to grant officers a “presumption of legality” when using their firearms. Rights groups warn the changes risk lowering the threshold for police to resort to use of firearms and shielding police from judicial scrutiny. French authorities should stop treating peacefully protesting children as a danger that needs to be neutralized. Instead, the government should uphold its obligations to protect children and their right to protest and listen to the demands of young people on the streets. To restore trust, the government should also thoroughly and promptly investigate all incidents of police use of force and end police tactics and reform the powers that foster police violence.

Kazakhstan Women Need Action on Domestic Violence. Click to expand Image Participants at the international Women's Day rally in Almaty, Kazakhstan, March 8, 2022. © 2022 Stanislav Beketov During its October 6 review by the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), Kazakhstan pledged new legislation to make domestic violence a standalone crime – a timely commitment. Now the government should turn words into action. On September 23, Zhazira Adauova, a mother of two, died after her ex-husband stabbed her 16 times in Astana, Kazakhstan’s capital. Zhazira’s family told the media she had repeatedly reported threats and violence to police. Four former police officers are under investigation for alleged negligence in handling her case. Elvira Erkebayeva, from western Kazakhstan, endured two decades of domestic violence, including having boiling water thrown in her face. Instead of protecting her and holding her former husband accountable, authorities prosecuted Elvira in 2025 for allegedly conspiring to murder him because she wanted to “find a firearm.” As in manyother cases, Kazakh authorities failed to protect women who sought protection against further violence, even when they had obtained multiple protection orders. Perpetrators are often held accountable only after killing their victims. Kazakhstan no longer has a dedicated law on domestic violence, and the latest reforms still did not establish domestic violence as a standalone criminal offense. The 2009 Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence was repealed by the Law on Prevention of Offences, which entered into force in March addresses domestic violence within a broader prevention framework. The Kazakh delegation claimed during its CEDAW review that “enforcing zero tolerance for violence had become … the cornerstone of ongoing reforms,” and that in 2024 Kazakhstan had “intensified legal accountability for domestic … violence.” Yet CEDAW experts rightly questioned the effectiveness of existing measures, and the Committee’s Rapporteur for Kazakhstan underscored that domestic violence is still not a standalone criminal offence. Under CEDAW and the Committee’s General Recommendation No. 35, states must prevent, investigate, prosecute, and ensure accountability for gender-based violence. Kazakhstan should adopt reforms to make domestic violence a standalone offence, strengthen and improve enforcement of the protection order mechanism, ensure interventions are effective and perpetrators held accountable, and guarantee survivors’ access to justice and services. Kazakhstan’s international partners should press for these reforms. Accountability after a woman is dead is no substitute for timely protection and prevention. Kazakh authorities need to ensure that women in Kazakhstan receive meaningful protection and assistance before violence escalates or turns fatal.

World News in Brief: Russian attacks continue in Ukraine, Gazans shelter in flood-prone areas, keeping sight of eye health. UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Thursday he was appalled by a wave of attacks that have killed civilians across Ukraine over the past four days.

World News in Brief: ‘Horrific’ attack in Sudan, Israeli incursions in Syria intensify, most women and girls homeless in Gaza. A suspected drone strike has left at least 40 dead in Sudan’s Blue Nile State – near the Ethiopian border - according to initial reports from the ground, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric. Most of the casualties were women and girls.

Global trade reaches record $35 trillion despite conflicts. World trade reached a record $35 trillion in 2025 – but developing countries were held back from greater participation in the global economy because of new technological and policy barriers, the UN trade and development agency UNCTAD said on Friday.

Livestreaming US execution would breach prohibition of torture, UN rights office warns. The UN human rights office (OHCHR) on Friday warned that livestreaming a planned execution by firing squad in the United States would amount to a public execution and breach the absolute prohibition on torture.

Security Council LIVE: Cycle of escalating attacks on civilians in Ukraine ‘must end now’. Escalating violence and human rights violations in the four-year-old Russia-Ukraine war are in the spotlight in the Security Council on Friday following a spate of Russian attacks against civilian targets and infrastructure in recent days.

‘Serious blow’: Guterres condemns new US sanctions on International Criminal Court. The United States has imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing on Friday to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick” unless it ends what Washington regards as a “threat” to its citizens.

Amid heartache of Nepal flooding disaster, fear remains. Six weeks after Nepal’s deadly flooding disaster, communities are still struggling to rebuild their lives, but they will need sustained help as global warming increases the risk of another Himalayan catastrophe, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday.

Security Council LIVE: Yemen has fallen back into full-scale war, warns UN envoy. The Security Council met to discuss the crisis in Yemen Friday, where a Houthi offensive launched in September has sharply escalated the 12-year-long war for control of the country and spillover from the US-Iran war has provoked a new displacement crisis. Live coverage below and for full meetings updates, go here.

Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize. South African jurist and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay was on Friday announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

Giving a dam: Cultivating peace in Côte d’Ivoire. Adam Ouattara and Makongo Traoré have four children and a home on the edge of Torla village in Côte d’Ivoire. He herds cattle. She grows vegetables on a small plot nearby. For years, the dry season pitted their two livelihoods against each other.

India: UN rights office urges release of ‘arbitrarily detained’ protesters. The UN human rights office (OHCHR) has voiced concern over reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists, before and during large-scale protests in Delhi on Saturday.

In the Mekong Delta, a push to grow food with saltwater. For generations, farming in Viet Nam’s Mekong Delta has depended on a delicate bargain. The river flooded, retreated and flooded again, carrying freshwater and sediment across a flat landscape whose vast fields helped turn the country into one of the world’s leading rice exporters.

UN chief ‘gravely concerned’ by renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, warns against escalation. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has called for an immediate end to the renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, saying he is deeply worried by reports that Eritrean forces are present in the country.

Djibouti shipwreck: Death toll rises to 139 as 84 remain missing. At least 139 migrants have died after their boat capsized off Djibouti, with a further 84 people still missing, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Sunday.

Sustaining livelihoods amid crisis in Gaza. Nidaa, Hanaa and Hanin have different stories, but share a common thread: the determination to build something of their own and keep it going despite extraordinary challenges facing them in war-ravaged Gaza.

‘These attacks must cease immediately’: Guterres condemns deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has condemned a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s main airport that Saudi authorities say killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.

General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, but not by consensus. The General Assembly on Monday adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, by 153 in favour to three against (Argentina, Israel and United States) with two abstentions (New Zealand and Paraguay).

Colombia peace deal must endure as insecurity grows, Security Council hears. Nearly 10 years after Colombia signed a historic peace agreement to end a decades-long insurgency, the deal is under strain from growing insecurity – and the UN’s top official in the country says it cannot be allowed to falter.

Security Council LIVE: Syria’s fragile transition – economic strain, Israeli incursions and progress towards elections. The Security Council met to debate Syria's thorny transition Monday as it faces pressure on several fronts. Economic hardship is fuelling unrest, Israeli incursions continue in the south and sectarian tensions persist in Sweida, even as Damascus reports progress on its chemical weapons programme and talks about future elections. Millions, meanwhile, remain displaced. Follow live below and go here for full meetings coverage.

Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine. The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan already torn apart by war, as a severe El Niño drought makes life even harder in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the UN-backed global hunger monitor warned on Monday.

UN aid operation underway in Nepal following fresh floods. The United Nations has rushed to assist Nepal following new flash floods in the central Gorkha district on Sunday that swept away homes and bridges just weeks after catastrophic flooding in the north.

‘Efficiency has limits’: UNHCR chief warns refugee protection is buckling under cuts. The money is running out faster than needs are growing: with 117 million men, women and children now forced from their homes, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) has received just $3 billion of the $8.5 billion it needs this year – and its chief, Barham Salih, warns that the global support system for asylum-seekers risks buckling.

Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says. The number of people living in “multidimensional” poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.

Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs. Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.

800 million young people face a future without jobs. Approximately 800 million young people entering the labour market in developing economies over the coming years will not find jobs unless countries act, the head of the UN Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Tuesday, as the agency launched two initiatives to boost investment and employment.

World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update. Fewer people from West Africa are reaching Europe by sea, but the journey has not become safer, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Tuesday.

CALABRIA: SALVIAMO LO SCOGLIO DEL DELFINO. L'iniziativa è stata promossa dalle varie associazioni nazionali e internazionali affinché l'erosione calcarea e la stupidità d alcuni turisti non rovini questa meravigliosa forma d'arte scultorea che Madre Natura ci ha regalato. ORIGI, MESSIAS, ADLI E 25 MILIONI PER MILINKOVIC-SAVIC. LOTITO NE CHIEDE 35!!!. Il Milan, dopo lo scioccante siluramento di Paolo Maldini, punta al grande colpo per il calciomercato estivo: Sergej Milinkovic-Savic della Lazio . Lo ha riferito ' SportMediaset '. Il Diavolo, dunque, ha intenzione di andare all'assalto del centrocampista serbo, classe 1995 , che gioca nella Capitale dal 2015 e che ora sembra arrivato al momento dei saluti. Nonostante il contratto di Milinkovic-Savic scadrà tra un anno, il 30 giugno 2024 , il Presidente della Lazio, Claudio Lotito , continua a valutarlo molto. Si parla di 35-40 milioni di euro, per un giocatore che, in fin dei conti, in questa stagione con le Aquile di Maurizio Sarri si è riconfermato come uno dei centrocampisti più forti e completi del panorama calcistico mondiale. Motivo per cui il Milan, pur di metterlo a disposizione di Stefano Pioli in questo calciomercato estivo, sarebbe pronto ad offrire alla Lazio 25 milioni più ben tre contropartite tecniche individuati in Junior Messias , Divock Origi e Yacine Adli. Le contropartite tecniche sarebbero di gradimento per Mister Sarri e si adatterebbero facilmente al suo gioco spettacolare: Adli può ricoprire diversi ruoli del centrocampo e sarebbe un sostituto ideale del capitano biancoazzurro; Messias , visto il flop di Romero e l'età avanzata di Pedro, sarebbe un'ottima alternativa di fascia visto i tanti impegni che aspettano la Lazio; Origi sarebbe una discreta opzione a Ciro Immobile, lasciando crescere con tranquillità il talentuoso Cancellieri. La palla passa a Lotito che attende un rialzo di offerta magari intorno ai 30 milioni e l'inserimento di tre contropartite tecniche di buon livello per concludere l'affare.

Tra le questioni affrontate anche quella dell’interruzione della partita e del 3-0 a tavolino, provvedimenti su cui l’arbitro Del Cerro Grande, da norma, non può nulla. Tra i casi in cui i club devono rispondere delle azioni della tifoseria c’è anche “il lancio di oggetti che possa mettere in pericolo l’integrità fisica di altri presenti alla partita o pregiudicarne lo svolgimento”. Il paradosso è che Biraghi, per sperare in un 3-0 a tavolino, avrebbe dovuto accentuare il dolore e farsi sostituire, invece è stato “colpevole” di essersi grintosamente rialzato. Per dare un’idea del modo in cui viene messo in pratica il regolamento, prendiamo in esame un caso simile: il famoso petardo in testa a Dida nel derby di Milano del 2004-2005. In quel caso le autorità capiscono che la situazione non può avere seguito e inoltre il brasiliano resta a terra. Per questo motivo, viene assegnato il 3-0 a tavolino ai rossoneri. In sostanza, il West Ham al momento rischia solo una pesante sanzione pecuniaria e la squalifica del campo nella prossima edizione dell’Europa League. Un caso simile, alla Fiorentina , è capitato nella stessa competizione contro il Sivasspor, in Turchia. Alessandro Bianco riceve un pugno in faccia da un invasore di campo della squadra di casa. Il calciatore rimedia la frattura del setto nasale. Per i turchi è arrivata una dura sanzione, più l’impossibilità di andare allo stadio per una giornata per i tifosi.

LAGIORNATA MONDIALE DELLE TARTARUGHE MARINE. Sono già una dozzina i nidi censiti dal network tartarughe marine del WWF in Sicilia (proprio in queste ore sono in corso le operazioni di verifica e messa in sicurezza degli ultimi), e uno in Calabria. Il Mediterraneo, sebbene rappresenti solo una piccola percentuale della superficie totale degli oceani, lo 0.82%, ospita una straordinaria varietà di vita marina. Con oltre 17.000 specie diverse, questa regione è un importante hotspot di biodiversità marina. E tra questa vasta varietà di specie, le tartarughe marine occupano un posto speciale. Nel Mediterraneo, tre specie di tartarughe marine hanno fatto di queste acque la loro casa: la tartaruga comune (Caretta caretta, l’unica che vi si riproduce), la tartaruga verde (Chelonia mydas) e la tartaruga liuto (Dermochelys coriacea). Le tartarughe marine trascorrono la maggior parte della loro vita in mare, ma, come altri rettili, respirano aria tramite i polmoni. La deposizione delle uova è l’unica fase vitale che avviene sulla terraferma, di solito tra maggio e agosto nel Mediterraneo. Dopo l’accoppiamento, le femmine raggiungono la spiaggia per deporre le uova, che vengono incubate dal calore del sole (e del suolo) per circa due mesi. La temperatura influisce anche sul sesso delle tartarughe neonate: temperature superiori a 29°C tendono a produrre femmine, mentre temperature inferiori generano maschi. Dopo la deposizione delle uova, le femmine ritornano alle loro zone di alimentazione, che possono trovarsi anche a migliaia di chilometri di distanza dalle zone di riproduzione. Una volta raggiunta la maturità sessuale, intorno ai 20-30 anni, le tartarughe ritornano alle stesse aree di riproduzione per deporre le uova. La loro capacità di orientarsi durante queste lunghe migrazioni è influenzata dall’incredibile abilità di percepire il campo geomagnetico terrestre, una sorta di sesto senso di queste antichissime specie. L’impatto dei cambiamenti climatici. L’aumento delle temperature globali influisce direttamente sull’habitat di queste creature e sulle risorse di cui dipendono per la loro sopravvivenza, oltre che sulle correnti. Uno degli effetti più evidenti è l’aumento della temperatura dell’acqua. Le tartarughe marine sono specie ectotermiche, il che significa che la loro temperatura corporea dipende dall’ambiente circostante. Con l’aumento delle temperature marine, le tartarughe possono trovarsi in situazioni di stress termico, poiché non sono in grado di regolare la propria temperatura interna. Questo può influire sul loro metabolismo, sulla loro capacità di digerire il cibo e sull’efficienza riproduttiva.

BONUS VACANZE: SCADENZA DELLE DOMANDE IL 30 GIUGNO. La procedura per la richiesta del Bonus vacanze va effettuata solamente online tramite la app “Io” da smartphone. Basta munirsi di Spid o della carta d’identità elettronica. Lo possono richiedere soltanto i nuclei familiari con un reddito Isee sotto i 40.000 euro e può essere speso solo per un soggiorno in Italia entro la fine dell’anno. Una volta ottenuto il Bonus, la prenotazione della vacanza non può essere effettuata su siti online: quindi non è possibile prenotare né con Booking né con Airbnb o con altri siti di prenotazione. Bisogna, invece, prenotare tramite agenzie viaggi o o tour operator tradizionali o direttamente con la struttura scelta nella meta di villeggiatura. Ecco gli step per fare la richiesta del Bonus vacanze: se non si è già scaricata la app “Io” in passato sul proprio smartphone è possibile farlo sia per telefoni Apple sia per Android; la prima volta che si scarica la app viene richiesta la registrazione che è possibile fare più facilmente digitando un Pin a scelta o, per chi è più pratico, attraverso il riconoscimento biometrico (impronta digitale o riconoscimento del volto); una volta entrati nella app, bisogna selezionare la sezione “pagamenti” e quindi il Bonus vacanze; a questo punto è necessario inserire le informazioni richieste, tra cui il valore dell’Isee; se tutte le informazioni inserite sono corrette, la app genera un codice associato al vostro Bonus vacanze con un QrCode; sia il codice sia il QrCode devono essere mostrati alla struttura al momento del pagamento. N.B. Prima di effettuare la richiesta del Bonus vacanze è bene tenere sotto mano sia la propria identità Spid sia la carta d’identità elettronica e i dati del proprio Isee (chi non lo ricorda può recuperarlo all’Inps o al proprio Caf). Il Bonus di un valore massimo di 500 euro è rivolto alle famiglie italiane composte da almeno tre persone. Per i nuclei familiari composti da due persone il Bonus vacanze scende a 300 euro, ma lo possono ottenere anche i single, in questo caso il valore è di 150 euro.

"È una rettiliana": come una donazione da 6,5 miliardi si è trasformata in un caso di cyberbullismo. Susan e Michael Dell, fondatore e amministratore delegato di Dell Technologies, hanno destinato 6,25 miliardi di dollari ai conti d’investimento per l’infanzia introdotti dall’amministrazione Trump: 250 dollari per 25 milioni di bambini fino a dieci anni, residenti nelle aree americane a reddito medio-basso ed esclusi dal contributo federale riservato ai nuovi nati. Durante l’intervento nello Studio Ovale, Susan Dell, filantropa e cofondatrice della Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, ha invitato genitori e nonni ad attivare i conti.Sui social, però, l’attenzione si è rapidamente spostata dalla donazione al suo aspetto. Su TikTok, Threads, Facebook e X sono comparsi insulti, ipotesi non confermate sulla chirurgia estetica e teorie complottiste secondo cui quella ripresa alla Casa Bianca non sarebbe stata la vera Susan Dell, ma un clone, un robot o persino un “glitch della simulazione”. Movimenti degli occhi, espressioni e posture estrapolati da brevi clip sono stati usati per paragonarla anche a un’aliena, uno skinwalker o un rettiliano. Non esiste alcun elemento a sostegno di queste fantasie, mentre Dell non ha mai confermato di essersi sottoposta agli interventi estetici ipotizzati online. Un caso che mostra come persino una delle più grandi donazioni private mai rivolte ai bambini americani possa essere oscurata dal body shaming e dal cyberbullismo.

Navi Pillay, il Nobel per la Pace e una lezione sul coraggio. «Perché mai ci vorrebbe coraggio per dire la verità?». Se lo domanda Navi Pillay, la giurista sudafricana che ha vinto il Nobel per la Pace 2026. Cresciuta in una famiglia di origine tamil durante l'apartheid, da bambina non poteva nemmeno andare in spiaggia per il colore della sua pelle. Grazie a una colletta del quartiere riuscì a studiare legge e, quando nessuno volle assumerla, aprì uno studio tutto suo. Da allora ha difeso gli oppositori del regime sudafricano, contribuito a una sentenza storica sugli stupri durante il genocidio in Ruanda e presieduto la commissione ONU che ha accusato Israele di genocidio a Gaza. La sua storia, raccontata in questa puntata, attraversa anche quella del diritto internazionale, oggi sotto attacco da più fronti. Proprio nel giorno del Nobel, l'amministrazione Trump ha annunciato nuove sanzioni contro la Corte penale internazionale, di cui Pillay è stata giudice. Passeggero precipita dalle montagne russe: l'evacuazione dei passeggeri vista dall'alto. Un uomo è precipitato dalle montagne russe del parco divertimenti Six Flags Over in Georgia; secondo le prime ricostruzioni l'incidente sarebbe avvenuto nel tratto in corrispondenza della zona in cui vengono scattate le foto ricordo. Stando alle prime testimonianze il sedile o il sistema di ritenuta dell'uomo si sarebbe sbloccato. Le immagini aeree mostrano il personale del Six Flags Over Georgia aiutare i passeggeri rimasti bloccati sul Goliath - nome della montagna russa in questione - a scendere lungo le scale di servizio. L'altezza massima dell'attrazione, stando al sito web, è di 60 metri, e le carrozze viaggiano a una velocità che raggiunge i 112 chilometri all'ora. Secondo il sito web di Six Flag, gli standard di sicurezza per le montagne russe Goliath si basano su rigidi protocolli che prevedono sistemi di ritenuta (un sistema di barre di protezione cosciali individuali e imbracatura che scendono dalle spalle) e un programma di sicurezza multilivello che prevede controlli quotidiani, verifiche degli operatori prima di ogni partenza e regolari ispezioni di parti terze.

"Finisce una storia durata vent'anni. Raccolgo i ricordi che mi hanno accompagnato in circa 500 puntate di Report". Scrive il giornalista. "L'avevo messo in conto e ho sempre cercato di immaginare come sarebbe andata: mi sono figurato tanti scenari, ma mai avrei pensato a modalità così mostruose. Tuttavia non rimpiango nulla di quello che ho fatto. Rifarei tutto, perché ho scelto di difendere dei principi, ho scelto di non piegare la schiena davanti a nessuno, neppure davanti alle mie paure o incertezze, anche quando mi sarebbe stato più comodo, e mi avrebbe portato delle utilità", ha proseguito. La Guardia di Finanza ha scoperto a Napoli una stamperia clandestina articolata in due laboratori: le banconote venivano prodotte vicino all’aeroporto di Capodichino e rifinite a Chiaia, sotto un poster de “La banda degli onesti”, il film in cui Totò e Peppino diventano falsari. Sequestrati oltre 12mila pezzi da 20 e 50 euro, per un valore nominale di circa 400mila euro, insieme a macchinari professionali e materiali per contraffare passaporti e carte d’identità. Arrestati tre uomini, tutti con precedenti specifici; secondo gli investigatori, la tecnica utilizzata sarebbe riconducibile al cosiddetto “Napoli Group”, noto per la qualità delle falsificazioni.
